Texans (No. 17; 0-4): Where did the Houston defense go? – Mike Florio Average Ranking: 24.67 (Last Week: 22.56) Yeah, ouch. The Texans started the season as one of the Super Bowl favorites in the AFC, and now they’ll be lucky to dig themselves out of the 20s by January. What are the chances that they even mount a comeback? Well, like SI’s Conor Orr stated, they’ll be getting quality players back from injury soon, and the 0-4 Tennessee Titans (the same team that kickstarted Houston’s comeback last year) are up next. By comparison, that 1992 0-4 Chargers team that made the playoffs was led by QB Stan Humphries, WR Anthony Miller, RBs Ronnie Harmon, Marion Butts, (current Chiefs offensive coordinator) Eric Bienemy on offense, and DE Leslie O’Neal and LB Junior Seau on…
author: fizzyjoe

title: Houston Texans Defense: Serious Problem?
summary: The Houston Texans entered the 2026 season with sky-high expectations after their dominant display the season prior. They are pretty much stacked at all three levels of the defense, but somehow, things have not looked the way they used to. Regression is always possible in the NFL, but the drop-off from one year to the […]
full_text: The Houston Texans entered the 2026 season with sky-high expectations after their dominant display the season prior. They are pretty much stacked at all three levels of the defense, but somehow, things have not looked the way they used to. Regression is always possible in the NFL, but the drop-off from one year to the next, especially without losing much talent, has been troublesome. If you look back at the start of last season, the Texans’ defense also started somewhat slow and did not immediately become the dominant unit we eventually saw. The offense could not get much of anything going, and the defense was doing everything it could to keep Houston in games. This year, it has been almost the complete opposite. Houston’s offense has looked far better when fully healthy. The Texans have put up 30 points per game when their best wide receiver, Nico Collins, has been on the field. He missed two games this season, and the offense struggled tremendously without him, but that is a story for a different day. The reality of the situation is that quarterback C.J. Stroud gave the Texans a late fourth-quarter lead in three of their first four games. In each of those situations, the defense had an opportunity to get a stop and close out the game, but they were unable to do so. That is a major reason why this team is sitting at 0-4. Defensively, the Texans have immense talent, and there is no questioning that. The issue is that it feels like the players are not always being put in the best situations to succeed, especially when it comes to the scheme in certain situations. This is a defense loaded with players who have already proven they can play at an elite level. When a unit this talented continues to struggle in crucial moments, eventually you have to look beyond the players themselves and figure out what needs to change. In order for Houston to have any chance of turning this season around, the defense simply has to be better. The good news is that there is plenty of reason to believe that will happen. There is far too much talent on this roster for this unit to continue playing at this level. Defensive end Will Anderson Jr. is already having a Defensive Player of the Year-caliber season and has been practically unstoppable through the first four games. He has established himself as the anchor of this defense and continues to make an impact on a weekly basis. The Texans now need the rest of the defense to follow his lead. Starting 0-4 is obviously far from ideal, and Houston has put itself in a difficult position moving forward. However, this does not feel like a team that is completely lost. They have been in position to win several of these games and have simply failed to finish them. They are close. Now, they have to prove that being close can eventually turn into winning football games.
author: Nickschwager

title: Value of Things: Life on the hot seat
summary: Last week I started the whole notion of the stages of suck and that continues unabated as the Texans drop to 0-4 for the first time in franchise history. Even the David Culley experience managed a victory in week one. Since this is unchartered waters it is impossible to see everyone in the key spots […]
full_text: Last week I started the whole notion of the stages of suck and that continues unabated as the Texans drop to 0-4 for the first time in franchise history. Even the David Culley experience managed a victory in week one. Since this is unchartered waters it is impossible to see everyone in the key spots making it out alive. So, the question is exactly how warm is everyone’s seat getting? Naturally, this is just one observer’s opinion. People are free to flood the comments with their own. However, let’s start on top. Nick Caserio These reports come out on Wednesday for a reason. Ultimately, we want to avoid making irrational decisions. Someone wise once said that perfect is the enemy of good. What they meant is that we can discard good way too easily in the search of perfect. The perfect general manager doesn’t exist. The hot name this week will be on the chopping block next month. Howie Roseman is a perfect example. One or two years ago he was the best general manager in sports. Now, Eagles fans are looking at him with side eye. On balance, Caserio has taken this organization from the land of Bill O’Brien hell into constant competitiveness the last three years. Even three of these four games where down to the final possession. Yes, there are cracks in the veneer. Everyone focuses on the offensive line for obvious reasons, but there are other free agency misses as well. There have been draft misses as well. I would challenge any detractor to look at the records for any of the other general managers and name me ten better ones. It would be a difficult task. However, the GM’s job is about much more than players. The coaching staff has his fingerprints all over it. In particular, the offensive coordinator and offensive line coach appear to be buddy hires. Interesting how those two units are coming under more scrutiny than any of the others. If we are looking at this from the Goldilocks zone of cold, warm, and hot then we would have to put Caserio in the warm category. I can’t see much of a case for firing him at this moment, but once this debacle is over he will be put on notice to get coaching hires and the offensive line right. Another year of this and he could be out. Seat: Warm DeMeco Ryans Like with Caserio one should consider whether you can do better. That is a very reasonable question. For some, simply having an offense first coach is always preferable and that is more than fair. However, it is fair to ask what Ryans has done to deserve the axe. It is only one man’s opinion, but I see him as 2010 Gary Kubiask. Kubiak was a gifted offensive mind and had one of the more prolific offenses in the NFL at the time. In fact, the Texans offense has never been better than it was in 2010. He just couldn’t figure out the defensive side of the ball. The McNairs stepped in and hired Wade Phillips and forced him on Kubiak. It might be that time for Ryans. 2010 was year four for Kubiak and 2026 is year four for Ryans. My personal view is that Caley was selected for him. He failed when he brought in his own guy. So, that means Hannah McNair needs to come to the rescue and hire someone for Caserio and Ryans. The decision needs to be taken out of their hands. No more buddy hires. The Colts game was rife with clock management issues, but those were cleaned up this week. He is growing as a football coach and he should be here for the long haul. Obviously consecutive losing seasons would change the calculus on that, but I see him on the Kubiak track. He will recover with a better offensive staff and hopefully Stroud will stay healthier than Matt Schaub. Seat: Cold Nick Caley The life of a teacher can be cruel. Teachers are usually put into three different buckets. There are those that are pros and we just leave them alone and let them do their thing. There are those that show promise, but have areas where they can definitely grow. We keep them around and offer them training and support until they figure out what they need to figure out. Then there are those that are lost causes. You bide your time and get rid of them when you can. I have been all three in my teaching career. The differences were based on the situation. I am built to do specific things well and when allowed to do those things I will be great. There are other things I don’t do well and situations where I will struggle. So, I get Nick Caley more than most people. Caley isn’t an idiot. He is just in a bad situation for him and his skill set. Sometimes it is a location thing. Sometimes it is a question of what is being asked. Sometimes it is a question of the tools that are given to him. Either way, we are beyond the stage of hoping and working towards growth. I have little doubt that Caley could potentially succeed in a different situation. He just isn’t the right guy for this job. Even in his good weeks there are too many instances where he is overmatched. The hook and lateral play in the fourth quarter was a moment of brilliance in a sea of mediocrity. There just aren’t enough of those moments to make up for the mediocrity. Looking back he probably should have been one and done, but they wanted to give him a chance to grow and I can’t fault them for that. It just didn’t work. Seat: Scalding Hot
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Their record is improving, but are the Colts?
summary: I don’t intend to mess with karma, as a win is a win and we will need 10 or more of them to make the playoffs. I recently reminded a coworker about tempting said karma. He had been to the casino and returned “even”, which upset him. He said that he had won the previous […]
full_text: I don’t intend to mess with karma, as a win is a win and we will need 10 or more of them to make the playoffs. I recently reminded a coworker about tempting said karma. He had been to the casino and returned “even”, which upset him. He said that he had won the previous three trips, so a “tie” was like a loss. I told him that he had a free evening of entertainment and that complaining about coming out even, would likely see his fortunes change. It did, as he lost the next three trips. I only tell that brief story because I am aware that complaining after a win, could be tempting fate. The biggest thing to remember is that we are only four weeks into the season, or just short of the quarter pole in this season’s race. Many say that the season doesn’t start until Thanksgiving weekend, so that is nearly two months away. You can’t win a division in the first four weeks, but you can lose it. The Colts have positioned themselves into the middle of the pack and have not played themselves out of the race. While I am against complaining about a win, I do think it is fair to look at strengths and weaknesses, evaluate the probability or possibility of seeing a decline, or anticipating improvement. In short, I think it is okay to point out shortcomings, even if you managed to get a win on the ledger. I am not exactly cracking the code, as many are seeing the same things that I am. Most team conversations revolve around the QB, so that is a logical place to start. Daniel Jones has flat out turned the ball over too often. From comments, I’d guess around 1/2 would put all blame on Jones and point to past turnover difficulties, while the other 1/2 would split blame between the offensive line and Steichen’s play calling. All can be legit. Jones history does show that he has fumbled 63 times in 86 starts. He fumbled last week without actually getting hit. Can a QB learn ball security on the fly? It is also hard not to notice that the OL is not holding up as well as it did last year. The truth is, the line has been under siege, since the Steelers made attacking the backfield work, last year. From that point, you have to determine whether Travis’ insertion into the lineup is more the cause, or is our HC/OC failing to put us in the best position to counter what has turned into Colts opponents game plan. Generally, if you can determine your weakness, you should be able to find a way to fix it, or at least reduce the negative affects. QB play is not the only place where improvements are needed. We have to find some quick strikes. Jones needs to air it out, or find a way to punish teams that bring so many to the line of scrimmage. I hate to think that we have to wait and count on a healthy Pierce return to accomplish this. Honestly, he may not be ready to do that until next year. Marvin, Reggie, and even T.Y. found a way to get behind the defense, and with the way teams are coming after us, there has to be a way for someone on the roster to do this. Both offensive deficiencies seem like something Shane is going to have to address. My dead horse is going to have to take another beating, because I believe that staying under center more often and incorporating some no-huddle series, would help offensive efficiency all around. When JT and DJ are both in the backfield, they are easier targets. Having the entire play clock to diagnose what the D wants to do and keeping them in their base personnel would both be benefits of the no-huddle. How can the defense get better? We have shown some improvement, although against a bad offensive line and a 3rd string QB, but we have tackled better and need to continue to do so. Our LBs could get better with sheer reps. Davis-Gaither has 28 starts over his 7 year career. Carlies has 10 in just over 2 years and Ajiake, Boettcher, and Allen have never started. We need the game to slow down for all of them and play the best two, no matter their draft status or contract. With Keys’ injury, we may see the same thing by allowing inexperienced Edges to hone their craft on the fly. I actually thought I saw glimpses of better penetration in the first two games of the season, than I did in our wins. I may be way off base and I know that we all see plays differently, but I do not think the DL is allowed to “win however you can win”. Lane integrity seems more important than blowing up a play or at least the timing of the play. Maybe we could just find a way to get the same kind of effort that we get from Buck. More Adebawore? Going into the season, it was thought by many, myself included, that the secondary would be the strength of the team. The unit is not performing to that level. I think it is a group effort, as only Ward and Bynum have escaped looking bad at times. We do have to remember that 3/5ths are playing their first full season with the team and the other 2/5ths are just in their second year as Colts. The secondary is like the O-line in that they operate as a unit and there are still some lapses in assignments. In short, they are getting to know each other on the fly. There will be no new toy brought in to save a position group. If you are hoping for a Booger McFarland such upgrade, I think you are believing that Ballard may have that option. I not only think that he needs to win the division or a playoff game to keep his job, I think he has to do it with the group he has on the roster. (I don’t think that I can put Carl Lawson in that new toy category). As an optimist, I know that younger players can get better. Some also respond to higher pressure situations. The Colts need for both to happen. Shane and Lou do not seem to be implementing new tricks, so there needs to be physical or mental improvement from some players. The Colts can have 11 full contact practices, during the first 11 weeks of the season, so it is hard to imagine a player showing well enough in those limited opportunities, to “take” a job from someone. It feels like once the season starts, only an injury can see you lose your job, so we may not see the personnel changes that some are suggesting. There does seem to be a little more fire on D and I attribute that to Buck’s inspired play recently. Maybe Q could work a little of the same magic on the offense? As far as the Steeler game goes, I’ll take a win in the ugliest of fashions, as long as it does not include see any of our guys go down. As a 2.5 point underdog on the road, we may actually be seen as the better team, but not enough to compensate for having to play in a historically difficult environment. I think we can win this with a cleaner game from the offense. Moving the ball is not easy for the Steelers, so don’t give them short fields. Has the two game winning streak changed how see the Colts’ chances moving forward?

Wednesday’s practice report for #INDvsPIT pic.twitter.com/eKhvetDPhZ — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 7, 2026 Center Tanor Bortolini (ankle) missed practice today. Bortolini was seen at practice wearing a walking boot/ankle brace. Bortolini looks like he is set to miss time maybe even beyond this week. Linebacker Jaylon Carlies (ribs) missed practice today. Fellow linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither knee) also missed practice today. The Colts two starting linebackers both missing practice doesn’t bode well for a defense that has just started to turn a corner. However, if they do both miss Sundays game it could mean rookie linebackers Bryce Boettcher and CJ Allen get more snaps. Defensive end Arden Key (hamstring) missed practice today. Colts Head Coach Shane Steichen told the media earlier in the week the team expects Key to miss some time with the injury. The team announced today they had signed defensive end Carl Lawson to the practice squad to join the defensive end rotation. Wide receiver Ashton Dulin (hamstring) missed practice today. Dulin looks like he may be missing a third game with the injury. Wide receiver Keenan Allen (rest/groin) and running back Jonathan Taylor (rest) were both killed at practice today due to veteran rest days. It will be interesting to see how Allen managed with tomorrow’s practice as he missed Sundays game due to the groin injury. Tight end Will Mallory (thumb) was a full participant at practice today. The Colts announced they have opened the 21 day practice window for Mallory to return from injured reserve. title: Alec Pierce’s prolonged absence is killing the Colts
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are facing a bit of a crisis at the wide receiver position. Michael Pittman Jr. was traded this offseason. He didn’t seem to have his best stuff anymore, but that one still hurt. Alec Pierce was tabbed to be the next man to take over the reins as the number one receiver. […]
full_text: London, United Kingdom - October 4: Daniel Jones of Indianapolis Colts in action during the Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders match between Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 4, 2026 in London, United Kingdom. (Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images) | DeFodi Images via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are facing a bit of a crisis at the wide receiver position. Michael Pittman Jr. was traded this offseason. He didn’t seem to have his best stuff anymore, but that one still hurt. Alec Pierce was tabbed to be the next man to take over the reins as the number one receiver. Since cashing his check, we have hardly seen him on the field. The Colts are feeling the effects. Statistically, Daniel Jones had his worst quarter and a half against the Commanders. There was pressure, but his attempts were the shortest in the league at 3.8 per play. Going 19/34 for only 143 yards and multiple turnovers proves Jones is struggling. Josh Downs is the twitchy man the Colts need underneath, but no one can take the top off the defense. Laquon Treadwell has been the Colts’ best downfield threat. No offense to Treadwell, but he isn’t going to cut it. Pierce was the deep threat. Last year, he added more routes and became more of a well-rounded receiver. That made his deep threat even more lethal. Jones averaged over 8 yards per attempt last year with Pierce in the fold. Not only would Pierce provide an option for a deep shot, he also opened the rest of the field by taking defenders with him away from the line of scrimmage. His presence on the outside changes everything. Another heel injury is crippling the Colts. Alec Pierce may or may not be a true number one, but his importance to the Colts is real. Occupying a corner and safety deep while providing an option to pick up huge yards in a hurry is something the Colts can’t replicate without him. He was supposed to be the guy. Missing time this year doesn’t mean he can’t be going forward, but being without him means the offense, Daniel Jones very much included, is going to feel the effects.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Colts sign veteran pass rusher Carl Lawson to practice squad
summary: The Colts added some veteran help to their defensive front Wednesday, signing defensive end Carl Lawson to the practice squad. Indianapolis also released tight end Kenny Fletcher Jr. from the practice squad to make room for Lawson, who had previously worked out for the Colts on Sept. 23. The timing is pretty easy to understand. […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - DECEMBER 22: Carl Lawson #55 of the Dallas Cowboys looks on from the field after an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium on December 22, 2024 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts added some veteran help to their defensive front Wednesday, signing defensive end Carl Lawson to the practice squad. Indianapolis also released tight end Kenny Fletcher Jr. from the practice squad to make room for Lawson, who had previously worked out for the Colts on Sept. 23. The timing is pretty easy to understand. Arden Key is expected to miss time with an injury, while Micheal Clemons is already on injured reserve, leaving the Colts thinner than they would like at defensive end. Lawson gives them an experienced option who already has familiarity with defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo’s system. Lawson played under Anarumo in Cincinnati during the 2019 and 2020 seasons, and 2020 was arguably the best year of his career. He recorded 64 pressures that season and continued to establish himself as a disruptive rotational pass rusher. That familiarity should help if Indianapolis eventually needs to elevate him to the active roster. The 31-year-old has played eight NFL seasons with the Bengals, Jets, Cowboys and Ravens, appearing in 90 games with 34 starts. Over that span, he has recorded 32 sacks, 122 quarterback hits, 32 tackles for loss and four forced fumbles. His role has decreased in recent years, though, and he played just 26 defensive snaps for Baltimore last season. This should not be viewed as some major solution to the Colts’ pass-rush problems. Lawson is being added to the practice squad in October for a reason, and expecting him to suddenly become the player he was several years ago would be unrealistic. Still, the move makes sense considering the state of the defensive line. Indianapolis enters its Week 5 matchup against Pittsburgh ranked 31st in total defense, allowing 423.8 yards per game. The Colts have struggled to consistently affect opposing quarterbacks, and injuries have now taken away two veterans from an edge group that was already short on proven difference-makers. Lawson at least gives Anarumo another player he knows and trusts, along with someone who has shown in the past that he can create pressure when used in the right role. If Key remains out for multiple games, it would not be surprising to see Lawson elevated and given rotational snaps sooner rather than later. For now, he gives the Colts some needed insurance at a position that has quickly become even thinner.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Where’s CJ Allen?
summary: The Colts used their first pick of the 2026 NFL Draft on CJ Allen because they believed he could play early. Chris Ballard called him an athletic, fast MIKE and said Allen would be a “green-dot guy for us from the get-go.” Indianapolis liked him enough at No. 53 overall that Ballard considered trading down […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20: Indianapolis Colts linebacker CJ Allen (53) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Colts used their first pick of the 2026 NFL Draft on CJ Allen because they believed he could play early. Chris Ballard called him an athletic, fast MIKE and said Allen would be a “green-dot guy for us from the get-go.” Indianapolis liked him enough at No. 53 overall that Ballard considered trading down again and decided against it because the Colts did not want to risk losing him. Four games into his NFL career, Allen has played 11 defensive snaps. He played zero against Washington. That needs an explanation. Akeem Davis-Gaither played 62 of the Colts’ 64 defensive snaps Sunday. Jaylon Carlies played 30, Bryce Boettcher played 18 and Austin Ajiake played 17. Allen, the first player Indianapolis drafted five months ago, never got on the field defensively. So, where is CJ Allen? The Colts have boxed him into one position Lou Anarumo was asked about Allen’s lack of playing time Monday, and his answer gave us a pretty clear idea of how the Colts currently view their linebacker room. “Two totally different positions… Austin went out there in a pass situation, we were anticipating a certain thing and he plays DIME and CJ plays backer. Akeem is playing well and we were playing well. CJ is getting better each week in practice and he will get his opportunities in practice. Play count was low at one point so no need to rest Akeem, but not down on CJ. Not down on CJ, he’s working his tail off and he’ll have his opportunities.” Technically, that explanation makes sense. Davis-Gaither is playing MIKE and wearing the green dot. Carlies, Boettcher and Ajiake are being used in different roles, primarily at WILL or in sub-packages. Allen is currently being treated as the direct backup to Davis-Gaither, so Ajiake getting 17 snaps does not necessarily mean the coaching staff thinks Ajiake is a better linebacker than Allen. The problem is the Colts created that problem themselves. If Allen is only going to play MIKE, and Davis-Gaither is going to play 62 of 64 snaps whenever he is healthy, then when exactly is Allen supposed to play? You have essentially taken your top draft pick and placed him behind one of the few defenders on the roster who almost never leaves the field. That makes no sense to me. Davis-Gaither has played better over the last couple of games, and because he has the green dot, he naturally needs to be on the field more than most linebackers. Fine, but he also was not particularly good during the first couple weeks of the season, and nothing he has done should make the Colts terrified of taking him off the field for a handful of snaps. Allen does not need to replace him, but he needs to play. Allen is not a raw developmental linebacker Allen’s background makes the situation even harder to understand. He started at Georgia as a freshman and eventually became a First-Team All-American. He played three seasons in Kirby Smart’s defense and was the green-dot linebacker for a program that has produced Roquan Smith, Quay Walker, Nakobe Dean and a ridiculous number of NFL defenders. Colts linebackers coach James Bettcher specifically praised Allen’s communication and football intelligence before the season, noting that he was constantly making coverage checks and adjusting the front at Georgia. This is not a converted safety trying to learn linebacker and this is not a small-school prospect who spent Saturdays playing against guys who are now selling insurance. Allen played linebacker in one of the best and most complicated defenses in college football. Indianapolis drafted him in the second round in large part because the team believed his intelligence would allow him to transition quickly. Now we are being told he essentially has to wait behind Davis-Gaither because he is a MIKE. Allen did miss roughly a month of training camp, and that deserves to be mentioned. Missing that much time as a rookie absolutely hurts development, especially in a new defense. I would understand if he were behind where the Colts originally expected him to be, but we are also four regular-season games into the season now, not two days removed from his return. At some point, practice has to turn into playing. There is a difference between sitting and developing I am probably more sympathetic than most people when teams choose not to immediately throw young players onto the field. I argued for patience with Anthony Richardson when almost everyone wanted him starting immediately. Quarterback is difficult, and putting a young player on the field before he understands what he is seeing can do more harm than good. There are plenty of positions where sitting, watching and learning can be extremely beneficial. Linebacker is also much easier to rotate than quarterback. Nobody is asking the Colts to bench Davis-Gaither and give Allen 64 snaps next week. Get him eight. Then 12. Then 15. Give him a series at MIKE. Put him at WILL in another package. Let him cover. Let him play downhill against the run. Find out what translates and what does not. There is a huge difference between protecting a young player and burying him and right now, Allen is being buried. Boettcher has already played 79 defensive snaps this season. Allen has played 11. There is no reasonable argument that the talent difference between those two players should result in that kind of gap. And if Davis-Gaither is apparently playing too well to come off the field, then stop treating Allen as a MIKE-only linebacker. Why can’t he play WILL? This is the part of Anarumo’s explanation that bothers me the most. Why are the Colts rotating three different players through the WILL spot while keeping Allen glued to the bench as Davis-Gaither’s backup? Carlies is the obvious player whose snaps should be available. He played 42 defensive snaps against Baltimore earlier this season and did not record a single statistic. Not one!! His interception against Washington was a nice play, but one interception does not erase years of very little production. If the choice is between continuing to give Carlies 25-30 snaps a game or using some of those snaps to develop the player you just selected 53rd overall, I know which direction I am going. Allen has enough athleticism to run and cover. His college tape showed a player comfortable operating in space as well as inside the box. Nothing about his profile suggested a linebacker who could only stand in the middle of the defense and call plays. If Anarumo wants Davis-Gaither at MIKE because of the green dot, then work Allen in elsewhere. That is coaching! The answer cannot simply be, “They play different positions,” as if those positions were assigned at birth. Other rookie linebackers are already producing The rest of the 2026 linebacker class also makes Allen’s usage look strange. Jacob Rodriguez, who went 43rd overall to Miami, was one of my favourite prospects in the entire draft. Through three games he already had 28 tackles and an interception and had taken over defensive communication duties for the Dolphins. He is now the betting favourite for Defensive Rookie of the Year at +300. Anthony Hill Jr. went seven picks after Allen at No. 60 overall. He immediately won a starting job with Tennessee, recorded 34 tackles in his first three games and was named NFL Defensive Rookie of the Month for September. Sonny Styles was obviously drafted much earlier at No. 7 overall, so the expectations are different, but he has already become an important part of Washington’s defense. He has started all four games, played more than 200 snaps, intercepted a pass, forced a fumble and earned NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors. Every prospect develops differently, so this is not…

title: Jaguars Reacts Survey: Is it time to trade WR Brian Thomas Jr.?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country. Through the first four weeks of his third NFL season, Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. has played 47.3% of offensive snaps. That figure was […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 27: Brian Thomas Jr. #7 of the Jacksonville Jaguars warms up prior to a game against the New England Patriots at EverBank Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country. Through the first four weeks of his third NFL season, Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. has played 47.3% of offensive snaps. That figure was at 80% during his rookie season and 78% last year. According to PFF, Thomas only has 1 deep target (20+ air yards) this season. He had 30 deep targets as a rookie and 23 last year. When he is targeted, he’s not producing as well. Thomas’ yards per target has dropped from 9.6 to 7.8 to 7.0 this season. With Thomas, the Jaguars have a young player trending downward in snap share and target efficiency. And they don’t even deploy him on the stuff he’s best at (deep targets). Wouldn’t it make sense to trade him to a team that would actually use him as a full-time wideout? The shine of Thomas’ first-round pedigree and first-year success will only last so long. The fact that he still has multiple cheap seasons on his rookie contract is as much a reason for another club to acquire him as it is for the Jaguars to keep him. And several playoff contenders already need receiver depth (Rams, Chiefs, Patriots, 49ers). In a way, the Jaguars would be selling low on Thomas Jr., but his trade value might evaporate entirely if they continue to hold. They could recoup a Day 2 draft pick and give more opportunities to players drafted by the current regime, like Josh Cameron and CJ Williams, without really missing a beat. I feel kind of slimy for posing this question. Of course, I hope Thomas has a great career, preferably in Jacksonville. And if you watched the team’s latest production of Sounds of the Game , you’d know that Jacksonville’s players and coaches still believe in BT. #Jaguars HC Liam Coen said he showed this block by Brian Thomas Jr. to the team today along with another key block on third and short. A good performance yesterday by BTJ after only playing 23 snaps vs. New England. https://t.co/TiGFmy5nPU — Juston W. Lewis (@JustonLewis_) October 5, 2026 The stats from the top of this article are pretty telling, though. Thomas is not being fully maximized in Jacksonville. At this point, if another team thinks they could get the best version of him, I don’t see why a change of scenery wouldn’t be a win-win for both sides. What do you think? title: Numbers Never Lie: Can the Chiefs’ defense be the best in the AFC?
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs have a week off during the fifth slate of games on the NFL’s regular-season calendar. After four games, the team leads the AFC standings with a 96% chance of making the playoffs, according to ESPN’s up-to-date NFL playoff picture. It’s time to start comparing the team to the rest of the […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs have a week off during the fifth slate of games on the NFL’s regular-season calendar. After four games, the team leads the AFC standings with a 96% chance of making the playoffs, according to ESPN’s up-to-date NFL playoff picture . It’s time to start comparing the team to the rest of the AFC playoff field, all the opponents it could potentially face on the way to a potential return to the Super Bowl. It’s hard not to feel confident putting the Chiefs’ offense up against any opponent it faces, given how running back Kenneth Walker has helped quarterback Patrick Mahomes regain his form. But how good is the defense? The Chiefs arguably have the best defense in the AFC through 4 weeks. Conference ranks: Points/Game: 2nd Yards/Play: 2nd Pass Yds/Att: 1st Rush Yds/Att: 3rd Red Zone conversion rate: 3rd JAX rivals them in most of these stats, but rank 15th in yards allowed/play in the AFC — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) October 6, 2026 Looking at the team’s season-long statistics, the unit stands out as one of the best in its conference in many major categories. Points per game allowed Jacksonville Jaguars (13.3) Chiefs (19.3) New England Patriots (19.3) Yards per play allowed New York Jets (5) Chiefs (5) Baltimore Ravens (5.1) Passing yards per attempt allowed Chiefs (6.2) Jets (6.5) Patriots (6.5) Rushing yards per attempt allowed Jaguars (3.3) Houston Texans (3.4) Miami Dolphins (3.6) Chiefs (3.6) Red zone conversion rate allowed Jaguars (29%) Cincinnati Bengals (31%) Chiefs (44%) However, the Chiefs rank eighth among the 16 AFC teams in third-down conversion rate allowed (37%) and have the lowest sack rate in the conference (2.6%). It’s worth considering the team’s opponents include some of the league’s lowest-ranked offenses so far in the Dolphins and Denver Broncos . Kansas City has found a strength in being a bend-but-don’t-break defense under coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. With the offense clicking on all cylinders, all anybody can ask from Spags’ unit is to allow under 20 points per game. That’s all he cares about, too. However, as the season wears on and the stakes rise, the defense needs to get off the field more on third down and find a way to finish pressures. The Chiefs have the seventh-best pressure rate in the conference (24%) and are just behind the Jaguars; however, Jacksonville has six more sacks in the stat line. Here are some defensive stats through week 4, starting with each team's missed tackle rate 🧵 pic.twitter.com/vBsCSKShj2 — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) October 6, 2026 Another encouraging statistic for the Chiefs’ defense is its missed tackle rate, the lowest in the NFL, according to Sumer Sports . There is reason to believe the tackling will only get better as the season goes on, so already being one of the league’s most reliable in that area says a lot about the effort and intensity of the young, new-faced defense. The bottom line The Chiefs’ defense has never needed to be one of the league’s best in order for the team to succeed. When the offense is finding the rhythm it has in 2026, the defense simply needs to be good enough in any one matchup, making situational plays on late downs and in the red zone. When you consider the Chiefs’ potential path through the AFC playoffs, which of the conference’s defenses would you take over Kansas City’s to make enough plays in win-or-go-home fashion? Jacksonville has flashed in that respect, but Spags and his coaching staff make a huge difference. The Chiefs haven’t been perfect on defense, especially on pass-rush downs, but there’s reason to believe this unit can be good enough to win the crucial games in December and January.

title: Are the Chiefs’ offseason bets on offense paying off 4 games in?
summary: The offseason gave the Kansas City Chiefs fans plenty of reasons to ask what came next. Familiar faces departed, established defensive starters found new homes, and the Chiefs placed significant responsibility on players who had yet to take an NFL snap. Four games later, the Chiefs enter their bye week at 4-0. That makes the […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) The offseason gave the Kansas City Chiefs fans plenty of reasons to ask what came next. Familiar faces departed, established defensive starters found new homes, and the Chiefs placed significant responsibility on players who had yet to take an NFL snap. Four games later, the Chiefs enter their bye week at 4-0. That makes the changes easier to embrace, but an undefeated record does not automatically give every offseason decision an “A.” The better question is whether Kansas City improved the roles it needed to improve through outside additions and the development of players already on the roster — and whether the early production supports the risks Brett Veach took. We’ll start with the offensive changes: Running back: Kenneth Walker has changed the conversation Moving forward without Isiah Pacheco and Kareem Hunt meant turning the page on two familiar pieces of the offense. Both had helped Kansas City win games, but signing Kenneth Walker III raised the expectations for what the running game could provide. So far, he has exceeded them. Walker has rushed for 537 yards on 87 carries, averaging 6.2 yards per attempt. Add his 84 receiving yards and two touchdown catches to his four rushing touchdowns, and he has produced 621 yards from scrimmage and six total touchdowns through four games. His impact has been consistent enough to matter beyond one highlight. Walker topped 100 rushing yards against the Denver Broncos , the Indianapolis Colts and the Las Vegas Raiders . In Las Vegas, his 177 rushing yards and two touchdowns helped Kansas City win a game in which its passing offense was far from its best. That is the value of this addition. The Chiefs have another player who can carry the offense when Mahomes needs help. Walker’s explosiveness also gives opponents a reason to respect the handoff, creating opportunities for the under-center and play-action concepts Kansas City can build around him. The remaining question is how the Chiefs manage his workload over a full season. As an early evaluation of the decision itself, however, this is the easiest grade on the board. Early grade: A+ Offensive tackle: A quiet signing became a major investment in protection Walker has been the most obvious offensive upgrade, but rookie Kahlil Benson belongs among the offseason’s most consequential additions. Kansas City signed Benson as an undrafted free agent. With Josh Simmons sidelined by a back injury, the rookie has started all four games at left tackle, taking responsibility for protecting Patrick Mahomes’ blind side much earlier than the Chiefs expected. That is a significant return from a signing that required no draft pick. An injury at left tackle can force an offense to devote extra resources to protection and limit its options. Benson has given Kansas City a player it can turn to at one of the game’s most demanding positions while Simmons recovers. His September performance earned NFL Offensive Rookie of the Month honors . That recognition strengthens the case for treating his acquisition as a major part of the offseason evaluation. As our own Caleb James detailed in his four-game Benson breakdown , he assigned the rookie a 77% overall grade, with 74% in true pass protection and run blocking and 85% in assisted pass protection. James credited Benson’s power in the running game while identifying speed rushes and inconsistent hand placement as areas to improve. His evaluation shows both Benson’s contribution and how Kansas City’s scheme has helped him succeed. There will still be growing pains, and four starts do not answer every question about his pass protection. But when we ask whether the Chiefs found meaningful help for Mahomes, Benson deserves a prominent place in the answer. Early grade: B The small-scale changes Kansas City also moved forward without receivers Marquise Brown and JuJu Smith-Schuster, changed its offensive-line personnel and acquired Justin Fields from the Jets for a 2027 sixth-round pick. Some of those decisions need more time before they can be graded usefully. A backup quarterback acquisition, for instance, is difficult to evaluate through an undefeated start led by Mahomes. Receiver depth is a more immediate question. Against Las Vegas, Jalen Royals played 38 offensive snaps without recording a reception, while rookie Cyrus Allen played five. Injuries to Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton have made the players behind the starters more consequential moving forward. That doesn’t mean retaining Brown or Smith-Schuster would have been the right answer. It does mean the Chiefs’ confidence in their younger depth will face a more demanding test after the bye. Early grade: Incomplete Let us know how you feel these changes grade out so far! We’ll look at the defensive decisions later this week!

title: Chiefs Rookie Report: Grading Kahlil Benson through four games
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs head into their bye week with a perfect 4-0 record. A tight win in Las Vegas on Sunday helped the Chiefs remain unbeaten and put them at the top of the AFC and the AFC West. Many players have stood out this season, but rookie offensive lineman Kahlil Benson has played […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs head into their bye week with a perfect 4-0 record. A tight win in Las Vegas on Sunday helped the Chiefs remain unbeaten and put them at the top of the AFC and the AFC West. Many players have stood out this season, but rookie offensive lineman Kahlil Benson has played one of the most important roles on the team. A training camp standout, Benson seemed poised to compete for the starting right tackle job, but with returning starter Josh Simmons out, Benson started every game at left tackle to begin the 2026 season. In a move not often seen, the Chiefs brain trust has felt confident enough to line up Benson as Patrick Mahomes’ blind-side protector after Mahomes came off a serious knee injury. So far this season, the Chiefs have one of the NFL’s most potent offenses, and while the team has helped Benson, he’s reciprocated and put together solid tape. Grad ing Benson For game grades, I broke them into three categories to create an overall grade. My criteria were run blocking, true pass protection, and assisted pass protection. Run blocking is as black and white as it can be, but to keep his pass-blocking grade from getting oversaturated, I included true pass protection, which is traditional drop-back passes or plays where Benson is in a classic pass-blocking set. Assisted is where I included plays like RPO’s, screens, play-action looks, and other plays that can give offensive linemen easy plays to win. The Chiefs have used plenty of these, but the true pass-blocking grade tells us whether Benson has what it takes to keep playing the position in the NFL. Through four weeks—against formidable pass rushers—Benson has graded a 74% for true pass protection , with an assisted pass protection grade of 85%. His run game has been good as well, with a 74% grade as a run blocker . Overall, this puts his season grade at a 77% The team has definitely played to his strengths as a player with quicker passing patterns and an uptick in running the football, but Benson has delivered for what he has been asked to do this season. Pass protection Benson has been solid in pass protection so far this season and has yet to allow a sack. This has been largely because the Chiefs have emphasized getting the ball out of Mahomes’ hands more quickly. In 2023, Mahomes averaged 2.5 seconds of pocket time per throw, the seventh-longest in the NFL. Three seasons later, Mahomes is at 2.2 seconds of pocket time and below the league average. It has taken the Chiefs some time to get here, but the emphasis on a quick passing game has helped players like Benson, who rely on physicality. Benson wants to win snaps quickly; this is where he can put his power on full display. In his first game, he faced one of the NFL’s best edge rushers, Nik Bonitto. Bonitto relies on speed and bend and looks to rush wide. Benson is patient out of his stance, and quarterback Patrick Mahomes is only taking a three-step drop, so Benson knows he can run Bonitto wide if needed. As the two meet, Benson fires a big shot and blasts Bonitto upfield, finishing him to the ground. The clean pocket allows Mahomes ample time to run and pick up yards with his legs. Benson can have issues with quickness at times, but when he gets his hands on a defender, he ends snaps quickly with powerful grip strength and a strong base. A few snaps a game, Benson shows his pass-protection deficiencies. Knowing he has issues with the speed of the game—many undrafted rookies do—the Chiefs have been careful to give him help when needed, but one inconsistent area is his striking and hand placement. Solid out of his stance, Benson goes wide with his hands and gives up his chest to the edge rusher. He can’t recover and ends up on the ground as Mahomes is hit. Benson’s pass blocking is still a work in progress, but with the new-look Chiefs offense, his strengths are maximized, and much of this starts with the run game. Run blocking Running back Kenneth Walker has run wild this season, and Benson has been instrumental in this with his blocking. Benson’s strength and power translate well to the new run game, and so far he has delivered. While his technique still needs refining, he plays with a nasty streak and can move a man off a spot, opening lanes for his running back. His background as a guard during his underclassman years in college helps him create leverage from his stance and drives his feet through contact. Sealing the backside of the zone has become extremely important with Walker running the ball, given his vision and cutting ability. Backs with patience require offensive lines that give tremendous effort, play in and play out. The bottom line The Chiefs have tried to play young tackles with varying degrees of success, but this has culminated in finding a solid player in Benson. Perfect? No, but far from bad. Benson has benefited from a Chiefs team that is running the ball at the same rate they once did with greats like Priest Holmes and Jamaal Charles, and is helping Kenneth Walker to what could be a remarkable season. Benson might not be the left tackle of the future, but he has a bright future with the team, at either guard or tackle. Brute strength, physicality, and maximum effort can mask weaknesses, and Benson grades highly in all three.
author: Caleb James

title: Chiefs Mailbag: How could the Chiefs address wide receiver?
summary: Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs! The Chiefs will enjoy some early time off with a Week 5 bye after going to 4-0 with a 30-27 defeat of the Las Vegas Raiders. Let’s see what […]
full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs ! The Chiefs will enjoy some early time off with a Week 5 bye after going to 4-0 with a 30-27 defeat of the Las Vegas Raiders . Let’s see what questions (about wide receivers and other topics) are on our readers’ minds. Andyreidsmustache_ asks: Rashee Rice has a hamstring injury, and Tyquan Thornton is out for, at minimum, a significant portion of the year if not the entirety of it. Who are some possibilities at WR available, and more importantly, who would we realistically be able to get from a salary cap and scheme fit? The big unknown right now is Rice’s status. There does not seem to be significant concern that his hamstring injury is a long-term problem. By some accounts, Rice could even suit up in Week 6 against the Los Angeles Chargers . A heavily rumored wideout addition will be covered in the next question, but the initial focus should be on Rice given how much of the offense runs through him. If his hamstring is unlikely to stretch into a month-long absence, the Chiefs would do well to get a serious look at Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen. Neither looked great in brief moments against the Raiders, but the sample is too small to draw real conclusions. With Rice headed for free agency after the season, Kansas City should want to know more about how the pair perform. A couple of interesting low-cost options are Cedric Tillman — currently on the New Orleans Saints’ practice squad — and current Cleveland Browns afterthought Jerry Jeudy. Both played for Chiefs wide receivers coach Chad O’Shea in Cleveland. Tillman could be signed outright to a minimum salary. Jeudy would come with a very affordable salary in a trade, and the Browns likely would prefer to cut ties with Jeudy sooner rather than later. If Rice is available, however, it’s hard to see a path to either having a major role. Arizona Cardinals wideout Marvin Harrison Jr. has not lived up to his lofty draft status and seems a good bet to be traded soon. Harrison would come with an affordable 2027 salary. However, the Cardinals will likely drive a hard bargain to recoup the value spent to draft Harrison in 2024. He also has some of the limitations that sometimes leave Chiefs fans frustrated with Rice. Thornton himself seemed an irredeemable bust after washing out with the New England Patriots . I would be interested in seeking Kansas City look at a similarly profiled player in former third-round selection Jalin Hyatt, currently on the New York Giants ’ practice squad. At any rate, I expect preseason favorite Andrew Armstrong to get called up to help at wide receiver in at least one of the Chiefs’ upcoming games. Kansas City bringing back a player like Justin Watson or Mecole Hardman to the practice squad would also hardly be surprising. JoBackson asks: Where will KC find the money to pay Cheetah? At this point, it would be an upset if former Chiefs wideout Tyreek Hill — apparently in the final stages of recovering from a gruesome knee injury — does not return to Kansas City. I fully expect that to happen within the next few weeks. Hill forced a trade out of Kansas City to receive a monstrous $120 million extension from the Miami Dolphins in 2022. I don’t think anyone expects him to command even average wide receiver money on an in-season contract after multiple surgeries. In four games last season, Hill caught only 21 passes for 265 yards and a single touchdown. Whatever contract he signs will likely be built around a guaranteed minimum base salary (prorated for the weeks he signs for) plus incentives. Given his low stats from a year ago, it would be really easy to build easily attainable incentives that would be categorized as Not Likely to be Earned for cap purposes. My biggest question about Hill’s signing is whether he will be willing to accept a practice squad contract initially to acclimate his body to football activities while waiting to make his actual debut. KCMagic asks: Is it time to bring back running back Kareem Hunt and see if he has anything left in the tank. Bye week is perfect time. It’s now a trend (3 straight games) where the Chiefs have failed to run for 1-2 yards on third and fourth downs. I think the Chiefs need to try to find new things to do with the current room. Yes, it has been frustrating to see the Chiefs stopped short multiple times, and Hunt was automatic last year. But it is also hard to fit another running back on the team, from the standpoint of both the 53-man roster and the 48 players who dress for game day. It is really hard to have a player designated for one job who rarely will call for more than four or five snaps per game. It is even harder when that hypothetical player would offer no value on special teams. Third-string running back Brashard Smith hasn’t moved the needle much on either offense or special teams. However, with Thornton out and Hill probably a month away from contributing if he returns, Smith is the only real option on the Chiefs’ roster to add speed on offense. Papajazz asks: Did the Raiders show some of the better teams how to beat us? The blueprint to beat the Chiefs has long been to get pressure with four defensive linemen and stack coverage on the back end. Kenneth Walker has largely made that plan obsolete. The Raiders exploited some things in the Chiefs’ defense that were concerns entering the game. I do think some of the issues we are seeing will improve as the unit gets more experience playing together. How much it improves will likely determine Kansas City’s ultimate 2026 ceiling. I hope the Chiefs have learned the dangers of beating themselves, especially on defense (and frustratingly on special teams). The defense missed chances to get off the field on third down before two Raiders field goals, although one likely still would have resulted in a successful try. Both drives were kept alive by penalties on cornerback Nohl Williams. Another Las Vegas field goal came after only a 19-yard drive that started inside Kansas City territory because of a long kickoff return. At least six points for the Raiders probably come off the board without self-inflicted Chiefs blunders. GoChiefs70 asks: This is a question pertaining to the questionable call in last night‘s game at the end where it looked like the ball hit the ground on that very last Raider drive. They rushed up and spiked it, so I guess it could not be reviewed at that point. If Andy Reid had thrown a red flag before the ball was spiked, would it have been eligible to review? Shockingly, the NFL finds new ways for officiating controversy to arise each and every week. The Chiefs were trapped by the NFL’s own rules, as coaches can’t challenge in the last two minutes of a half. Even though the most severe of ophthalmology patients could see that Raiders wideout Tre Tucker did not actually catch the ball, Kirk Cousins spiking the ball counted as a play, and the window to review the pass to Tucker expired. Obviously, the league avoided an embarrassing scenario since Kansas City won. If the league had gone ahead and contradicted its own rules by reviewing the play after the first-down spike, we would never have heard the end of how they bailed out the Chiefs. The best solution would be to make a rule that spiking the ball doesn’t count for replay rules and to give the league until an actual play is run to initiate a review. Given how rare this situation seems, I doubt fixing it will be a high offseason priority. If Reid or any coach faces such a scenario going forward, they should throw the red flag at the nearest official and get onto the field even though they aren’t allowed to. Give the league extra time to start the review process, and if the coach is ultimately fined, that is just part of the job. Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! We will…

Tyreek Hill’s estranged wife details abuse allegations in Day 1 of civil trial | The Athletic During direct examination, Vaccaro Hill described an incident in July 2024 after she and Hill visited ESPN headquarters in Bristol, Conn. She said Hill became upset when Vaccaro Hill declined to get professional hair and makeup done for potential interviews there. Vaccaro Hill said later, at the hotel, Hill remained upset when he tried to punch her stomach. She said she put her hands on her stomach to block the strike, which made contact with her hands. She said Hill told her then that he didn’t want the baby. Vaccaro Hill described the day as “probably the worst of all these abuse times.” She also alleged Hill pulled her hair and ripped it out that same day. Because of a shoulder injury he suffered during OTAs, Delane had an up-and-down training camp. But he began his NFL career with a bang, recording an interception against the Denver Broncos on the third play of his career. The problem was that he aggravated the shoulder in the process. Three Things Andy Reid and the Chiefs Need to Correct Going Into the Bye | Sports Illustrated Rushing the Passer Despite having the immobile Kirk Cousins wrapped up multiple times this past weekend, the pass rush still failed to capitalize on its opportunities. George Karlaftis was the star of the show as he finished with 11 quarterback pressures, tied for the most in a game all year, yet even his fourth-quarter sack was wiped away by a penalty. Simply put, KC needs more from pass rushers like Chris Jones, Felix Anudike-Uzomah, and rookie R Mason Thomas. Finishing with a goose egg in the sack column every week isn’t a sustainable formula for success. Around the NFL Eagles All-Pro Lane Johnson retires, ending 14-season NFL career | ESPN “I deeply wanted to gut it out for one more year; to take the field with my brothers for one last season. But after a lot of reflection, I’ve realized that my personal and family priorities have changed. Right now it is critical that I focus on my mental health,” he wrote in a statement posted to social media. “I owe it to my teammates, coaches, the organization and the fans to have my head and heart 100 percent in the game. And right now my heart is telling me that it’s time to say goodbye to football.” Report: Seahawks opt against signing RB Joe Mixon following physical | NFL.com The Seattle Seahawks have decided to not sign the veteran running back to their practice squad following a physical, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported on Tuesday. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald told reporters on Monday that the team was “going through the process” of adding Mixon. That process evidently has ended without a signing. Mixon missed the entire 2025 season with the Texans due to a foot injury, and Houston released him this past offseason. Chargers fire sale at NFL trade deadline? They have a few intriguing trade targets teams will be looking at — especially when it comes to pass rusher. Let’s take a look at some Chargers players who could be traded in the near future, and a couple of potential landing spots for them as well. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride The good and the bad about the Chiefs’ win against the Raiders Kirk Cousins wasn’t sacked in this game, which might lead you to think the Chiefs’ defensive line didn’t get much pressure. However, the Chiefs did get pressure on Cousins in this game 34.6% of his dropbacks, which was 16th in the NFL for Week 4. Without blitzes, the Chiefs were 12th at 34.2%. Two players led the charge in getting pressure in this game: defensive ends R Mason Thomas and George Karlaftis. Thomas finished the day with eight pressures, including five in the fourth quarter. Thomas took time to get into this game, but his speed and explosiveness off the edge showed up when it mattered. title: Whatever happens against Bills, Rams are ready to go on a run
summary: The Los Angeles Rams would obviously prefer to pick up a Week 5 win against the Buffalo Bills on Monday Night Football. They currently sit at 2-2. 3-2 sounds better than a losing record. Regardless of the outcome Monday, the Rams are in a position to go on a run in Week 6 and beyond. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 04: Puka Nacua #12 and Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams celebrate after a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on October 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams would obviously prefer to pick up a Week 5 win against the Buffalo Bills on Monday Night Football. They currently sit at 2-2. 3-2 sounds better than a losing record. Regardless of the outcome Monday, the Rams are in a position to go on a run in Week 6 and beyond. That’s not to say their schedule lightens up overall. It doesn’t. There are still plenty of tough games to come. It will just be a while before LA is tested to a severe degree, and that will allow time for key starters to nurse back to health. Week 6 vs Arizona Cardinals Arizona is 1-3 and in last place of the NFC West. They are on pace to position themselves for a quarterback in the 2027 NFL Draft. The Rams must keep the Cardinals on that trajectory. Week 7 at Las Vegas Raiders It’s no secret that the Raiders fans would probably dominate SoFi Stadium if the Rams were playing at home. LA would likely rather travel to face Las Vegas on the road. Are the Raiders better than expected? Absolutely. Should the Rams still be expected to win? Yes, and easily. Week 8 vs Los Angeles Chargers The other LA team led by Justin Herbert is still winless. They have enough talent to be dangerous and hang around in games they shouldn’t. The Rams can’t get caught by surprise. Week 9 at Washington Commanders The NFC East isn’t exactly a murderer’s row. The Commanders are still solidly in last place. The health of their quarterbacks is a major ongoing question. Even then, they are an older team who looks like their window has closed. The Rams can’t let it spring back open—even for a week. Week 10 at Arizona Cardinals Week 11 – BYE Week 12 vs Green Bay Packers While the Packers are 2-2, they might be one of the worst .500 teams across the NFL. Their offensive line is historically bad. Jordan Love is operating under a high degree of difficulty and his situation may not even be operable. LA’s pass rush could be back in full force and that could be a disastrous scenario for Green Bay. When can Rams expect reinforcements? Jaylen Watson and Aaron Donald could return as early as this week. Myles Garrett is able to come back as soon as Week 6 against the Cardinals, although it’s probably safe to assume he’ll be healthy no later than the Week 11 bye. The defense is already tough to face without Watson, Donald and Garrett. Re-adding these players in the mix should help them restore their “super team” status. We have not seen all three healthy and on the field together. And while the defense is performing well, the offense has yet to fire on all cylinders. Matthew Stafford and company put together two strong drives to take down the Eagles. Was this a sign their best weeks have yet to come? Even if the Rams fall to 2-3 against the Bills, by Week 13 they could realistically find themselves at a 8-3 record based on their schedule. The closing stretch will be tough. The next two months could provide some wiggle room.

title: Former Rams receiver lands with 49ers, weeks after playing against them
summary: The San Francisco 49ers signed Xavier Smith to their practice squad on Wednesday, less than a month after he played against them as a division rival with the Los Angeles Rams. Another indication that the Rams’ offseason plans to get better on special teams has backfired, as the Rams waived Smith last week following an […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers signed Xavier Smith to their practice squad on Wednesday, less than a month after he played against them as a division rival with the Los Angeles Rams. Another indication that the Rams’ offseason plans to get better on special teams has backfired, as the Rams waived Smith last week following an underwhelming performance as L.A.‘s punt and kickoff returner. Smith will go down as “modern Az-Zahir Hakim” but for only the wrong reasons, as he muffed two punts against the Seattle Seahawks in the 2025 NFC Championship game, the second of which being recovered by the other team. Wide receiver shuffle continues: 49ers have signed former Rams WR Xavier Smith to their practice squad. — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 7, 2026 Smith had a surprising 303 yards as a receiver in 2025, but Sean McVay obviously sees no-to-little potential in him on offense despite the Rams needing help at the position at various points of the season already. With Puka Nacua’s return in Week 4 against the Eagles, and Smith’s disappointing performances on special teams, it was more likely than ever that he would be a healthy scratch or get waived to make room for players like C.J. Daniels and Alex Bachman, the latter of whom being the team’s new return man. Xavier Smith ranked 49th in average kick return yards (20.6) out of 50 qualified players. He now joins a 49ers team that is constantly churning through options at receiver, including another former Rams player, Brandin Cooks. The 33-year-old Cooks made his 49ers debut in Week 4 and had one target with no catches. Smith will start on the practice squad but could be a quick elevation as a returner. Current punter returner Jacob Cowing is averaging only 5.0 yards per return on five attempts. They once said “X gonna give it to ya”, but once he gave it to the other team, he was gone.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Rams vs. Bills features rare MVP matchup
summary: When the Los Angeles Rams face the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, the game will feature the last two MVP winners. Josh Allen won the award in 2024 and Matthew Stafford won the award in 2025, and this will be the fourth time that the quarterbacks have played against one another. It will also be the […]
full_text: When the Los Angeles Rams face the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, the game will feature the last two MVP winners. Josh Allen won the award in 2024 and Matthew Stafford won the award in 2025, and this will be the fourth time that the quarterbacks have played against one another. It will also be the first time since 2015 that the last two MVPs have faced off against one another and they don’t play in the same conference. Inter-conference MVPs have not faced off since Aaron Rodgers played against Peyton Manning in 2015. QBs with the highest passing yards O/U for Week 5: Jared Goff 280.5 Matthew Stafford 280.5 Jacoby Brissett 270.5 Dak Prescott 263.5 Josh Allen 244 Jordan Love 233.5 C.J. Stroud 231.5 Trevor Lawrence 229.5 Drake Maye 227.5 Sam Darnold 227.5 — Parlae | Fantasy Desk (@parlaeio) October 7, 2026 MVP quarterbacks who play in the same conference is obviously more common, but still doesn’t happen every year. The last four instances featured either Lamar Jackson or Patrick Mahomes: 2025 Allen vs Jackson 2024 Jackson vs Mahomes 2020 Jackson vs Mahomes 2019 Mahomes vs Brady 2017 Matt Ryan vs Cam Newton (twice) To find the next-most recent example of quarterbacks in different conferences before Rodgers-Manning, you have to go back to the 1976 Super Bowl between the Vikings and Raiders; Fran Tarkenton and Ken Stabler. In Allen’s 10th career start, he faced Stafford’s Lions and won 14-13. The next time they faced off was 2022, as the Bills blew out the defending Super Bowl champions 31-10 in Week 1. Two years later, Allen had 342 yards and three touchdowns against the Rams in Week 14 and scored three more touchdowns on the ground. However, the Rams won 44-42, holding off Buffalo’s comeback attempt. Allen still won MVP that season, a controversial close victory over Lamar Jackson. The Bills lost to the Chiefs in the AFC Championship game. In 2025, Stafford led the league in passing yards and touchdowns and won an even closer MVP vote over Drake Maye. Allen finished third. The Rams lost to the Seahawks in the NFC Championship. Allen is off to another crazy start, as he leads the NFL with seven rushing touchdowns, which is even more than his six touchdown passes. Home teams are 8-2 in the 10 previous meetings of the last two MVP winning quarterbacks.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: What did you think of Makai Lemon against the Rams?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams could’ve taken Makai Lemon instead of Ty Simpson in the latest NFL Draft, so it was fitting that Lemon took on the Rams in Week 4 to give him a chance and the show the Rams what they missed out on. How did you think he did? Lemon didn’t have the […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams could’ve taken Makai Lemon instead of Ty Simpson in the latest NFL Draft, so it was fitting that Lemon took on the Rams in Week 4 to give him a chance and the show the Rams what they missed out on. How did you think he did? Lemon didn’t have the biggest day as the Eagles offense as a whole struggled. He did make a few catches including a nice fourth down conversion. No, Lemon hasn’t lit his rookie season on fire to this point, but he has played more than Simpson, and that may not sit right with some fans who wanted the Rams to get players who can help them in 2026. Perhaps the Rams didn’t think Lemon could help them enough. It will be interesting to see if Lemon catches fire at some point this year, or ever, really considering the Rams could’ve had him. It’s all rather interesting when it comes to the NFL. Rams Rookie Report Cards After Week 4 (And an Update on the Ones That Got Away) (si.com) “The player that many wanted the Rams to take at 13th overall was wide receiver Makai Lemon. Given the Rams’ shift to 13 personnel and the fact that he would have been WR3 at best, Lemon didn’t make sense at that spot. Lemon struggled during the summer with the Philadelphia Eagles and through four games, he has 10 receptions for 65 yards. The Rams’ current third wide receiver, Konata Mumpfield, has six receptions for 112 yards. Now, Lemon is undoubtedly the better player than Mumpfield, but the early production proves that the Rams were right not to take the USC wide receiver.“ The rare fiery Sean McVay moment that saved Rams’ season from spiraling vs. Eagles (clutchpoints) “ESPN’s Lindsey Thiry called out one fiery moment from head coach Sean McVay that sparked the impressive fourth quarter comeback. “Yeah, I definitely think this is really helpful. And the moment I think we will all look back on if the Rams go on the run that they’re expected to go on is Sean McVay gathering that offense around,” Thiry said on Tuesday via Good Morning Football. “… He was proving as the head coach what he’s always preaching to his players and they needed something to really get them going. And you don’t really see that from Sean McVay. You don’t see him get the entire offense around in the middle of the game and get after them like that. But he did and it clearly sparked a change in that team.” Week 5 Consensus NFL Power Rankings: Are Rams Contenders or Pretenders After Comeback Win? (si.com) “With 8:16 to play, the Rams had a 3.2 percent chance to win, and they somehow overcame the odds to come out on top 24-20. Quarterback Matthew Stafford led another fourth-quarter comeback and the two late touchdown drives were enough. Still, how the Rams are winning is not sustainable. Stafford has thrown an interception in every game this season. He currently ranks 20th in EPA per pass and needs to be better, especially as the Rams get ready to play the Bills. Let’s take a look at how the media feels about the Rams in this week’s consensus power rankings. ESPN – 7th The Rams don’t move this week in ESPN’s Power Rankings and stay in the No. 7 slot after coming back from 10 points to beat the Eagles. Again, one of the biggest questions around this Rams team is its consistency. The Rams haven’t found a way to play for 60 minutes outside of their Week 2 win against a New York Giants team that was led by Jameis Winston for most of the game.“ Rams Week 5 Power Rankings Round-Up: LA Stays Mostly Amid Top 10 (sports.yahoo) “ NFL.com sees no change for the Rams from Week 4 to Week 5. The reigning MVP threw another two interceptions on Sunday, pushing his total to six for the season. He had a total of eight in the 2025 regular season. Yahoo! Sports – No. 8 Yahoo! Sports has the Rams as being a top 10 team, but they have fallen two spots down from No. 6.“ Former Chargers 14-Game Starter Signs with NFC West Practice Squad (sports.yahoo) “According to NFL insider Adam Schefter, former Bolts linebacker Eric Kendricks has signed with the LA Rams’ practice squad. “Rams signed veteran ILB Eric Kendricks to their practice squad.” Kendricks signed with the Chargers to a two-year, $13.25 million deal in the 2023 free agency, but was released after one season. Now, after three years, Eric Kendrick returns to the City of Angels with the opportunity to play for a Super Bowl contender.“ BEST PHOTOS: Kyren Williams’ back-to-back touchdowns, Byron Young’s critical sacks & more | Best of the Rams’ Week 4 road win over the Eagles (therams.com) “The Los Angeles Rams beat the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 4 at Lincoln Financial Field. Several assistant coaches were seen pounding on glass windows and gesturing toward spectators seated below their stadium box. Sean McVay said he spoke directly with his staff about maintaining professional standards. He stressed that emotion must come with composure, insisting the behavior will not happen again.“ Rams report card: Grading every position after first 4 games (ramswire) “That’s what makes now a good time to share a report card from the first quarter of the season. We graded each position group, evaluating their performance through Week 4. Quarterback: B- Matthew Stafford hasn’t been at his best this season. He had five interceptions in the Rams’ first 15 games last season and he already has six this year. His eight turnover-worthy plays rank as the fourth-most in the NFL this year, though he’s also tied for seventh with seven big-time throws.“ NFL Power Rankings, Week 5: Cowboys, Pats rising at quarter mark; unbeaten Vikings fall out of top 10 (nfl.com) “For three quarters, serious, nearly existential questions began to build for these Rams. They’d fallen behind in Philadelphia and couldn’t get out of their own way offensively, raising the specter of a 1-3 start to a season that began with immense hype. title: Klint Kubiak leans on learning as Raiders move on from 1st loss
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are onto Week 5 and the New England Patriots and they are doing so with a new feeling in the early days of the Klint Kubiak tenure. They are begining are going through a work week coming off a loss for the first time under Kubiak. The Raiders are now 3-1 […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are onto Week 5 and the New England Patriots and they are doing so with a new feeling in the early days of the Klint Kubiak tenure. They are begining are going through a work week coming off a loss for the first time under Kubiak. The Raiders are now 3-1 after losing a closely contested 30-27 home game to the Kansas City Chiefs. The theme of this week for Kubiak is learning. Kubiak is stressing to his players and coaching staff that they must learn from the experience and the mistakes made in the defeat to improve as a team. Kubiak has said he is having honest covnersations with the team this week to ensure they learn. “I just think that’s the easiest way,” Kubiak said. “Here’s the tape. Here’s what we got right. Here’s what we got wrong. Here’s where we’re not correct as coaches. Here’s where we didn’t make the play as a player. And if we can just put it in front of those guys and everyone sees it, and as a team we can learn from it and get better, then we’re going the right direction.” Kubiak is pleased how his team has responded this week thus far. “They’re disappointed, and they’re a very mature group that wants to win,” Kubiak said. “So, we’re fixing the corrections. We’re trying to make ourselves better. Whether we win or whether we lose, we’re telling each other the truth and just seeing what we can do to be a better team moving forward.” So, while Kubiak is clearly not pleased to lose, he does value this opportunity to make everyone better because of it. “Yeah, (the games) all are. They all are,” Kubiak said. “Every game you learn more about your team, you learn more about yourself as a coach, and you have to go make the corrections, get better.”
