title: Vic Fangio says it’s possible the Eagles are playing Jalen Carter too much
summary: The Eagles are having a rough week, and as they prepare for the Jaguars in London, defensive coordinator Vic Fangio spoke to reporters about their late-game struggles against the Rams, what he thinks of the secondary, and about Jalen Carter’s work load with a cast. As the injuries continue to stack up, Fangio was asked […]
full_text: Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images | Getty Images The Eagles are having a rough week, and as they prepare for the Jaguars in London, defensive coordinator Vic Fangio spoke to reporters about their late-game struggles against the Rams, what he thinks of the secondary, and about Jalen Carter’s work load with a cast. As the injuries continue to stack up , Fangio was asked how he feels about the depth on defense: “It’s being challenged right now, so we’ll see. But I think in certain places we’re good and others, you cross your fingers.” When later asked about which positions lack depth, he coyly replied, “You’ll have to figure that out yourself.” Here’s what else the DC had to say: On the late game struggles Fangio said that they struggled to make a play and he struggled to make the right call late in the game against the Rams, and with a veteran QB like Matthew Stafford, that’s a bad combination. “We didn’t get it done. You know, we played great for 10 drives, but the last two, we didn’t.” The DC clarified that the defense played 83 total snaps, including penalties, and while it might have a small affect on things, ultimately, they need to find a way to finish. On the secondary Fangio thought that Michael Carter did a good job on Sunday. He was asked about Jonathan Jones having to come in after Quinyon Mitchell was sidelined, and the DC said he was happy with how the CB stepped up. “I thought [Jonathan Jones] did good for really his first action in a long time. If you remember, he missed the tail end of training camp and hadn’t had any action since whenever, one of the early preseason games and though he’d come in there and did a good job. He does a good job preparing and he was ready to go.” The DC said that they are hopeful that Quinyon Mitchell will be available this weekend, but said they’ll find out more as the week goes on. He was also complimentary of new DB Kenny Moore and how he’s preparing to contribute. “[Kenny Moore]‘s getting closer. He’s done a great job learning, [we’re] trying to get him to learn two positions to be part of nickel or dime, and safety. But he got in there for a play or two at the end.“ On the pass rush “I thought it was inconsistent.” The DC said that they haven’t been consistently really good in one-on-ones, and while they might be affected by chips, when they are getting one-on-ones, they’re not getting it done on a consistent basis. Ultimately, though, Fangio said that he’s still confident that the pass rush will get to a level that he wants to see. “I just believe in the guys. A lot of times too, we’ve lost two sacks the last two games due to penalties. Sometimes the ball’s coming out quick, like previous some games. I know you guys have a love affair with the sack stat, but the ball’s coming out quick a lot.” On playing time for players Fangio said that LB Jeremiah Trotter Jr. played very well against the Rams, and probably earned some more playing time as a result. The DC was also asked about Jordan Davis only taking 35 percent of the defensive snaps, to which Fangio admitted that they probably need to get him on the field more. He explained that it was more of a result of personnel the Rams were in — they had been playing a lot of three tight ends in the weeks before the Eagles game, but then went with more three receiver looks on Sunday, which changed the game. He admitted that Jalen Carter ’s wrist injury affected him more on Sunday against the Rams than in previous games, and when asked if the DT is playing more than he should be, Fangio replied, “Possibly.” On the Jaguars offense “They’re really good on offense. The quarterback is athletic, got a big arm, he’s got a good group of receivers to throw it to. Their running back, 33 [RB Bhayshul Tuten] runs really good, kind of a new guy on the scene and they do a good job. They got a very varied running game, a lot of different types of runs, multiple run game and they’re good at it.” Other notables Fangio said that safety Andrew Mukuba has been playing well all season, and he’s real pleased with where he is in his development. He noted that Jalyx Hunt just needs to continue doing the little things consistently. The DC said LB Jihaad Campbell has been coming along, and is getting better each game against both the run and pass game.

title: Steelers reunite with young CB
summary: Pittsburgh has filled the final slot on its practice squad, bringing back second-year cornerback Doneiko Slaughter, the team announced early Wednesday. Slaughter has already had a busy stint with the Steelers this year after starting his NFL career as a Jaguars undrafted free agent in 2025. Originally signed to a futures deal with Pittsburgh in […]
full_text: Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Pittsburgh has filled the final slot on its practice squad, bringing back second-year cornerback Doneiko Slaughter, the team announced early Wednesday. Slaughter has already had a busy stint with the Steelers this year after starting his NFL career as a Jaguars undrafted free agent in 2025. Originally signed to a futures deal with Pittsburgh in January, Slaughter was thrust into starting duty at the nickel position for some of the summer as Jalen Ramsey and Brandin Echols dealt with injury. Slaughter made the Steelers’ initial practice squad following cutdown day, and then was elevated to the team’s active roster for the first three games of the season — the maximum number under NFL rules. However, Slaughter was then signed to the Steelers’ 53-man roster ahead of the team’s Week 4 matchup in order to play against the Cleveland Browns. While he still hasn’t appeared in a defensive snap this year, Slaughter has played in four games and 23% of Pittsburgh’s special teams snaps. The Steelers waived Slaughter following the Browns game, but after the cornerback cleared waivers, he was re-signed back to the practice squad. Steelers beat writers such as Alan Saunders and Chris Halicke have reported that the team cannot elevate Slaughter again.

Dowdle, who said he dislocated a toe in Week 2 against the Patriots and had it pop out of place twice in the game, was held out of Pittsburgh’s following games against both the Bengals and Browns after being a non-participant in practice. Veteran defensive backs Jamel Dean (ankle) and Jalen Ramsey (wrist) did not participate in Wednesday’s practice. On Tuesday, Dean was seen without the walking boot he used after Pittsburgh’s loss to the Browns, the same game in which Ramsey played through a broken wrist. Defensive lineman Cam Heyward rounded out Wednesday’s report as a non-participant with a rest day designation. title: The Steelers offense can be great, but they need to lean into what’s working
summary: Inconsistency has been the name of the game for the Pittsburgh Steelers’ offense and defense through the first quarter of the 2026 NFL season, leading to a fitting 2-2 record through four weeks. And after another recent low point, a 27-24 loss to the rival Cleveland Browns and Deshaun Watson last Thursday, Read and React […]
full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Inconsistency has been the name of the game for the Pittsburgh Steelers’ offense and defense through the first quarter of the 2026 NFL season, leading to a fitting 2-2 record through four weeks. And after another recent low point, a 27-24 loss to the rival Cleveland Browns and Deshaun Watson last Thursday, Read and React is here to take a look at if there might be a light and the end of the tunnel to one of the Steelers’ struggling units. Is there hope for the Steelers’ offense? RP : The Steelers have been an undoubtedly frustrating watch through the first quarter of the NFL season. While their record of 2-2 is certainly not reason to give up on the season — they are just one game back from the division lead after all — we can certainly empathize with any fans who think this Steelers team has proven they aren’t good enough to be taken seriously. You could argue the offense has only played one good game this year, Week 3’s win over the Bengals. That’s a tough pill to swallow considering the organization’s hiring of offensive-minded coach Mike McCarthy was supposed to finally fix what has been the glaring weakness of this team for the entirety of the 2020s. But what makes the whole thing more maddening is that there have been glimpses of a promising offense. The Bengals game was a stellar performance from start to finish, and even the Browns game featured an immaculate first drive of the game, as well as a late-game surge that saw the Steelers score two touchdowns in the fourth quarter to tie the game. The issue again and again has been that the Steelers have lacked consistency. On one drive they’re Jekyll, the next they’re Hyde. Naturally, fans are left wondering why that is. Are the players simply not good enough? Or are the coaches failing to utilize them well? Truthfully, the answer lies somewhere in the middle, but for the sake of this column, we’d like to argue, with film and data, that there is still a chance for this offense to be not only a fun one, but maybe even an above average one too. But to do so, the two most influential people in this offense, McCarthy and quarterback Aaron Rodgers, need to put ego aside, and embrace not the offense that they’ve enjoyed in the past, but the offense this roster is currently built to be. The Steelers need to lean into playing bully ball. And by that, we mean they need to get under center more and, to use an old coaching adage, they need to run the damn ball. Steelers are starting to embrace their size up front, their skill position players willingness to scrap, and even Warren's running style. They ran the Duo run concept 12 times last night against the Browns with 8 of them ending up successful, per @NextGenStats . Bully ball! pic.twitter.com/FMs7nQd7L0 — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) October 2, 2026 The Steelers gotta lean all the way into playing bullyball. Washington and Nowakowski handle the EDGE, DK Metcalf gets a solid block on the LB, and then Fautanu and Mason McCormick really help spring this run pic.twitter.com/7zKZtvTeBF — JP Acosta (@acosta32_jp) September 30, 2026 But it’s more than just what the eye test is telling us. The Steelers have been dominant when they line up under center. Whether it’s run or pass, Pittsburgh is averaging 6.8 yards per play when they do so. That trails only the Kansas City Chiefs through the first four games of the season. Steelers aren’t just a good offense when they’re under center, they’re literally the 2nd best under center offense in the league https://t.co/1EnJbRiB7c — Nick Farabaugh (@FarabaughFB) October 6, 2026 RB : Under center isn’t a magic bullet fix to an offense, but it does offer some advantages over shotgun in certain instances (and vice versa, of course). The most obvious is a more direct, downhill run game. The quarterback-center exchange is cleaner, the running back gets a running start and a wider field of view, and linemen have a tick longer to land their blocks. The results can be a fun watch, even if some more of less boil down to hitting a narrow crease at full speed for four or five yards. Steelers under center run game pic.twitter.com/4N11KtLxI4 — Ryland Bickley (@_Ryland_B) October 7, 2026 And the Steelers have the personnel to pull this style of play off. The addition of Brock Hoffman and Max Iheanachor on the Steelers’ offensive line has added a much-need infusion of extra physicality to a group that already includes maulers Mason McCormick and Zach Frazier, as well as a good left tackle in Troy Fautanu. Tight end Darnell Washington is, of course, one of the biggest bullies at his position in the NFL, and both running backs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle (when healthy), are physical ball-carriers with the latter having even more of a decisive, downhill playing style. And while this hasn’t been a great postgame week regarding the reputation of the Steelers’ wide receiver room, names such as Germie Bernard, Michael Pittman Jr. and Ben Skowronek have been putting some work in as blockers in recent weeks (including a lot of C-gap inserts), upping the “bully ball” potential of the offense as a whole. Yeah the Steelers O-line can be pretty cool, but check out these receivers in the run game pic.twitter.com/Xk8ySEGiGn — Ryland Bickley (@_Ryland_B) October 7, 2026 But why under center? A mid-September article from ESPN’s Bill Barnwell further broke down why the league as a whole has been seeing increased usage of this concept. The explanation matches the eye test — defenses have become incredibly modern, and to beat them, sometimes you have to break out the old-school concepts. Defenses have become unpredictable, meaning offenses need to follow suit. And under-center runs have far less tells of where the run will go as the running back is directly behind the quarterback to start the play. And in the passing game, play action and ball fakes are easier to pull off. Barnwell points out that the uncertainty of reacting to an under-center offense has been the “natural response” to NFL defenses using increasingly exotic zone coverages. As the adage goes, it’s a game of inches, and hard play-action fakes can provide the extra millisecond of hesitation in the secondary needed to break a big play. Little bit of hesitation from the safety opens up big play to DK Metcalf pic.twitter.com/UUgJAh9G9k — Ryland Bickley (@_Ryland_B) October 7, 2026 The Steelers have been especially productive in this aspect of the game. According to DK Pittsburgh Sports’ Chris Halicke , the Steelers run play action on 89% of their under-center drop backs — meaning almost every snap from that alignment starts off looking like a run play. As uninteresting as the Steelers’ offense has looked at times, the under-center concepts have found some success in confusing opposing defenses. RP : Frankly, for as impressive as the Steelers look under center, they’ve been just as dreadful from shotgun. Here's how effective NFL offenses have been when under center vs. shotgun pic.twitter.com/9zbgy01Xda — Ben Baby (@Ben_Baby) October 5, 2026 Historically, both McCarthy and Rodgers have preferred not only a passing-dominant approach to offense, but they’ve preferred a heavy dose of 11 personnel (three wide receivers) and from shotgun. But as the chart above indicates, this version of Rodgers, mixed with this current collection of players, is simply not built to live in that style of offense. A recent article from Mike DeFabo of The Athletic pointed out some of the key data points that can help contextualize the struggles we’ve seen play out on the field: The Steelers have used 11-personnel at 10th highest rate (63.8%) When doing so, they rank 30th in EPA per dropback (-0.23) That ranking drops to 31st when the defense rushes 5 or more (-0.68) 12 of the Steelers 13 sacks allowed have come while using 11 personnel When using 12 personnel, the Steelers improve to 18th in EPA per dropback (-0.05) They also improve against 5+ rushers in 12…

If Dean cannot go, Asante Samuel Jr. and rookie Daylen Everette will continue to see expanded roles. The fact that Dean is already out of the boot is a step in the right direction, but his practice participation will be the biggest indicator of whether he has a realistic chance to return Sunday. The biggest news on the Seattle Seahawks side is that defensive tackle Leonard Williams is a limited participant with an ankle injury that he suffered late in the game last week. This is welcome news and will be something to monitor the rest of the week. When asked if Williams can play against the 49ers, head coach Mike Macdonald stated that “ we’re optimistic for the game. ” The other names to keep an eye on throughout the week include linebacker Chazz Surratt, who did not practice with a calf injury. Right guard Beau Stephens (knee), cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett (ankle) linebacker Tyrice Knight (ankle), and running back George Holani (ribs) were all limited participants as well. Running back Zach Charbonnet (knee) was limited in practice again this week as he works his way back from the PUP list. Macdonald noted that Charbonnet will get team reps this week but that he will not play against the 49ers . The other new name that is exciting news is wide receiver, and special teamer Irv Charles, who was limited in practice as well. Charles was placed on injured reserve due to a knee injury, but has since been designated to return to practice . He too has a 21-day window to practice before the team decides to activate him to the active roster or shut him down for the season. Ty Okada (hamstring) and Patrick O’Connell (thumb) were full participants in practice. Meanwhile Jaxon Smith-Njigba (veteran rest day) did not practice. As for the 49ers, edge rusher Nick Bosa and fullback Kyle Juszczyk did not practice due to injury, however, neither is expected to play against Seattle. However, some other names who sat out practice and are worth keeping an eye on are safety Marques Sigle (ankle), cornerback Upton Stout (shoulder), and defensive tackle James Thompson (ankle).

title: Seahawks All-22 rookie review: How Beau Stephens performed vs. Chargers
summary: After a Week 3 in which Jadarian Price and Beau Stephens were the only Seattle Seahawks rookies seeing meaningful playing time, the situation changed considerably against the Chargers. Price was already on injured reserve with a chest injury, and with Avery Smith inactive again, only two Seattle rookies took the field on Sunday. Stephens played […]
full_text: After a Week 3 in which Jadarian Price and Beau Stephens were the only Seattle Seahawks rookies seeing meaningful playing time, the situation changed considerably against the Chargers. Price was already on injured reserve with a chest injury, and with Avery Smith inactive again, only two Seattle rookies took the field on Sunday. Stephens played 25 of Seattle’s 60 offensive snaps , continuing to rotate with Christian Haynes at right guard. Neal, meanwhile, did not play a single defensive snap but logged 23 special teams snaps . In total, Seattle’s rookies accounted for just 25 snaps (offense/defense) in a game in which the Seahawks ran 60 offensive plays and played 59 defensive snaps. The state of Seattle’s 2026 rookie class is becoming increasingly unusual. Price, the team’s best chance at immediate impact, is on injured reserve. Clark is still sidelined as well. Neal has yet to find a role on defense, while Stephens remains the only rookie consistently seeing offensive snaps. Jadarian Price, Running Back — 0 snaps, Injured Reserve Price missed the game against the Chargers after being placed on injured reserve with a chest injury. After opening the season as Seattle’s primary rookie running back and carving out a meaningful role during the first three weeks, he now has to watch from the sideline while Emanuel Wilson and George Holani handle most of the backfield workload. The timing of the injury is particularly frustrating for Price. The rookie was coming off a difficult Week 3 against Washington, when his second lost fumble in three games drastically reduced his playing time. Now, just when Seattle could have used a response from the rookie, he is sidelined. The good news is that Price showed enough explosiveness early in the season to justify the expectations surrounding him. The problem is that he will have to earn his role back when he returns. Price remains an important piece of Seattle’s future on offense, but he will have to find his place again in a backfield rotation that could look very different by the time he is healthy. Bud Clark, Safety — 0 snaps, Injured Reserve Still on injured reserve. Julian Neal, Cornerback — 0 defensive snaps, 23 special teams snaps The third-round pick did not play a single defensive snap against the Chargers, repeating what happened against Washington. Neal did see 23 special teams snaps, nine more than he played in the loss to the Commanders, but he was also flagged for illegal use of the hands. For now, special teams remains his only avenue onto the field. The next step is finding a way to turn those opportunities into defensive playing time. Beau Stephens, Guard — 25 snaps For the third consecutive game, the fifth-round pick rotated with Christian Haynes at right guard. This time, Stephens played 25 of Seattle’s 60 offensive snaps, while Haynes played 35. This was easily Stephens’ roughest performance of the season so far. title: Seahawks designate standout special teamer Irv Charles to return to practice
summary: Through the first month of the season, the Seattle Seahawks rank near the bottom of the league in yards per kickoff return allowed (29.4), but they’re poised to regain a key special teams piece in the the coming weeks. The team announced on Wednesday they’ve designated wide receiver and special teams gunner Irv Charles to […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JUNE 11: Irv Charles #85 of the Seattle Seahawks catches the ball during practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on June 11, 2026 in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through the first month of the season, the Seattle Seahawks rank near the bottom of the league in yards per kickoff return allowed (29.4), but they’re poised to regain a key special teams piece in the the coming weeks. The team announced on Wednesday they’ve designated wide receiver and special teams gunner Irv Charles to return to practice, meaning they have a 21-day window to activate him to their active roster. If they opt not to, he’ll remain on injured reserve for the remainder of the season. Charles was acquired from the New York Jets on May 27 but has yet to suit up for Seattle after he sustained an undisclosed injury during training camp and missed the entire preseason before being placed on injured reserve prior to the start of the regular season. The fourth-year pro has already missed the minimum four-game requirement and is eligible to return to action as soon as Sunday. Although, the team’s Week 7 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs is seemingly the most realistic return date considering the Seahawks have a quick turnaround against the Denver Broncos next Thursday. Charles, 29, missed the entirety of last season after he tore his ACL in December 2024, but emerged as a key special teams contributor over two seasons with the Jets, during which time he recorded 14 tackles and a blocked punt.

title: Ernest Jones IV breaks down Justin Herbert pick, talks ‘Call of Duty’ in Field Gulls interview
summary: One of the pivotal moments for the Seattle Seahawks in transforming from a below-average defense to the consensus best defense in the NFL was the trade for linebacker Ernest Jones IV. Once a rival on the Los Angeles Rams, Jones was traded to the Tennessee Titans before the start of the 2024 season, then acquired […]
full_text: One of the pivotal moments for the Seattle Seahawks in transforming from a below-average defense to the consensus best defense in the NFL was the trade for linebacker Ernest Jones IV. Once a rival on the Los Angeles Rams, Jones was traded to the Tennessee Titans before the start of the 2024 season, then acquired by Seattle midseason for a fourth-round pick and Jerome Baker . Jones has become one of the league’s best linebackers, earning All-Pro second-team honors last season, and he’s off to a stellar start in 2026, most recently dominating the Los Angeles Chargers with his 12-tackle, 1 interception, 1 sack outing. Field Gulls had the opportunity to talk to Ernest on Tuesday about his Chargers performance, his relationship with Bobby Wagner, and how his second Super Bowl felt compared to the one he won with the Rams. But before we get into the football aspect of our conversation, this interview was all made possible by Call of Duty , who will soon be releasing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on October 23. Jones is a big-time gamer, and his experience playing CoD dates back many years ago. “I think it’s World at War ,” Jones said. “That was my first [ Call of Duty game]. I remember playing that in my living room and I’d tried to be playing it up until 3-4 in the morning knowing I had school the next day and my mom would be on my butt. That’s my early remembrance of playing Call of Duty. Ever since, I’ve been getting more into it, playing it a lot more, having teammates makes it a lot more fun. So that’s kind of my history with Call of Duty . Beta gameplay has been out for a bit, but Ernest said he hasn’t had the opportunity to give the game a test run, so he’s going to be waiting until worldwide release date for MW4. He admits that his play style throws caution to the wind, but he just loves playing the game. “With time and with playing I get better, but I say I’m pretty reckless. A lot of my teammates, especially when we’re playing Warzone , I’m the guy that’s—if I see you, I’m pushing, I’m coming up, so that’s me!” While Jones said the whole Seahawks team gets into CoD, he shouted out Devon Witherspoon and Tyrice Knight as a couple of teammates who play regularly. And yes, the idea of ‘Spoon talking trash in video games is exactly what you probably thought. Ernest Jones revealed Devon Witherspoon is a big Call of Duty guy. And I know what you're thinking, and the answer is "yes" as far as trash talking. But Ernest's response makes it funnier. pic.twitter.com/nWxeNLmbQd — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) October 7, 2026 “It’s worse,” Jones said when asked if he trash talks as much in CoD as he does on the football field. “It’s worse because he’s actually like a real good Call of Duty player. He’s annoying at times when he’s out there and he’s talking trash and you may be down or you may be dying a lot. He’s on your head because he’s playing good. He’s more of a trash talker through the game for sure.” Alright, let’s get to football now! Ernest Jones IV on being the first Seahawks LB with a sack/pick double since Bobby Wagner “That’s great company to be in right there. Bobby’s a legend, somebody I’ve got tremendous respect for, played with, so to be in that company that’s great. That puts a smile on my face, for sure.” “I think it was a big key coming in my year two and being able to learn from Bobby [when we were on the Los Angeles Rams]. Just seeing how he works, seeing what it took to be a Hall of Fame linebacker in this game. To have everything that he has going for him, to have him be able to come in and speak life into me and coach me and teach me things was really beneficial, and I think it’s carried me to this point.” What was Ernest’s coverage responsibility on the Justin Herbert interception? “I’m the hook player there, and I think Justin may have thought that I was taking the tight end up vertical, and when I squared back up he threw the ball right there to my hook window. “That’s something that we worked, that’s something that we see on film that quarterbacks just don’t think linebackers are going to get to those windows and be in those sports, so they kind of just throw the ball a thinking that we’re not going to be there. Fortunately, I was there.” Quads vs 3×1 with a “trix” safety backside. Looks like “stump” to the trips. Nickel takes 1 under, Jones as the hook player takes 3 up until he peels off on the dig under it. Specific coaching point in Macdonald’s offense is play on top the dig bc that’s how so many O’s pair… https://t.co/4CnvYcKKHT pic.twitter.com/xj9g4rhEmq — rich madrid (@richjmadrid_) October 7, 2026 Sack, tackle for loss, or turnover? What’s Ernest Jones’ favorite thing to do as a linebacker? “For me, it used to be tackles. It used to be tackles, tackles, tackles. But ever since I found the joy, I see why people like playing offense and catching the ball. When you get those interceptions it’s just fun to have the ball in your hands and be running the ball back. I think it’s still tackles, but it’s probably like 60-40 tackles-interceptions. Was winning the Super Bowl sweeter this time because it was at the 49ers stadium? “I think it was more so that—it took me five years in between to get close to this moment again. So I just think I understand what it takes to get to that part of the pinnacle of an NFL career, the NFL season, to be playing in the Super Bowl, let alone win it. I think I understood the importance of that this time. “I was just truly grateful, no matter the opponent, no matter where it was, just grateful for the opportunity and grateful that I was fortunate enough to be here for a second time.” Preparing for Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay offenses “I think when you’re playing Shanahan and McVay there’s definitely different wrinkles you got to prepare for, but it all gets down back to what they’ve practiced for six months, what they’ve been practicing the entire year, and what they’ve been showing on film. It always comes back to that. We’ve got a got a good idea on what we have to do to win these teams against both of those teams. “Specifically talking about the Niners this week, man, they’ve got a really good team. I think they’re playing the best ball of all the teams. Offensively they’re making a hell of [a lot of] plays. [Brock] Purdy’s playing really good. We’ve got our hands full. Defensively they’re no slouch either; they can go out there and get turnovers. Fred [Warner] is a really good linebacker in the middle with Dre [Greenlaw]. I expect it to be a war like it’s always been. We expect nothing less, and I’m sure they expect the same thing.” Has Ernest Jones IV ever ridden in Derick Hall’s monster truck? And how was Hard Knocks ? “No I haven’t ridden. I honestly don’t even want to get that high up in the air while a car is being [driven]. Might as well get in a plane at this point. “Hard Knocks was fun. We had a really great time. I think it truly showcased what we’re about, what we’re doing, what we’re striving to do here in Seattle. We’re just trying to have fun every day at work, Put the work in and go win football games, and if it takes us to the Super Bowl, that’s perfect. That’s where the hard work pays off. “Each day we’re just fighting to strive, and I believe it showed that, Showed personalities. Derick Hall’s truck, his shorts, Coach [Macdonald]—his side of him that you don’t get to really see. I think it was a really good time, I think guys enjoyed it, and I really enjoyed it, as well.” There’s a little more from this interview I’ll sprinkle here and there over the next couple of days and maybe into next week. Thanks to Ernest for his time and thanks to the folks at Call of Duty for setting this up! And now I have to ask the most obvious question in the world to our readers: Do you play Call of Duty and are you hyped for Modern Warfare 4? Check out the campaign mode trailer here . title: Seahawks Week 5 power rankings: Seattle eyes top spot, which currently belongs to 49ers
summary: Entering Week 4, the Seattle Seahawks took a hit in the power rankings after their surprising loss to the Washington Commanders. However, will Seattle start to make a move back up the rankings after defeating the Los Angeles Chargers (albeit in a rather sloppy manner)? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, […]
full_text: Entering Week 4, the Seattle Seahawks took a hit in the power rankings after their surprising loss to the Washington Commanders. However, will Seattle start to make a move back up the rankings after defeating the Los Angeles Chargers (albeit in a rather sloppy manner)? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (BR), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle. There are a lot of similarities between three of the national media sites who all moved the Seahawks up one spot, from fourth to third best in the league. In this ranking, NFL.com noted that Seattle took their foot off the gas too early against the Chargers , yet were still able to rebound after their loss to the Commanders a week earlier. B/R, which also moved Seattle up to number three , brings up Sam Darnold’s bumpy start (referencing his three interceptions in two games). However, B/R also notes that the Seahawks defense continues to get the job done, citing their four quarterback sacks and 10 hits on Justin Herbert. While ranking Seattle the third best team in the NFL, ESPN used four words to describe the Seahawks first four weeks of the season: “ Eventful – not always positive .” To add some context to these four words, Brady Henderson of ESPN brings up the many different events that occurred over the first month of the Seahawks 2026 season. Including Sam Darnold and Jadarian Price’s injuries, a franchise-record 150 penalty yards against the Chargers in week four, and even Mike Macdonald’s interview mishap regarding Sean Payton . Not every national media site has the Seahawks ranked as the third best team in the NFL. CBS, which moved Seattle up one spot from 5 to 4 , also cited Seattle’s impressive defensive performance as the reason they were able to defeat the Chargers. Meanwhile, PFT has the Seahawks ranked the lowest among these five national media sites, leaving Seattle as the fifth best team in the league, one spot up from last week. In their reasoning, PFT simply states “Let Rashid cook .” Overall, the Seahawks moved up slightly after defeating the Chargers. Entering week four, the average power ranking between the five polled sites was 4.6. Entering Week 5, that average has risen to 3.6. Next week against the San Francisco 49ers will be the biggest test Seattle has faced all season. In all five of the national media site’s power rankings, the 49ers came in as the number one team in the league. If Seattle can pull off the victory, it may be tough for any of these national media sites to keep the Seahawks out of that number one spot.

Buccaneers (0-4): DT Vita Vea. The big defensive tackle hails from nearby Milpitas, Calif., and would reunite with Evans. Maybe the 49ers will send Florida native Mac Jones in a home-state swap? Cardinals (1-3): Edge Josh Sweat. He had 12 sacks last season and won’t turn 30 until March. Chargers (0-4): Edge Khalil Mack. He turned 35 in February, but the fact he has three sacks so far (no 49er has more than two) shows he’s still got it. Commanders (1-3): DT Daron Payne. A rotation including Payne, Osa Odighizuwa and Gracen Halton wouldn’t be too shabby. A result of the 49ers’ long list of D-line injuries is that Odighizuwa has logged 123 snaps in the past two games. That’s a lot for a defensive lineman and ought to set off alarm bells for the 49ers. Dolphins (0-4): DE Joshua Uche. Uche, who has bounced around the league, has one sack so far in Miami. He turned 28 last month. Jets (1-3): DE Will McDonald IV. McDonald is just 27 and had 18.5 sacks over the past two seasons. The Jets picked up his $13.8 million fifth-year option this season, but a long-term deal appears unlikely. Saints (1-3): None. Texans (0-4): DE Danielle Hunter. The 49ers have been linked to the veteran pass rusher in free agency in the past. He had 15 sacks last season and two so far this year. Titans (0-4): DT Jordan Elliott. I know you wanted me to put Jeffrey Simmons. But what would he cost the 49ers?” 49ers Week 4 Trench Grades: They may have stumbled into gold (paywall) “The 49ers may have stumbled into something incredible with the trio of Naquan Jones, Sebastian Valdez and Gracen Halton. Halton’s not perfect, but he can anchor down well in one-on-ones, and possesses a violence to shed blocks uniquely. Jones and Valdez possess that violence and double-team splitting ability. Ironically, all the 49ers’ injuries may have helped their run defense. Just wait until Mykel Williams is playing run snaps instead of Ogbo Okoronkwo. HOO BOY.” 49ers top pick Mykel Williams eager to make up for disappointing rookie season (paywall) “Another focus for Williams during his recovery: getting leaner. He did not specify his current weight but said he began taking his diet more seriously after the injury. To reach his desired weight, though, Williams had to make some tough sacrifices. He gave up peach cobbler — his favorite craving when he has a sweet tooth — in addition to ice cream, in favor of protein shakes.” Is it time to panic about 49ers’ injuries? Breaking down IR, trade deadline plan “There’s a scenario in which those practice squad players hold their positions throughout October. Then, the return of injured players could set up the 49ers well for the stretch run. But that assumes there won’t be more injuries in the meantime. With this team, that would be a bold assumption….San Francisco would be smart to invest in insurance policies for Bosa, West, Thompson and Okuayinonu in case their recoveries don’t go as planned. A run-stuffing defensive tackle and another edge rusher capable of getting after the quarterback have to be among the top priorities for the Niners as the season goes on. Currently, they’re 22nd in defensive rushing success rate and 26th in sacks per dropback.” At least four 49ers players will miss Week 5 NFC West showdown vs. Seahawks “[Stout] begins the practice week with his status unclear for the 49ers’ Week 5 game against last season’s Super Bowl champions.” Kyle Shanahan reveals injury updates, previews 49ers-Seahawks matchup “No, you put the ball in Deebo’s hand and he can execute it. He runs as good as anyone. That’s why I like him at kick returner, possible punt returner. There’s a game you used to play when you were younger that I can’t say the name of it anymore. It’s tackle the guy with the ball with no rules to it. I always say he’d probably be my first pick in the draft if that was the game.” After big-game beatdowns, 49ers’ thoughts on Seahawks are hard to believe (paywall) “When pressed on his just-another-week outlook, Warner smiled, suggesting his real emotions were just beneath the surface, when reminded of the Seahawks celebrating a title in the 49ers’ locker room shortly after trouncing them twice. Before Warner roared like a lion, feigning fury, he asked: “Are you trying to rile me up?” How Kaelon Black’s heads-up instincts bailed out Jake Brendel on big 49ers play “Brendel, known among his teammates as someone who rarely has a missed assignment, did not hear Purdy signal he was making the shift to 5 yards behind center. Brendel thought Purdy was directly behind him. Brendel snapped the ball, and he immediately knew something had gone awry. “As soon as I didn’t feel his hands, I kind of gave a little flick of the wrist,” Brendel said. “That’s kind of a big no-no to do as a center, but I just wanted to get the ball back there.” The ball fluttered in the air, and that is when the rookie did not act like a rookie during the chaos that followed. What was Black thinking in that split-second? “Just get the ball and make a play,” Black answered. “I couldn’t let it hit the ground. I feel like it was just instincts at that point. If something goes wrong, you just try to make it right, as best as you can, especially in that situation where we needed to convert that fourth down.” 49ers sign former Rams wide receiver to the practice squad “Smith, 5’9”, 180 pounds, had been with the Rams since 2024. He was waived by Los Angeles on October 2. He’s speedy. Smith ran a 4.38-second 40-yard dash at Florida A&M’s Pro Day. This move tells me that the 49ers want to surround their core passing targets, Mike Evans and George Kittle, with as much speed as possible. Of course, the plan probably isn’t to play Smith, but they’ve only worked out or signed guys who can run or have return experience at wide receiver.”

title: How similar are the 49ers and Seahawks through 4 weeks?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers head to Seattle for the biggest matchup of the season as the two best teams in the NFC are set to do battle. The 49ers are 4-0 following a gritty win over the Denver Broncos, and the Seahawks are 3-1 after dismantling the Chargers. The two teams are far more similar […]
full_text: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers head to Seattle for the biggest matchup of the season as the two best teams in the NFC are set to do battle. The 49ers are 4-0 following a gritty win over the Denver Broncos, and the Seahawks are 3-1 after dismantling the Chargers. The two teams are far more similar than anyone expected. The margins will be thin, and the team that makes more plays and fewer mistakes will leave with a win. This feels like the rivalry from 2012 with two evenly matched teams. What are the similarities between the two teams over four weeks? Explosive play rate allowed on defense Now, the 49ers aren’t to be confused with a top-flight defense, but they currently sit at the top of the league with a 2.7% explosive play rate allowed (passes or rushes over 20 yards). How are they doing this? A combination of things, actually. First, the secondary has done a great job keeping everything in front of them. Raheem Morris has dialed up the right calls at the right time, and the offenses they have faced so far aren’t exactly vertical passing attacks. Miami creates passing explosives diagonally with screens. Arizona has no desire to go downfield with Jacoby Brissett under center, and the same goes for Denver, although I’m sure Sean Payton wants to attack downfield; Bo Nix has no desire to. Seattle is currently third in explosive play rate allowed at 4.9% and has allowed 2.2% of explosive passes, which is good for third in the NFL. Now, the run defense is seventh in rushing explosives allowed at 8.2%. That is where the 49ers have to take advantage on Sunday. Coverage percentages The 49ers have a new defensive coordinator in Morris, but the team has largely kept their zone coverage principles, with 45.8% of their calls being for Cover 4. With 18.7% of the coverage played as Cover 6, the only new real wrinkle is that the 49ers are up to 25% Cover 1 man. Seattle is literally a full-on zone coverage defense. With 34.9% of their coverage being Cover 3, 20.8% is Cover 4, and 24.8% is Cover 6, Seattle’s defense gets home with four and will sit in a suffocating zone if the opposition doesn’t have vertical threats or separators. The 49ers will have to find the soft spots in the zone and protect up front to beat Seattle through the air on Sunday, but running the football will loosen the depth of the linebackers and safeties.
author: Jason Aponte

title: 49ers-Seahawks: 3 major differences from last year’s roster
summary: The San Francisco 49ers faced the Seattle Seahawks three times in 2025. Kyle Shanahan’s offense had 30 drives against Mike MacDonald’s defense. They scored two touchdowns. In the first matchup, Ricky Pearsall had over 100 receiving yards, while Zach Charbonnet led Seattle in rushing. Neither player will be in uniform this Sunday. In the second […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers faced the Seattle Seahawks three times in 2025. Kyle Shanahan’s offense had 30 drives against Mike MacDonald’s defense. They scored two touchdowns. In the first matchup, Ricky Pearsall had over 100 receiving yards, while Zach Charbonnet led Seattle in rushing. Neither player will be in uniform this Sunday. In the second matchup, the 49ers’ leading receiver was Jauan Jennings. Cornerback Riq Woolen had a pass breakup. Those two are on different teams. In the playoff matchup, Kenneth Walker ran for 116 yards, while Jake Tonges had a team-high in receiving for the Niners. Walker is with the Chiefs, while Tonges is on the injured reserve. Having a WR1 like Mike Evans Even in that Week 1 matchup, 45 of Pearsall’s 108 yards came on one play. Christian McCaffrey and Kyle Juszczyk each had 25-yard receptions. For the most part, the passing attack was held in check because, as they showed in the next two games, no wideout could consistently get open. Mike Evans is seventh in the NFL in EPA per target and fifth in targeted success percentage. He’s what a true WR1 looks like. The only reason he’s seventh in Sumer Sports’ impact plays metric is because he’s only been targeted 24 times. For reference, the six receivers ahead of Evans have at least 39 targets. Kyle Shanahan moves Evans around the formation enough that defenses can’t key in on him. That has led to incredible efficiency. Of Evans’ 17 receptions, 14 have resulted in either a first down or a touchdown. The struggles against Seattle are why you go out and get a receiver of Evans’ caliber. In Week 18, the 49ers wide receivers were Jauan Jennings, Kendrick Bourne, Demarcus Robinson, and Skyy Moore. It’s a completely different group this time around. There’s speed around Evans, which has opened things up and allowed the 49ers to stretch the field both vertically and horizontally. Evans isn’t catching intermediate passes with Bourne or Jennings on the field, because teams like Seattle aren’t threatened deep. Brock Purdy will also have George Kittle and Deebo Samuel, two players who weren’t available in the playoffs. A little better at linebacker In those final two matchups, the 49ers started two players who had signed to the roster as recently as Thanksgiving, plus Dee Winters. The fact that the Niners were so eager to move on from Winters this offseason, despite his rookie contract, tells us how they felt about him internally. Raheem Morris views Garret Wallow as a nickel linebacker, while Kendricks is 34. There were plays where Seattle ran to the outside, and Kendricks, understandably, was a step slow. Wallow would get swallowed up, while Winters’ best work came on plays right at him or in coverage. Quietly, the 49ers have been one of the best teams at defending outside zone — the Seahawks run some variation outside of the tackles 60% of the time. The Niners have allowed 3.7 yards per play on outside zone runs, with a -0.045 EPA per play. On 16 attempts, they’ve had nine defensive stops. It’s been a mix-and-match of players on the edge. They’ve done their jobs, but Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw are winning the foot race when running backs try to beat them to the sideline. In Week 18, Tatum Bethune and Winters combined for three missed tackles. Seattle torched Bethune in coverage, to the tune of 64 yards. Bethune allowed six of his seven targets to be completed. Wallow got lost on one play in coverage, leading to a critical first down. It goes without saying that Warner will impact where Sam Darnold throws the ball. If he targets Warner seven times, Raheem Morris will take that all day. The upgrade at linebacker cannot be undersold heading into this matchup. Interior pressure + an edge presence Yetur Gross-Matos was the only player to generate interior pressure against the Seahawks during the regular season. In those three games, five defensive tackles recorded seven run stops and five missed tackles. Let’s look at the past two games this season, since those are the defensive tackles who will play this week for the 49ers. Osa Odighizuwa has eight pressures. Gracen Halton and Sebastian Valdez have five impact plays. Naquan Jones has a couple of run stops and is holding his ground. The four defensive tackles on the field this year are all upgrades from last year. One of the most impressive areas from Week 3 was seeing the edge players play the run. Matt Judon played one snap, and it looked great. Romello Height is wiry strong, while Keion White has been a pleasant surprise. The edge presence who didn’t play in the final two games is Mykel Williams. The 49ers’ run defense allowed a half-yard-per-play more with Mykel off the field last season. The first-down rate and EPA per play were marginally better. What you can’t quantify is having a player his size going up against tight ends. Those are wins for Williams. Or having Mykel take on pulling blockers instead of your designated pass rushers, like Height. Even if Williams plays only 30 snaps, you get to keep Height, Okoronkwo, and Khalid Kareem fresh. The domino effect of getting a first-rounder back has immense benefits for the Niners’ defense.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 quarter season takeaways for the 49ers: How the Niners are putting it all together so far
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are just about a quarter of the way into the season, and they’re undefeated so far, starting off 4-0 with wins over the Los Angeles Rams, Miami Dolphins, Arizona Cardinals, and Denver Broncos. Through four games, the 49ers have been exceptional offensively, ranking first by a wide margin in EPA/play, while […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers calls a play in the huddle in the second quarter against the Denver Broncos at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are just about a quarter of the way into the season, and they’re undefeated so far, starting off 4-0 with wins over the Los Angeles Rams, Miami Dolphins, Arizona Cardinals, and Denver Broncos. Through four games, the 49ers have been exceptional offensively, ranking first by a wide margin in EPA/play, while coming together strongly defensively, all while dealing with a large number of injuries. Still, they’ve beaten two contenders, while establishing themselves as a real threat in the NFL behind MVP-level play from Brock Purdy. So, through four weeks, let’s look at five quarter-season takeaways for the 49ers. Brock Purdy excelling in several key categories The Brock Purdy train has taken off, as the quarterback is currently the odds-on favorite to win MVP, being No. 1 on NFL.com’s MVP Ladder through four weeks. He’s played extremely well thus far, including in a performance against the Denver Broncos where he still played quite well despite it being his “worst” game of the season. Purdy kept the ball out of harm’s way, took what the defense gave him, and still threw for 218 yards, two touchdowns, and no interceptions. Through four weeks, Purdy is the clear leader in EPA per play and success rate at quarterback. He’s No. 1 in QBR. And he is also leveling up in key moments. Breaking it down by quarter, Purdy is the NFL’s top quarterback in EPA per play in both the third and fourth quarter, while ranking third in the NFL in the first quarter. Purdy is also pushing the ball downfield, ranking first in yards per attempt, while completing nearly 70 percent of his passes and ranking fourth in completion rate over expected. One category really caught my eye, though: Purdy’s excellence against the blitz. Thus far, when blitzed, Purdy has completed 27 of 35 passes for 427 yards and seven touchdowns when blitzed, while not being sacked once on 11 pressures. He’s been the NFL’s best quarterback against the blitz and has seen the field very well, not making any turnover-worthy plays, which have been the issue in years past. In 2025, Purdy’s completion rate dropped to 62.6 percent, and he had six of his 13 interceptions when blitzed, despite being blitzed on just 26.6 percent of his dropbacks. This year, he’s being blitzed at a 31.5 percent rate, and playing even better. The story is simple: Purdy is making the plays while not taking any negative plays, regardless of situation. The 49ers run game has a foundation The Niners’ run game was an issue in 2025. They ranked 29th in EPA per rush and 24th in rushing success rate, as the explosives just weren’t there on the ground. This season, the 49ers are 10th in EPA per rush and eighth in rushing success rate. Thus far, the 49ers are averaging 4.8 yards per carry, seventh in the league, while getting to 137.3 rushing yards per game, a top-six mark in the NFL. That’s happened while Christian McCaffrey has averaged just 4.4 yards per carry and Kaelon Black has averaged 3.9 yards per carry, thanks to the wrinkles in the run game with Deebo Samuel and Brock Purdy’s ability to extend plays with his legs. More importantly, the 49ers run game seems to have built a foundation again. San Francisco’s offensive line has done a really good job over four weeks of keeping Brock Purdy up and limiting the pressure from opposing defenses. But they’ve also paved the way in the run game. San Francisco ranks fifth in yards before contact per rush (1.93 yards), and they’re also not getting negative plays in the run game, which was an issue last year. Instead, the 49ers also rank sixth in percentage of runs with zero or negative yards before contact at 37.2 percent. So, they’re avoiding negative plays and averaging nearly five yards per tote. The explosives still need to come. Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black also rank 24th and 45th, respectively, in yards after contact. But the 49ers are doing better on the ground and have a foundation there this year. Limiting explosive plays The 49ers have been the best team in the NFL at limiting explosive plays this season. In fact, their 3.5 percent explosive play rate allowed is the best of any team through four games since 2000. And that’s with a banged-up defensive line. Raheem Morris has been exactly what the 49ers needed, and I’m slowly starting to compare him to DeMeco Ryans back during that monster 2022 defensive campaign. The 49ers are the No. 5 team defensively in DVOA, which, matched with the No. 1 rank on offense, has created a clear-cut contender. Now, the 49ers are 26th in pressure rate, but part of that is attributed to teams looking to get the ball out quickly. Subsequently, they’re sixth in ESPN’s pass rush win rate, and it helps to limit explosive plays when linebackers Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw fly to the ball. I’ve been impressed with how Morris has created pressure with his personnel up front on the defensive line, but also with how the 49ers have played coverage through four weeks. After struggling last season at times, the 49ers secondary has looked the part in a big way so far. That includes growth from safeties Marques Sigle and Malik Mustapha, as well as from Renardo Green and the newcomer Jack Jones, who have all played roles in the secondary so far. Overall, you’re starting to see a defense gel in a new scheme, and this unit should only get better with healthy players. It’s been a very promising start to the 49ers season.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: Brock Purdy atop MVP leaderboard through four weeks
summary: It’s been only four weeks, but San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy has been playing the best football of his career so far here in 2026. Through four games, Purdy has thrown for 1,007 yards, 11 touchdowns, and only one interception, while completing nearly 70 percent of his passes and averaging 8.9 yards per attempt. […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers throws a pass against the Denver Broncos in the third quarter at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been only four weeks, but San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy has been playing the best football of his career so far here in 2026. Through four games, Purdy has thrown for 1,007 yards, 11 touchdowns, and only one interception, while completing nearly 70 percent of his passes and averaging 8.9 yards per attempt. While the 49ers receiving core has been hit with a flurry of injuries, Purdy hasn’t lost a step, leading this team to a 4-0 start as he’s done a good job of taking what the defense has given him. His main issue coming into the year was turnovers and some poor decisions that could overshadow a quality game. Well, he’s got just one interception this year, coming back in Week 1, and has continued to find ways to extend plays behind a strong offensive line. That’s why it’s not a surprise that Purdy sits atop the leaderboard of the MVP race through four weeks in NFL.com’s MVP tracker. “Purdy is on fire to open the season, and the catalyst for the 49ers’ 4-0 start,” NFL.com’s Kevin Patra wrote. “Playing pristine in Kyle Shanahan’s system, Purdy’s performance is a culmination of time on task, innate deft touch, exemplary pocket manipulation and heady playmaking. Each week he seems to drop a dime that makes me yelp and wonder how in heaven the ball got through to its target. “Through four games, Purdy is tied for the league lead with 11 touchdown passes and has allowed a banged-up 49ers offense to continue operating at a high level without a trove of assets. Sure, he still has Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle to lean on, but the receiver corps has been decimated, including Mike Evans clearly playing through a painful rib issue. Lesser QBs have crumbled. Carrying a club through injury is MVP pixie dust.” While Purdy didn’t have the biggest stat line against the Broncos on Sunday, he didn’t hurt his MVP case, and remains sack-free through four weeks while avoiding negative plays. “Sunday’s outing against Denver wasn’t his best of the year, but did little to take the shine off. Purdy still hasn’t been sacked this season,“ Patra continued. ”If we’re willing to say sacks are a QB stat when blaming players who take them in droves, we should credit Purdy’s uncanny ability to shake free and avoid negative plays. Avoiding disaster has been a Purdy specialty through four weeks. He’s thrown two touchdowns without an interception for the third straight week. He also became the first 49ers QB to start the season with multiple touchdowns in each of the first four games since Steve Young in 1998 (seven straight), per NFL Research. “Purdy has used keen accuracy to blow away the rest of the QBs through the start of the season. He’s No. 1 in passer rating (126.2), QBR (89.6) and net yards per attempt (8.9). His EPA per dropback of 0.53 is by far the top ( Lamar Jackson is No. 2 at 0.29), and his success rate of 60.7% is best among QBs with at least 100 dropbacks. There is nary an advanced stat Purdy isn’t dominating right now. Knock his opponents if you must, and yes, there could be a clunker coming, in which he splashes a couple of interceptions on high passes over the middle, but entering Week 5, no one is playing the position at Purdy’s level in 2026.” That final sentence has been echoed by a few national reporters this season. Purdy has been playing on a different level than his peers, as he’s pushed the ball downfield, been accurate, carried his offense, and avoided negative plays. Behind him on the MVP leaderboard are Josh Allen, Kenneth Walker III, Trevor Lawrence, and Jaxon Smith-Njigba to round out the top five. It’s only a quarter of the season in. But Brock Purdy has been playing at a very high level, and people are taking notice.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

summary: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers released their final injury report Wednesday ahead of Thursday night’s matchup against the Dallas Cowboys, and they will once again be without several key players. Quarterback Baker Mayfield, safety Antoine Winfield Jr., cornerback Benjamin Morrison and linebacker SirVocea Dennis have all been ruled out for the Week 5 matchup. Mayfield continues […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - SEPTEMBER 20: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Linebacker Rueben Bain Jr. (3) rushes t he passer during the regular season game between the Cleveland Browns and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on September 20, 2026 at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida.(Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Tampa Bay Buccaneers released their final injury report Wednesday ahead of Thursday night’s matchup against the Dallas Cowboys, and they will once again be without several key players. Quarterback Baker Mayfield, safety Antoine Winfield Jr., cornerback Benjamin Morrison and linebacker SirVocea Dennis have all been ruled out for the Week 5 matchup. Mayfield continues to recover from his injured right thumb, while Winfield will begin what is expected to be a two-to-four week absence due to a slight rib fracture suffered against Green Bay. There was some encouraging news for Tampa Bay. Rookie outside linebacker Rueben Bain Jr. was a full participant throughout the week and carries no game designation, putting him in line to return Thursday night. Kicker Chase McLaughlin was also a full participant Wednesday after missing Tuesday’s walkthrough with a right groin/hip injury. Tight end Ko Kieft and linebacker Josiah Trotter were full participants Wednesday, while outside linebacker Anthony Nelson remained limited with an illness but was not given a game designation. title: Where is TE Gunnar Helm in this Titans offense?
summary: Tennessee Titans fans entered the 2026 season believing sophomore tight end Gunnar Helm would play a big role in the offense. Fast forward through Week 4 and that hasn’t been the case. Let’s examine Helm’s early involvement in Brian Daboll’s offense. Helm ranks third on the Titans in receptions, but has just nine catches. The […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Gunnar Helm #84 of the Tennessee Titans runs out prior to an NFL football game against the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tennessee Titans fans entered the 2026 season believing sophomore tight end Gunnar Helm would play a big role in the offense. Fast forward through Week 4 and that hasn’t been the case. Let’s examine Helm’s early involvement in Brian Daboll’s offense. Helm ranks third on the Titans in receptions, but has just nine catches. The former Texas standout is also third in targets (12), but ranks fourth in receiving yards (60). Rookie Carnell Tate has essentially dominated all air-yardage opportunities, especially after his breakout performance in Week 4 further skewed the numbers. Helm has not scored a touchdown, but was on the receiving end of Cam Ward’s two-point conversion on Sunday. Helm has surprisingly not seen a single red-zone target. In fairness, the Titans have consistently run the football, even stubbornly, once inside the 20-yard line. Extrapolating Helm’s current production into a 17-game sample size, he’s currently on track for fewer receptions, yards, and touchdowns than he accumulated as a rookie in 2025. He was productive last campaign, catching 44 balls for 357 yards and two scores. Even his yards per reception (6.7) is down (8.1). The Titans signed veteran tight end Daniel Bellinger to a three-year, $24 million contract in free agency. His annual $8 million price tag suggested he might eat into Helm’s workload, but that hasn’t necessarily been the case. Helm has outsnapped Bellinger 179-85. Helm has been on the field for 78.85% of the offense’s snaps. That’s a noticeably bigger workload than his rookie season included (50.47%). Yet his production is way down. The Titans appear hellbent on using Helm as a blocker more frequently than they did last season. That’s confusing, because he’s a better pass catcher, and the presumption was Bellinger was signed to primarily handle in-line blocking duties. PFF has Helm with 67 run-blocking snaps, compared to Bellinger’s 49. The ball isn’t finding Helm enough in the passing game. Coach Daboll could also make personnel-related changes to how Helm is being deployed. The Titans’ inconsistencies on offense and time of possession issues surely haven’t helped, but Daboll hasn’t put Helm in the best imaginable positions to be successful yet.

title: Commanders QB Jayden Daniels working to ‘embrace the brace’
summary: Jayden Daniels was presented with a hypothetical situation during his Wednesday press conference.   Let’s say it’s third-and-8, respected Athletic reporter David Aldridge said, and the first-down marker is in clear and unobstructed view.   What do you do? How hard do you charge? Is the left elbow injury now protected by a big brace […]
full_text: Jayden Daniels was presented with a hypothetical situation during his Wednesday press conference. Let’s say it’s third-and-8, respected Athletic reporter David Aldridge said, and the first-down marker is in clear and unobstructed view. What do you do? How hard do you charge? Is the left elbow injury now protected by a big brace going to impact what you do? Daniels answered the question with a question. “Is it the fourth quarter?” “Sure,” Alridge responded. “Let’s say it is.” Daniels responded in typical JD5 fashion. “I mean, we have to do something to win, right?” That’s the conundrum Daniels will face as he returns to action following a Week 2 elbow dislocation that was a repeat of the one that ended his 2025 season early. Following that Week 2 injury in Dallas, Daniels traveled from coast to coast seeing specialists and getting medical opinions of what he should do next. He decided against surgery (during the season, at least) and to, instead, wear a protective element — a brace — over his elbow to help prevent another dislocation. Daniels practiced in a limited capacity during Week 4 and was a full participant on Wednesday with the expectation that he’ll play on Sunday against the New York Giants. On Wednesday, he was asked repeatedly about, and talked a ton about, getting used to the brace and his steadfast decision to play on and return quickly despite the injury. “I went through the process and it wasn’t the end of everything,” Daniels told on-site reporters during his weekly press conference, referring to his 2025 injury. “I was blessed enough to still be allowed to play this game. I’m just going to go out there and embrace it. I’m going to embrace the brace. I’m not really worried too much about it. I’m going to be the best version of myself.” The best version of Daniels is the 25-year-old playing free and having fun, with a style that’s productive and super fun to watch. He believes he can do all that despite the extra hardware, considering it’s his non-dominant hand. “It’s my non-throwing arm,” Daniels said with a smile, “So as long as I’ve got the right one, I think I’ll be all right.” Daniels was coy about the fact he’s not quite sure how he’ll react in a game, whether he’ll take it a little bit easier or whether he’ll end up going full throttle in the heat of the moment. He knows that the elbow brace is part of his playing existence now and it’s something he’ll have to handle. “I’m trying to get used to it,” Daniels said. “It’s a part of me for the time being, so I’m getting a feel for it and finding ways where it’s most comfortable and where I’m able to just go play.”

title: Dan Quinn: Marcus Mariota’s return expected sooner than later, no need for IR
summary: The Washington Commanders are home from their international game in London against the Indianapolis Colts. They lost the game, and injuries to Marcus Mariota (MCL) and Jaylin Lane (ankle/IR) deflated the team. Dan Quinn has said they plan on having Jayden Daniels back as a full participant with the expectation he can start this week […]
full_text: The Washington Commanders are home from their international game in London against the Indianapolis Colts. They lost the game, and injuries to Marcus Mariota (MCL) and Jaylin Lane (ankle/IR) deflated the team. Dan Quinn has said they plan on having Jayden Daniels back as a full participant with the expectation he can start this week at home vs the Giants. Daniels will be wearing a brace when he plays, and Quinn said they’ve talked about protecting the elbow. He traveled with the team and was limited in practice last week, but wanted to play. Marcus Mariota’s MCL sprain is expected to follow the same timeline as the one that sidelined him in the preseason. Quinn said they are hopeful he can return after missing next week, and then having the bye before the team returns in Week 8 for a home game rematch against the Philadelphia Eagles. The team didn’t place Mariota on injured reserve which would have kept him out for four games. Washington had QB Jack Plummer in for a workout, but seems confident in Jayden Daniels and Athan Kaliakmanis being available this week. The Commanders announced that three players who have been on injured reserve for the first four games have returned to practice, and their 21-day windows have opened. CB Trey Amos (ankle), DE Deatrich Wise (quad), and RB Jeremy McNichols (quad) will have their individual recovery plans as they return to the field. Quinn was asked about a return timeline for Amos, and he noted he has only practiced once since breaking his leg as a rookie. Quinn was asked about struggling players like CB Mike Sainristil and C/G Nick Allegretti having reduced roles and getting less snaps. He said they’re working on the best scenarios for each player and they would make moves to improve the team. He mentioned Allegretti missing time in training camp, and other injuries that have limited him as he moved to center. title: Trey Amos among three Washington Commanders opening practice windows
summary: Commanders reinforcements are starting to come in. Washington made those announcements on Wednesday afternoon. Wise (quad) is on the physically unable to perform list while Amos (ankle) […]
full_text: Commanders reinforcements are starting to come in. Cornerback Trey Amos, defensive lineman Deatrich Wise Jr. and running back Jeremy McNichols have had their 21-day practice window opened to return off of PUP and injured reserve. Washington made those announcements on Wednesday afternoon. Wise (quad) is on the physically unable to perform list while Amos (ankle) and McNichols (quad) are on injured reserve with a designation to return that was made way back when the original 53-man roster was formed. This is a positive development for the Commanders, who need reinforcements at all of those positions. Head coach Dan Quinn hasn’t said when those guys will be available for activation to the 53-man roster, but there is a maximum window of 21 days for activation, and it will probably take some time before we see any of those players get activated, especially considering how long it has been since any of them has practiced. Eyes will certainly be on Amos, considering how the cornerback corps has struggled, but the second-year pro has practiced just once since suffering a fractured fibula during the 2025 season. He incurred an ankle issue during that early August practice, which was a giant setback at the time. Amos is probably the team’s most talented cornerback, and he will be welcomed back with open arms when and if he’s ready for to return from IR. Under NFL rules, players returning to play from PUP or IR have 21 days to work their way to a point where they can be activated off of their respective lists. If a player is not activated by the end of that 21-day period, he reverts to IR/PUP, and is ineligible to play for the team for the remainder of the season.

Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Sonny Styles vs Colts [The video of the play described in the excerpt below is embedded in the tweet that is also pasted below] Despite the Commanders suffering another disappointing loss and falling to a 1-3 record, there were some positives to take out of this game. One of the biggest positives, in my opinion, was the play of rookie linebacker Sonny Styles. Styles has been playing well all season, winning NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his performance against the Seahawks [the week before]. He made some flash plays against the Eagles a few weeks prior too, and his coverage ability has already stood out as one of the best coverage linebackers in the NFL. But against the Colts, we saw a step forward from Styles in another area of his game. Styles is an incredible athletic and is terrific in coverage, but he’s still fairly fresh to the linebacker position, having transitioned from safety to linebacker in college a few years ago. So while he’s been fine in the run game, there has certainly been some room for growth in his first three performances. In this game though, we saw what was comfortably the best performance we’ve seen from Styles against the run. So let’s break it down to see why he was so good. Commanders rookie LB Sonny Styles had another impressive performance on Sunday. It was perhaps his best outing against the run so far. I broke it all down: https://t.co/AzV7Q767u5 pic.twitter.com/uh8OwqgWKh — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) October 7, 2026 This time the Colts run a gap scheme inside with the fullback kicking out the edge and the tight end working up to block Styles inside. Styles reads the run quickly and you can see how compared to Luvu, he’s the quicker linebacker to read the run and react. He identifies the tight end working up to him and closes the gap, using his momentum to get into the chest of the block and stack him up. Styles arrives at the block with a thump, landing both hands on the blockers chest and standing him up. From there, Styles has control of the block. He looks into the backfield and sees running back Jonathan Taylor cutting his run outside, so Styles works off the block and reaches out with one arm to make the stop for a one yard gain. Perhaps his most impressive play against the run came later on in the game in the second half. Commanders.com Kaliakmanis’ NFL debut contained plenty of lessons Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo didn’t make life easy on Kaliakmanis. He didn’t blitz the quarterback an excessive amount — per Pro Football Reference, Kaliakmanis was pressured on only 20% of his dropbacks — but he did choose moments in which Kaliakmanis needed to make a play. Most of the pressure came off the edge and led to a sack on third-and-9 that knocked the Commanders out of field goal range. Other times, Kaliakmanis got the ball out but was punished for it with hard hits on his release. But plays were open downfield thanks to that pressure, and Kaliakmanis started letting the ball fly in the second half. He tied with C.J. Stroud for the highest average depth of target at 14.1 yards and had six passes of at least 30 yards — the most for a quarterback in a single game so far this season. Two of those passes found their mark — a 48-yarder to Dyami Brown and a 47-yarder to Treylon Burks that resulted in his first career touchdown pass. The current expectation is that Kaliakmanis will not be under center for the first snap against the New York Giants this coming weekend. Daniels is expected to have a full week of practice, and if everything goes well, he will start and try to get his team one game closer to .500. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Do Commanders need to look outside the organization for a short-term veteran backup QB? Kaliakmanis will be available to stabilize the room in week five with the hope that Daniels anchors the room once more, yet given the Commanders have already watched its starting quarterback go down in two of the first four games in 2026, whether an addition needs to be made is the question. The irony? A familiar name looms as an available option given 33 year old Jeff Driskel, who also joined the Commanders’ practice squad to close last season, is an available name. Jimmy Garoppolo and Brandon Allen are two others who remain available, albeit both have limited experience over the last two seasons to add a question whether they would serve as viable stopgaps. Could Washington pull a page from last season’s book and sign someone off another team’s practice squad? Josh Johnson, who started the final two games of last season, is on the Bengals’ practice squad to serve as a low risk move. The upside is unlike Washington, the question isn’t about finding an answer atop the unit, rather ensuring depth is in place as offensive coordinator David Blough looks to find consistency [in the 2 games] ahead of the bye week.
