title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why you should use Texans, Cowboys
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and picks for Week 5 including the Texans and Cowboys.
full_text:
After the most-selected team in ESPN Survivor fell in each of the first three weeks, Week 4 knocked out only 11% of ESPN Survivor entries. The Buffalo Bills became the fifth 7-point favorite to fall this season, but just 6% of entries chose them.

 As expected, the Baltimore Ravens and Minnesota Vikings combined for 70% of the entries, but both teams won without a major sweat. Lamar Jackson 's injury complicates the Ravens' value going forward.

 Week 5 is fascinating because all the biggest favorites have barely been used, and most of them aren't among the top Super Bowl contenders. The Dallas Cowboys , Cincinnati Bengals and Houston Texans are all at least 7-point favorites, and all are available to at least 97% of entries.

 

 The Cowboys are the biggest favorites and, not surprisingly, they are the most popular pick. However, Dallas has much more future value than the Bengals and Texans. In addition to the Titans game in Week 11, the Cowboys still have home games against the New York Giants and Arizona Cardinals . That Cardinals game happens the same week the Bengals host the Tennessee Titans , so Survivor entrants may have the same decision between Cincinnati and Dallas in three weeks.

 The Texans get the Titans on the road this week, but the return matchup isn't until Week 18. However, the Texans also project to be one of the biggest favorites in two weeks when they host the Giants. Of course, Houston is 0-4, but the Texans must be motivated to beat one of the worst teams in the NFL, right?

 The other big favorites are the Jacksonville Jaguars in London against the struggling Philadelphia Eagles . However, they have the most future value remaining in the NFL according to my model, with two games against the Titans, home games against the Indianapolis Colts , Pittsburgh Steelers and Washington Commanders , plus a road game against the Giants.

 There are a few other options down the board, including the Detroit Lions visiting the Cardinals. But they also host the Titans and Giants, plus they also have a road game in Miami in Week 9.

 If your main goal is to preserve future value, particularly in double-pick contests like on Splash, this is likely the best spot all season to use the Commanders. The Atlanta Falcons surprisingly could mix in, as they are up to 3.5-point favorites against the Ravens due to Jackson's injury. 

 

 However, in ESPN contests, the Texans seem like the clear choice. If they are going to be significantly less selected than the Cowboys and Bengals, I will take that discount. It's slightly lower win equity, but you gain leverage against the Cowboys and Bengals entries while gaining future flexibility.

 The Bengals-Cowboys choice comes down to the injury reports for the Bengals. While they should be able to beat Miami without them, I would be much more comfortable if Ja'Marr Chase or Tee Higgins suited up on Sunday. Monitor injury reports, since you will need to make your choice by Thursday.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 1. Houston Texans (at Titans) 

 

 Taking an 0-4 team in Survivor sounds crazy, but this is not your typical 0-4 team. The Texans are the largest favorites for any team with an 0-3 or worse record in the Super Bowl era. They have played the fourth-toughest schedule in the NFL so far according to ESPN Analytics. And we've seen the Texans start slow and get hot. They were 0-2 in 2023 and 0-3 last season and made the playoffs both seasons. The Titans have been the best team to fade in Survivor over the past three seasons. They haven't beaten the Texans at home since 2020, while Cam Ward 's offense managed 13 points combined in two meetings last season. Just keep in mind in Circa Survivor that the Texans play on Christmas Eve in Philadelphia, a game which looks a lot easier now than it did a month ago.

 
 Chance to win: 66% (ESPN Analytics), 61% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Texans -7.5 (-375 moneyline) 
 Future value: 17th 
 Availability: 100% 
 ESPN Selection: 13% 
 

 2. Dallas Cowboys (vs. Buccaneers) 

 

 With the Commanders struggling, the Giants playing a backup quarterback and the Eagles falling well short of expectations, the Cowboys' future value has risen significantly. As a result, I lean towards saving them for later, especially with the Texans and Bengals looking like strong options. However, if you are simply looking for the team with the highest win probability, Dallas is probably the answer. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are 0-13 against the spread in their past 13 games, so betting models have been struggling to catch up to how bad Tampa Bay has been for almost two seasons now.

 
 Chance to win: 86% (ESPN Analytics), 83% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Cowboys -8.5 (-455 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fifth 
 Availability: 98% 
 ESPN Selection: 33% 
 

 3. Cincinnati Bengals (at Dolphins) 

 This is the easiest spot all season on paper for the Bengals, though a lot of it comes down to the health of Chase and Higgins. As bad as the Dolphins have been, the one area they have been good at is against the run, where the Bengals have struggled. Joe Burrow has a tendency to drop games as a big favorite, as he is just 7-6 outright when laying at least seven points. Still, one of the top strategies in Survivor this year is to simply fade the Dolphins, and even if Chase and Higgins are out, the Bengals are a top-three option for me.

 
 Chance to win: 80% (ESPN Analytics), 83% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Bengals -7 (-355 moneyline) 
 Future value: Eighth 
 Availability: 97% 
 ESPN Selection: 35% 
 

 4. Washington Commanders (vs. Giants) 

 

 The Commanders are only an option in the largest pools, especially ones with double-pick weeks. In pools where you need to pick 24 or more teams, you will need to pick some ugly teams. The Commanders are in their largest favorite role all season on paper, and they are 4-0 against the Giants under Dan Quinn. Obviously this is risky, but if you are able to sneak through with a win, you will have one of the more valuable remaining entries in big contests.

 
 Chance to win: 63% (ESPN Analytics), 56% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Commanders -3.5 (-175 moneyline) 
 Future value: 26th 
 Availability: 100% 
 ESPN Selection: 0.2% 
 

 5. Atlanta Falcons (vs Ravens) 

 Not too long ago, the Ravens would have been a possibility in Week 5 Survivor. But after Jackson's injury and back-to-back Falcons blowout road wins, Atlanta is now very live. The Falcons have one of the toughest remaining schedules in the NFL after this week, and unless they truly are a top-15 team like they've shown the last few weeks, you probably don't have another good chance to use them until late December. The Falcons are a logical contrarian pick, but among the smaller favorites, I lean Washington, just because I have more faith in Atlanta being a team you want to have later in the year.

 
 Chance to win: 48% (ESPN Analytics), 46% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Falcons -3.5 (-185 moneyline) 
 Future value: 21st 
 Availability: 99% 
 ESPN Selection: 0.2% 
 

 6. Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Eagles) 

 The Jaguars are big favorites, but they are not a strong consideration this week. They rank first in future value the rest of the season, with several easier games coming up. While they will be lesser selected, they have already been used by nearly 32% of entries, so you will have other opportunities to use them in better spots. Plus, the Eagles are 6-1 outright as underdogs over the past three seasons including the playoffs.

 
 Chance to win: 73% (ESPN Analytics), 80% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Jaguars -7 (-325 moneyline) 
 Future value: First 
 Availability: 68% 
 ESPN Selection: 1% 
 

 The Road to 18-0 
 
 Week 1: Jaguars (vs. Browns) - Win 
 Week 2: 49ers (vs. Dolphins) - Win 
 Week 3: Chiefs (at Dolphins) - Win 
 Week 4: Vikings (vs. Dolphins) - Win

title: NFL Week 5 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we're hearing
summary: Could injuries to Saquon Barkley, Lamar Jackson and others derail their teams? Which AFC teams should trade for a WR? Which coordinators could get head coach interest?
full_text:
It's already Week 5 of the  2026 NFL season ! Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 Injuries are starting to pile up as we hit the quarter mark of the season, and a few important players went down Sunday, including Lamar Jackson , Pat Surtain II , Ja'Marr Chase and Saquon Barkley . Which teams could be in trouble if they have to go without one of their stars? And which teams might have to make a trade sooner rather than later to either replace an injured player or quickly fix a weak spot in the roster? The trade deadline is approaching fast -- it is under five weeks out.

 Coaches are also under the microscope with four weeks of games behind us. Are any seats warming around the league? And have any coordinators shown enough in the early going to put themselves on the radar for head coach interviews if they keep this up? It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 5.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Key injuries | Teams needing a trade 
 Warming seats | Rising coordinators 
 Fantasy football advice 
 More notes, intel 

 
 

 Which player's Week 4 injury could be most detrimental to his team? 
 Graziano: Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson is the obvious answer if he has to miss time (which we don't know for sure yet). They're just so different without him. Having him on the field makes things easier for running back Derrick Henry , whereas defenses can lock in on Henry when they don't have to fear the QB run.

 Fowler: Can't understate that one. The Ravens are hopeful he won't miss time, but this week feels uncertain. I'll go with Broncos corner Pat Surtain II , who is set to miss multiple weeks with an ankle injury . With Denver's offense struggling to consistently score points, it needs the defense to reestablish its dominant form. But after ripping through the league with 68 sacks last season, the Broncos have eight through four games ... which heightens the importance of having a former Defensive Player of the Year such as Surtain in the secondary. Normally I would go with the star quarterback who's hurt, but Surtain's absence could have a sizable ripple effect for a team on the ropes.

 Graziano: A Saquon Barkley absence could exacerbate the Eagles' problems. I know Barkley isn't having the best season, but the Philadelphia offense is getting really low on good players. It had to play Sunday without right tackle Lane Johnson (who has since retired ), top wide receiver  DeVonta Smith  and, other than the first four plays, Barkley. It's a thin group around Jalen Hurts right now, and even at full strength it was trying to figure out a new offense under a first-time playcaller. If the Eagles are going to pull out of this, they're going to need as many of their stars as close to full strength as possible.

 

 Fowler: Yeah, the Eagles are depleted in the short term, and their healthiest back right now is third-stringer Will Shipley . Hamstring injuries linger, and unfortunately for Philly, their top two playmakers are managing them . Plus, tight end Dallas Goedert has missed two weeks and guard Cam Jurgens is in concussion protocol  (Update: Jurgens was traded to Baltimore on Wednesday). The Eagles could use reinforcements, so it might be worth it for them to explore the trade or free agency market for depth.

 An underrated absence is that of Vikings guard Donovan Jackson , who is undergoing season-ending knee surgery . He's a good player, which Minnesota can't afford to lose, particularly on an offense that ranks 31st in total yards. Either Joe Huber , who went undrafted in 2025, assumes the starting job, or Minnesota adds to the roster in short order.

 

 
 Which team most needs to make a trade -- and at what position? 
 Fowler: The Lions should make a move for a cornerback. They were in on Joey Porter Jr . before Pittsburgh traded him to Dallas . Detroit's secondary is swimming right now, and though safety Brian Branch is close to a return and safety Kerby Joseph should eventually be back, the Lions don't have enough corner help to run the coverages they want. This team has elite players on both sides of the ball and must embrace its window of contention, whether it's slipping away or not.

 One potential option is Kansas City's Kristian Fulton , who is in and out of the Chiefs' lineup. He is owed real money -- $5 million of his $9.75 million base salary is guaranteed -- but perhaps the Chiefs and Lions could split the bill to facilitate a deal. Is it worth calling Pittsburgh for Jalen Ramsey ? Not sure he's available, but the Lions' defense seems far from settled.

 Graziano: Stop me if you've heard this before, but the Chiefs could use another wide receiver . I'm not buying that Tyreek Hill is much of an upgrade over what they have at this point in his career. If players such as Marvin Harrison Jr ., Brian Thomas Jr ., Jerry Jeudy or Calvin Ridley become available, the Chiefs should poke around. But the other team I think should be turning over whatever rock it can to find wide receiver help is the team Kansas City barely beat on Sunday -- the surprising 3-1 Raiders.

 

 Before the season, who would have thought that the Raiders could be adding at the deadline? Tight end Brock Bowers is their top receiver and likely would remain so even if they did get somebody, but Las Vegas would love to have a true X receiver so teams can't put a top corner such as Surtain on Bowers.

 Fowler: Receiver is a need for the Raiders, but they've been inclined to preserve draft capital and develop their young receivers, and I'm not sure the 3-1 start changes that. Las Vegas operates in that space between rebuilding and contention, and with only five selections in April's draft, Vegas could opt to lean on second-year players  Jack Bech  and  Dont'e Thornton Jr ., who returns soon from injured reserve, to play bigger roles. Also, Bowers basically is a wide receiver, so him as the No. 1 and Tre Tucker as the No. 2 isn't a bad setup.

 Another team to watch at receiver is the Colts, who are 2-2 with Pittsburgh and Tennessee coming up. They could easily be sitting at 4-2 after those two games despite a depleted receiving crew, and Indy is not hiding from being all-in to win now. Perhaps there's not a splash move that fits, but how about one that brings an upside receiver for a quality Day 3 pick? (The Sauce Gardner trade last year drained Indy's capital.)  Marvin Harrison Jr . would be an obvious fit -- and not just for sentimentality -- but Arizona won't just give him away. A midseason return from Alec Pierce could assuage the need to make a move.

 Graziano: It's tough to swing trades for offensive linemen, since the demand massively outweighs the supply. But teams that could/should be in the market include the Patriots, Ravens, Eagles and, of course, the Packers, who have been signing dudes out of retirement the past couple of weeks because their line has completely fallen apart.

 The Bengals could use help at linebacker. The Jaguars don't need much, but I could see them looking to add another edge rusher if the opportunity presents itself. And the Bills could need some help in the secondary as they continue to transition to Jim Leonhard's defense.

 

 
 Are any coaches' seats warming a little early? 
 Graziano: Before starting, I need to stress that I am not reporting that any coach is in imminent danger of losing his job. I don't have information to suggest that teams are considering big changes at this point in the season. That said, I can't imagine you're feeling too good if you're Todd Bowles right now. The Buccaneers have lost 11 of their past 13 games dating to their 2025 bye week, when they were 6-2 and eyeing a fifth straight division title.

 The extent to which things have fallen apart for Tampa Bay, which entered 2025 thinking it was primed for a Super Bowl run, is…

title: NFL trade deadline grades: Cam Jurgens to Ravens, Joey Porter Jr. to Cowboys
summary: Will Cam Jurgens boost the Ravens' protection? Can Joey Porter Jr. clean up the Cowboys' defense? We're grading NFL trades ahead of November's deadline.
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline , which will pass on Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for the first three deals of trading season:  J.J. McCarthy  to the Giants,  Joey Porter Jr . to the Cowboys and  Cam Jurgens  to the Ravens. Check back right through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

 

 

 Eagles trade C Jurgens to Ravens 
 Ravens get: C Cam Jurgens , 2027 seventh-round pick 
 Eagles get: 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

 Ravens grade: D+ 
 Eagles grade: A

 First, Tyler Linderbaum walked in free agency . Then the Ravens lost Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic to injury , suddenly leaving them without a center. Last week, Baltimore moved first-round rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane to center but evidently doesn't see that as a long-term option.

 So Baltimore turned to the trade market and dealt for Jurgens. It's an interesting and unusual move, because Jurgens is no stopgap. He's only 27 years old and is already on a long-term deal after signing an extension with the Eagles in 2025.

 Jurgens moved from center to left guard in Week 2 after the Eagles placed guard Landon Dickerson on injured reserve . It has not gone well. Jurgens ranks in the bottom three in both pass block and run block win rate at guard. But the Ravens are trading for Jurgens to have him play center.

 In 2024, Jurgens was a Pro Bowl center who recorded pass block and run block win rates in the 80th and 50th percentiles, respectively. He made the Pro Bowl again in 2025, but his numbers slipped to the 65th and 39th percentile, respectively. He should be a stabilizing force for the Ravens -- perhaps an average to above-average center -- at what has suddenly become a position of need. But the cost is exorbitant.

 

 The Ravens are surrendering a second-round pick (plus a swap of fifth- and seventh-round picks) for the right to pay a non-premium position player market price after this season. Jurgens is due a fully guaranteed $16 million next year. He's due $17 million (non-guaranteed) in 2028 and 2029. Jurgens' $17 million average per year for the duration of his contract makes him the fourth-highest-paid center in the league, behind only Linderbaum, Creed Humphrey and Aaron Brewer , per OverTheCap.com . By comparison,  Connor McGovern , who had better numbers than Jurgens last season, makes a little over $13 million per year.

 One saving grace for Baltimore is that Jurgens' salary is cheap this season . The Eagles have already paid Jurgens' option bonus, so the Ravens should be on the hook for only the remaining portion of his $1.2 million base salary.

 For the Eagles, the loss of Jurgens is the latest blow to an offensive line that is already down Dickerson and recently retired tackle Lane Johnson . Jurgens hadn't played well at guard, but surely they saw him as their long-term center. Drew Kendall , who has played center after Jurgens' shift, has been below average in both pass and run block win rate this season. But the Eagles seemed to believe this was a price too good to pass up.

 I understand that the Ravens rightfully believe they are Super Bowl contenders, probably want Ioane to stay and develop at guard and thought they needed to fill their gap at center. Making a trade before the deadline to fix that issue makes sense. But almost certainly there would have been cheaper options out there than this. And the timing is odd, considering that Jurgens is currently in concussion protocol and not expected to play Sunday.

 So it seems like the Eagles sensed Baltimore's desperation and squeezed an overpay out of the Ravens. -- Walder 

 
 

 Steelers trade CB Porter to Cowboys 
 Cowboys get: CB Joey Porter Jr . 
 Steelers get: 2027 sixth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

 Cowboys grade: B 
 Steelers grade: C+

 This is the Cowboys' third trade with the Steelers in the past 18 months ( George Pickens  and  Broderick Jones ), and it's their third trade involving a star defensive player after acquiring Quinnen Williams at the trade deadline last season and shipping Micah Parsons to Green Bay last offseason.

 It's easy to see what the Cowboys are doing here. DaRon Bland , who first broke onto the scene as a slot corner, was playing on the outside given Dallas' lack of depth. By acquiring Porter, Bland can move back inside, which will allow the Cowboys to relocate 2026 first-round defensive back Caleb Downs , as well. He has been playing the slot, but his natural position is at safety. These are options, not guarantees. Bland might stay outside as the Cowboys instead pursue a strong 1-2 punch at outside corner, with Porter shadowing WR1s.

 The salient point is this: Porter can have a rising tide impact on the Cowboys secondary, clarifying the roles of other players and enhancing the whole unit in the process.

 Porter is not as tricky of a scheme fit in Dallas as people think, too. His strengths are certainly his length and physicality, such that he can line up in press -- but he has been in press alignments on only 30.6% of his snaps over his career, just above the league average for cornerbacks (24.1%). Porter is a much better man coverage defender than he is in zone, as his passer rating allowed in man coverage over the past four seasons is better than all but Derek Stingley Jr . But the Cowboys are actually running more man coverage (24.8%) under first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker than the league average (23.2%) over the first three weeks.

 

 Of course, early-season rate stats can be noisy. Parker's Vic Fangio-inspired defense will require Porter to play from greater depth than he did in Pittsburgh, and the communication and keys required in that match-heavy system will take some getting used to. But Porter has a valuable and rare skill set in his press-man ability, and premium picks should be spent on players with premium traits. The Cowboys got much, much better in the secondary -- though the move is not without risk.

 Acquiring Porter does not solve all their deficiencies; linebacker is still a big problem for this team, and the edge rush isn't far behind. But if the secondary needs less schematic help now that Porter is in play, more coaching tools can be used to hide those other weak spots.

 For the Steelers, Porter's recurring back ailments seemed incurable without an extension or a relocation -- what can you do? It's frustrating that GM Omar Khan invested more in third-contract players like Jalen Ramsey and T.J. Watt over a younger, second-contract player like Porter -- Ramsey and Watt will hit their athletic wall far sooner than Porter. Jamel Dean , another third-contract player signed to play corner opposite Porter, now has to cover WR1s alongside Asante Samuel Jr . and 2026 third-round pick Daylen Everette . Corner is no longer a strong position on Pittsburgh's depth chart.

 Porter reportedly had contract demands up at the top of the cornerback market, where Devon Witherspoon and Christian Gonzalez recently reset elite deals to clear $33 million annually. I'm not sold that Porter is a top-tier corner deserving of that top money. But because the Steelers let this go on for so long and bleed into the regular season, they were only able to acquire a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick for a young, ascendent cover corner. They could have -- and should have -- gotten at least a first-round pick by playing this differently and dealing Porter in the…

title: Kyle Monangai, Chuba Hubbard starred in superb week for Africa's running backs in NFL
summary: The Chicago Bears' Kyle Monangai (ties to Cameroon) and the Carolina Panthers' Chuba Hubbard (ties to Nigeria) starred in an NFL week which saw running backs with links to Africa impress.
full_text:
The Chicago Bears ' Kyle Monangai (ties to Cameroon) and the Carolina Panthers ' Chuba Hubbard (ties to Nigeria) starred in an NFL week which saw running backs with links to Africa impress.

 Monangai, Hubbard and New Orleans Saints running back Alvin Kamara (ties to Liberia) each scored two touchdowns. The Bears beat the New York Jets 23-12 and the Panthers edged the Detroit Lions 32-26, but Kamara's Saints went down 45-24 to the Atlanta Falcons .

 That game saw Nigeria's Samson Ebukam pick up a sack for the winning side, while his compatriot Basil Chijioke 'CJ' Okoye became the first NFL Africa IPP graduate to pick up a sack in a regular season game as his New York Giants beat the Arizona Cardinals 36-24.

 

 African Player of the Week - Kyle Monangai (Chicago Bears) 
 Monangai, whose parents are from Cameroon, racked up 146 yards across 30 carries in the Bears' win over the Jets at Soldier field, scoring two touchdowns.

 He is increasingly becoming an important part of the Bears offense in his second season. Having scored five touchdowns in his first season last year, Monangai now already has three this season.

 He racked up 100 yards across 10 carries and scored a superb touchdown in the 59-37 win over the Carolina Panthers in his first game of the season, in addition to 24 more yards gained across two receptions.

 This time, his four yards gained on a solitary reception took his total yards in the win over the Jets to 150.

 

 African Moment of the Week - Chuba Hubbard (Carolina Panthers) 
 Not only were Hubbard's two touchdowns in the win over the Lions vital in a game ultimately decided by a six-point margin, but both of them were easy on the eye and the second came off the back of a sensational marauding run through the Detroit defense.

 Hubbard shook off five tackles, weaving his way through the tightest of spaces in a 25-yard-run, before a sixth finally brought him down two yards from the goal line.

 To complete his Moment of the Week, Hubbard ran in for the touchdown off the very next play. It came at a crucial moment, as the extra point from Ryan Fitzgerald extended the Panthers' lead to 10 points in what proved to be the final notch on the scoreboard during the third quarter.

 The Lions did their best to claw their way back in the fourth, but largely due to the damage already done by Hubbard -- who was born in Canada to a Nigerian father and Canadian mother.

 

 Honorable mentions 
 There were several standout defensive performances by players with ties to Africa across the NFL in Week 4. However, the pick of the bunch was Foyesade Oluokun - a Jacksonville Jaguars linebacker with parental ties to Nigeria.

 Oluokun made seven tackles, one red zone interception, and one sack, as the Jags beat the Cincinnati Bengals 22-17.

 Another player of Nigerian heritage -- Seattle Seahawks safety Nick Emmanwori -- had an equally impressive game in the 30-23 win over the LA Chargers.

 Africa-born Player Watch 
 Okoye's sack for the Giants was certainly the underdog story of the week. Having come through the 2022 NFL Africa Touchdown camp and then the IPP Program, he had already shown his potential with the LA Chargers and then Baltimore Ravens , but the 24-year-old rising Nigerian star's first regular season sack was a moment to remember.

 The Giants held a slender 19-14 lead when Okoye pinned Jacoby Brissett back eight yards with around two minutes left in the first half.

 For a defensive lineman who only played his first organized football three years ago in the 2023 pre-season, it was yet another major statement of his ability - and arguably the most convincing of them all to date. He joined the Falcons' Ebukam as yet another Nigerian born player to pick up a sack in a Week 4 win.

 Meanwhile, the LA Rams' 24-20 win over the Philadelphia Eagles was a showcase of Zimbabwean brilliance.

 On the winning side, Nate Landman made 10 tackles for the Rams. However, the contribution of his Zimbabwean compatriot, Andrew Mukuba -- who also has family ties to DR Congo -- should not be overlooked. Mukuba picked up an interception for the Eagles.

 Perhaps the biggest compliment one could pay towards Africa's growing role in the NFL in recent years is that week on week, it is becoming increasingly difficult to fit the top highlights on both offense and defense into a single piece.

title: Early 2026 NFL trends for the 49ers, Vikings, Bucs, Texans, Giants, Browns
summary: Just how good are the 49ers? Are the Texans and Bucs better than their records? Are the Giants and Browns worse? We put the NFL season's first month in historical context.
full_text:
Early in every  NFL season , you hear a lot about the pace of certain stats. But most of the time when you see that a player or team is on pace to record a certain stat, you have no idea about issues for similar things in the past.

 Performance is usually going to regress toward the mean. Teams and players that started superhot will cool. Teams and players that were terrible early will get better. So we don't want to compare a team's performance after four games to what other teams have done over 16- and 17-game seasons. We want to compare that performance to what others have done in the same number of games.

 We can do that with DVOA ( defense-adjusted value over average ) stats. We've gone back and rerun every season since 1977 to see what DVOA would have looked like as of Week 4. Here, teams are rated solely based on what they did through four games (and what opponents did over that time). And every year of DVOA is normalized so that we're comparing teams to the averages of their own era, not to what teams do in today's game.

 This year, there's one team in particular playing at a historical level. You might not realize quite how good the San Francisco 49ers have been. But will their usual spate of injuries prevent them from living up to their September greatness with the franchise's sixth Super Bowl title? Let's look closer and explore three other early trends that I've noticed in the DVOA data.

 

 

 1. The 49ers are the 11th-best team overall through four games since 1977 (and have the third-best passing offense) 
 The 49ers shocked everyone when they not only beat the favored Rams in Week 1 but destroyed them. We've sort of written off that Rams performance because of the whole jetlag issue , but maybe a part of the 49ers winning was being really good?

 San Francisco has continued to win games, mostly decisively. It dominated the Dolphins in Week 2 and had a big fourth quarter to beat the Broncos in Week 4 . The Niners'  Week 3 victory over Arizona was 36-30, but a play-by-play breakdown suggests the 49ers outplayed the Cardinals by a much wider margin. They outgained the Cards 8.7 yards to 4.5 yards per play but had 31 fewer plays. The efficiency predicts future performance better than the raw number of plays.

 Put it all together, and the 49ers are No. 1 in my DVOA ratings with a historically high number. Only 10 teams since 1977 have been higher through the first four games.

 

 The 49ers' success is primarily being driven by their superb passing game, with quarterback  Brock Purdy leading the league in QBR. Sure, the 49ers rank fifth in defensive DVOA and ninth in run offense, but the passing game is historically good. Since 1977, the only teams with a better passing game through four games were the 1998 Broncos with John Elway and a shockingly strong 1999 Washington team with Brad Johnson at quarterback. Yes, Washington in 1999 scored 37.5 points per game over the first four weeks, while Johnson averaged 298 passing yards and 9.8 yards per attempt, nine touchdowns and zero interceptions.

 That puts the current 49ers slightly ahead of some all-time great passing clubs, including the "Greatest Show on Turf" Rams, the 2013 Broncos with Peyton Manning and the 1984 Dolphins with Dan Marino.

 

 What we can expect: Our first table shows that not every team that starts this hot is guaranteed to win the Super Bowl, but there are also some all-time great squads on that list. If we expanded it to 20 teams, we would add five more Super Bowl champions: 1977 Cowboys, 1985 Bears, 1990 Giants, 1998 Broncos and 2009 Saints. Overall, the previous 20 best teams by DVOA through four games won nine Super Bowls and lost three.

 The problem for the 49ers, of course, is the injury bug. San Francisco has been among the most injured teams in the league nearly every season since coach Kyle Shanahan and GM John Lynch took over. Already this season, they've been without top edge rusher Nick Bosa  ( calf ) and starting defensive tackle Alfred Collins  ( knee ). Four different wide receivers are on injured reserve, and veteran Mike Evans was limited in last week's practices with a rib injury . In fact, the 49ers are running out of space on their injured reserve list.

 It will be tough for the 49ers to maintain this type of all-time great performance as starters give way to backups ... who in turn give way to third-stringers.

 
 

 2. The Vikings are the eighth-worst 4-0 team since 2000 
 Everyone saw the 49ers dominate the Rams on national television, so their 4-0 start isn't such a surprise. Kansas City is also 4-0, and most observers expected a rebound from last year's down season.

 The Vikings (4-0) are the third undefeated team, but their record is perhaps a little more surprising. They can barely get any offense going. Three of their four wins came by a touchdown or less. And this week, they barely beat a Miami team that is widely considered the worst in the league.

 The offense-defense split for the Vikings is remarkable. They currently rank 31st in offensive DVOA, ahead of only the Chargers. They're second in defensive DVOA, barely behind only the Seahawks. And the Vikings have the benefit of this season's best special teams unit, with Myles Price leading the league in kick and punt return yardage.

 Add it all together and the Vikings are 10th in total DVOA despite going undefeated. (They're even worse in ESPN's Football Power Index , ranking 14th.) That makes them the eighth-worst 4-0 team by DVOA since 2000. If we go back to 1977, the Vikings are still 13th worst out of 136 teams to start 4-0.

 

 What we can expect: The bad news for the Vikings is that offense, in general, is more stable and predictive than defense or special teams. That means it is more likely that the Vikings offense will continue to struggle than it is that the defense and special teams will continue to be outstanding.

 The good news is that plenty of teams have ridden a suspect 4-0 start all the way to the Super Bowl. It's good to bank those four wins, no matter how well you play, and a number of teams on our list improved over the course of the season. Out of the dozen worst 4-0 teams since 2000, five made the Super Bowl and two won the Lombardi Trophy.

 The fact that the Vikings could go either way is emphasized by the two most similar teams on our list. The 2015 Broncos ranked first on defense and 30th on offense after four weeks. Peyton Manning never got his groove back, but the defense didn't regress and led the Broncos to a Super Bowl title. On the other hand, the Vikings are also similar to the 2012 Cardinals, who ranked 28th on offense and fifth on defense after four weeks. That team completely collapsed, constantly shuffling through backup quarterbacks after an injury to starter Kevin Kolb.

 
 

 3. The Texans and Buccaneers rank among the best 0-4 teams since 1977 
 The Texans were a popular Super Bowl pick out of the AFC before the season began. They are supposed to have one of the best defenses in the league and were hoping the offense would improve. Instead, the Texans have lost their first four games, three of them at home. Their season seems over.

 The same appears to be true for the Buccaneers. They weren't quite as popular as the Texans in the preseason, but plenty of observers believed they could return to the top of the NFC South. They've also started 0-4 and lost three games at home.

 What if I told you that the Texans and Buccaneers have actually been close to NFL average when you break down the play-by-play and look at their efficiency? Houston ranks 17th in the league and Tampa Bay ranks 18th. There are 150 teams since 1977 that have started the season either 0-4 or 0-3-1, and out of all of them, Houston and Tampa Bay rank third and fourth in DVOA.

 

 Houston's offense has been a lot better than you think, an unexpected 13th in DVOA this season. It's the defense that has disappointed, ranking only 15th. Meanwhile, in Tampa Bay, the young…

title: How Browns' defense reemerged as a strength after Week 1
summary: The return to its strength of playing man coverage has played a big role in the unit's resurgence.
full_text:
With a game ball in his hand and a smile on his face, Cleveland Browns cornerback Denzel Ward had only one complaint after the team's 27-24 home win against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday.

 "I'm going to talk to 'Rudy,'" Ward said with a grin, referring to Browns defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg. "All these man-to-man plays. I'm tired." 

 Ward and the Browns' defense had just completed a game in which the unit played man coverage on 73.3% of Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers ' dropbacks, the highest rate in a game by any team this season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

 The approach Cleveland's defense took on "Thursday Night Football" was the opposite of the one it had in Week 1, when the Browns were blown out  34-10  on the road by the Jacksonville Jaguars . In that game, the first under Rutenberg as coordinator, Cleveland's defense played a high rate of zone coverage -- 80%, its fourth-highest rate since 2023 -- but struggled as a whole, making mistakes and leaving open voids in coverage as Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence threw four touchdown passes.

 

 Since that defeat, the Browns (3-1) have returned to their strength of playing man coverage. Cleveland has used man on an NFL-high 50% of opponent dropbacks this season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. The return to the familiar style of defense has played a big role in the unit's resurgence, as the Browns enter their Week 5 road game against the New York Jets ( CBS, 1 p.m. ET ) with an opportunity to move to 4-1 for the first time since 2020.

 "[Rutenberg has] done a great job, and the staff has done a great job," Browns coach Todd Monken said. "We learned our lesson at Jacksonville; we're not just going to be able to be stagnant and not be aggressive. And that's part of what we do as coaching. ... We look at everything on a daily basis, what we're doing, how we're doing it, we look at it after the game, and schematically, how are we doing it, and what do we need to do to get better."

 When the Browns hired Rutenberg, who previously worked as the Atlanta Falcons ' defensive pass game coordinator, the appeal was the ability to keep Cleveland's attacking defensive front intact while also incorporating fresh ideas. As the season opened, most changes seemed to be taking place in the secondary. Safety Grant Delpit alluded to an "exotic" scheme that changed its pre- and post-snap looks.

 But when the season opened in Jacksonville, a Browns defense that had been one of the best playing aggressive man-to-man coverage under former coordinator Jim Schwartz looked unrecognizable. Jacksonville moved the ball with ease against a defense that struggled to get pressure, missed tackles and allowed too many explosive plays through the air.

 After the game, cornerback Tyson Campbell acknowledged Rutenberg's scheme is stylistically the same as last season "in some ways, but we got some more zone concepts that we run as well. So a little bit more diverse." Safety Ronnie Hickman said it felt like the team played more zone than man in the season opener but couldn't pinpoint why.

 "It's definitely a little bit of acclimating to it. ... There was a different play style or playcalling compared to last year," Hickman said. "... Most of it came down to just executing the plays that we know we can make as a defense and just playing our style of football that we know how to play."

 Both Rutenberg and Monken downplayed the man-zone fixation after Week 1.

 "It's all about getting the players in the best position," Rutenberg said. "Sometimes zone turns out to be man. Sometimes man can have zone feels."

 "I've gone against the previous Browns regime; they played a good amount of zone ... We're trying to figure out who we are, who we're going to be moving forward," Monken said. "And that's part of the process."

 Which means Cleveland is returning to a tried-and-tested formula.

 The Browns have not only played more man coverage than any other team; they've excelled at it this season. According to ESPN Research, the Browns ranked 30th in completion percentage when using man coverage in Week 1 and 27th in yards per attempt (12.7). And 57% of Jacksonville's pass attempts versus man coverage went for a first down, which ranked 29th in the league. But in Weeks 2-4, that figure for Browns opponents has dropped to 27%, the second-best mark in the NFL.

 "If you're going to play man, you're going to get beat every now and then, and that's just part of it," Monken said. "There are times you're going to force the quarterback to hold the ball, and you have got to live with it. Otherwise, you're going to second-guess every call that you have. Do all the work during the week, shrink the margin for error, and let it rip, and then let the chips fall where they may, and then reassess."

 Players and coaches have emphasized how rush and coverage go hand in hand, and as tight of coverage as the secondary has had, Cleveland's pass rush has also rebounded from Week 1, when it generated six pressures, tied for the fewest in the league and fewer than in any game the defense recorded under Schwartz. Even without two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett , the Browns now rank fourth in pressures (65) and sixth in pressure rate (40.4%), according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Cleveland's 12 sacks, led by defensive tackle Mason Graham 's four, are tied for fifth in the league. Graham, though, is expected to miss time after sustaining an MCL sprain and an ankle sprain against the Steelers.

 

 Rutenberg has been creative in designing Cleveland's pass rush, moving players such as defensive end Jared Verse and linebacker Carson Schwesinger around. Schwesinger has blitzed at a higher rate than in his rookie season (18% in 2026 compared to 15.6% in 2025, per NFL Next Gen Stats). He has also increasingly lined him up as an edge rusher to do so; 23% of Schwesinger's snaps have come at outside linebacker, an increase from 12.3% in 2025.

 "When you put speed up in the middle, it throws off the [offensive linemen] on the interior," Verse said. "When you got power rushes on the edge, [it] throws everybody else. And when they get something that they're not used to, I mean, the interior guys don't really do a lot of scout reports on me because I don't rush over them a lot. So when I am over them, it gets them in a stressful situation, and I think that's what we took advantage of."

 The Browns, though, are also showing increased comfort in a Rutenberg scheme that might call for zone coverages in certain moments. Cornerback Myles Harden 's Week 2 interception of Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield came from a disguised Cover 4 coverage, in which Harden dropped into a zone and read Mayfield's eyes before undercutting a pass.

 "We're all figuring each other out and figuring our scheme and everything out," Ward said, "and we've been doing that week by week, and we see man is working, so they're going to do that and call that. So we're all bought in, man. [Rutenberg] still sprinkles a little bit of his own in there. So I'm not going to say it's just all man-to-man. He does a good job of calling the game."

title: 2026 NFL quarter-season awards: MVP picks, top rookies, OPOY, DPOY, best coaches
summary: Brock Purdy for MVP? Klint Kubiak taking Coach of the Year? Will Anderson Jr. getting DPOY honors? We ranked the top candidates to win eight NFL awards through Week 4.
full_text:
Can you believe we're already four games into the NFL season ? It still feels like we're trying to figure out which teams have a real shot at competing for a Super Bowl . But today, I'm here to identify the players and coaches who have been at the top of their game in 2026. It's time for my annual quarter-season awards, where I hand out hardware for the best performances from Weeks 1 through 4.

 Keep in mind that these are my picks -- who I believe deserves each award through four games -- as opposed to my prediction for who will ultimately win each award at the end of the year ... two entirely different things. I'm basing my picks on data and what I've seen on film. I also have some slightly different rules and beliefs that I use in my picks than the end-of-season electorate does. I'll mention them as we go through each award.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 One broader one is that availability matters. Players who aren't playing aren't helping their teams. At the end of the season, missing anything more than a couple of games really hurts a player's chances of winning an award unless they've completely dominated the competition. Shrunk down to a four-game sample, missing even one half of football is enough to seriously poke holes in a player's résumé. There are a handful of stars, with Baltimore receiver  Zay Flowers as the most prominent case, where simply being unavailable for some part of the first four weeks is holding an otherwise impressive start back.

 Let's go award by award, from Defensive Rookie of the Year to MVP. I'll look back at these eight awards after Week 9 when I put together my midseason award rankings to see who held onto their crown and who fell off quicker than expected.

 

 
 Jump to an award: 
 DROY | OROY |  Coach of the Year 
 Comeback Player of the Year 
 Protector of the Year 
 DPOY | OPOY | MVP 

 
 

 Defensive Rookie of the Year 
 We've seen plenty of defensive rookies getting regular snaps this season. Through four weeks, 24 rookies have suited up for at least 50% of their teams' defensive snaps, up from 22 players in 2025, 13 in 2024 and 16 in 2023. Titans linebacker  Anthony Hill Jr . and Bears safety  Dillon Thieneman  have been on the field for every one of their teams' snaps this season, a relatively rare feat for a rookie at any position.

 No one has really separated from the pack yet. The best rookie defender I've seen on a per-snap basis has been Chiefs cornerback Mansoor Delane , who finished his first drive as a pro with an interception of Bo Nix . Unfortunately, Delane suffered a shoulder injury and missed all but three snaps of the first two weeks of the season. He has been an excellent two-way defender from the very first drive of the year and should climb back into contention if he can stay on the field.

 Others might be able to carve out larger roles after proving themselves early in the season. It's going to be tough for the Cowboys to take Jaishawn Barham off the field after what he has done against the run over the past two weeks. Gabe Jacas has flashed as a pass rusher and disruptor in the backfield for the Patriots. Sonny Styles has one of the most physically impressive plays of the season on his tape, with the Commanders linebacker trucking Saquon Barkley in pass protection and running through the star back for a sack in Week 1. They'll each have a shot at working their way into the top three in the weeks to come.

 
 

 3. Jacob Rodriguez , LB, Miami Dolphins 
 Given how many rookies the Dolphins are lining up on a weekly basis, it's probably inevitable that at least one of their young players was going to make it into the top three here. Rodriguez has had his issues handling play-action this season, but he has been an impact defender against the run. The second-round pick has made tackles on nearly 24% of designed runs against the Dolphins, the 12th-best rate among players with 150 defensive snaps or more this season.

 And while making tackles doesn't mean much if they're 10 or more yards downfield, 4.6% of Rodriguez's tackles have produced stuffs for no gain or a loss -- including three for loss on  Kenneth Walker III  when the Dolphins played the Chiefs in Week 3. In you haven't noticed, defenses haven't exactly had much success tackling Walker anywhere this season, let alone behind the line.

 
 

 2. Hezekiah Masses , CB, Las Vegas Raiders 
 While most of the talk about the Raiders 3-1 start has understandably been about the offense, Masses has been a bright spot for Vegas in what has long been a problem spot at cornerback. The fifth-round pick started the season as the understudy to Darien Porter on the outside, but when Porter suffered a foot injury late in the Week 1 win over the Dolphins, Masses took over the job and has made it his own. Porter has played just three defensive snaps over the past two weeks since returning to the lineup.

 

 Masses is tied for the NFL lead with three interceptions, which might overstate his impact. One of those picks was an almost comical example of a Chargers drop by David Njoku , while the other was a wounded duck that came off the hands of Tyler Shough as he was hit mid-release. Those interceptions count, though, and Masses has six passes defensed across 20 targets this season, per NFL Next Gen Stats. He has allowed about 40 receiving yards per game as the nearest defender in coverage and has held his own as a tackler.

 Masses probably isn't going to finish the season averaging close to a pick per game, but he looks like he belongs on the field as a starting-caliber CB, which isn't exactly commonplace for even highly touted rookies.

 
 

 1. Arvell Reese , LB/Edge, New York Giants 
 Reese is a very scary player. He has been on the field for over 99% of the defensive snaps for the Giants, opening the year in what has primarily been an off-ball linebacker role while leading the league in solo tackles (27). With Brian Burns suffering a season-ending torn ACL , though, the Giants moved Reese onto the line of scrimmage more often against the Cardinals in Week 4, with their first-round pick playing more than 46% of his defensive snaps as an edge defender, up from 34% over the first three weeks.

 The operative phrase with Reese is going to be "stuffing the stat sheet," and we're already getting there. Against the Cardinals, Reese recorded his third tackle for loss of the season, batted down a pass and caught an interception off a deflection at the line of scrimmage. Another Reese pressure on a blitz from the second level hit Jacoby Brissett as he threw and produced a pick by  Greg Newsome II  on an underthrown ball. Reese isn't the Micah Parsons -esque pass rusher Giants fans might have hoped they were landing when he fell to the fifth pick of this year's draft, but New York probably doesn't beat Arizona on Sunday without him being the best player on the field.

 

 

 Offensive Rookie of the Year 
 Many of the high-profile offensive draftees from 2026 haven't had a chance to really show what they can do. Raiders quarterback  Fernando Mendoza  hasn't played a single regular-season snap. Cardinals running back  Jeremiyah Love , recovering from a high ankle sprain, has been on the field for only 50% of the offensive snaps in Arizona and told his own coaches that other backs were in better shape to help the team against the Giants last week. Saints receiver  Jordyn Tyson  is on injured reserve with a hamstring issue . Those are three of the top four picks on the offensive side from this year's draft, and they've collectively played 131 snaps.

 The other player in that big four might be about to make his move. Receiver  Carnell Tate got off to a slow start as part of a struggling Titans offense, but the No. 4 pick is coming off his best game as a pro, with nine catches for 145 yards against the Ravens, albeit with two fumbles. Tate probably should have had at least one touchdown against the Giants the week before if not for some…

title: Experience Cowboys QB Dak Prescott directing a TD play
summary: From pre-snap to post-snap, Prescott processes dozens of elements before the ball leaves his hand and is caught for a 21-yard TD.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- For the briefest of moments between each play, Dak Prescott can take a breath. But only one. 

 Coach Brian Schottenheimer's voice is quickly in the quarterback's ear, calling the next play. From there Prescott delivers the call to the rest of the Dallas Cowboys players in the huddle.

 As Prescott walks to the line of scrimmage, he gets his first look at the opposing defense. What's the front? Where are the safeties? Where is the middle linebacker? Are the corners playing off or in press coverage? How many defenders are in the box?

 He considers whether those things force him to change the play.

 Then the game circumstances come to mind: the quarter, time remaining, the score, the down and distance. How about the weather? Or how a loud crowd can make communication more difficult? 

 With center Cooper Beebe , he sets the protection. He uses hand signals to his pass catchers. He might need to kill the original call and go to the second play he called in the huddle.

 The drama builds as thousands in the stands yell and scream as the seconds tick off the clock.

 All this -- and more -- happens in 40 seconds before the ball is even snapped, Prescott told ESPN this spring, when he sat down to go through a single play and everything it entails.

 At the snap, what can look like chaos to many is choreography to Prescott.

 His hours of film study -- learning the tendencies of the opposing coordinator, the subtle tells of a defensive tackle aligning over the inside shoulder of the guard or a linebacker mugging the A-gap -- give him all the information he needs.

 When he drops back, he sees players flash all around him. It happens in a blur, but he knows where things are supposed to be. On a pass, he needs to decide whether the throw needs to be layered over the top, away from a defender or low so only his receiver can catch it. Does it need to be a fastball or a changeup?

 All this happens in seconds.

 Prescott estimates a normal play will have anywhere from two to 10 decisions. He can see things the way Matt Damon's character saw things in "Good Will Hunting," solving the most difficult equations with ease and speed.

 "Some of those decisions you make are naturally from your practice and from the repetition and the work that you put in throughout the week," Prescott said. "It's just unconscious."

 

 Seeing a play through Prescott's eyes 
 To protect their current offensive calls, the play Prescott dissected was against an uncommon opponent for Dallas, the Cleveland Browns . The 21-yard touchdown pass to receiver Brandin Cooks took place in the 2024 season opener, hours after Prescott agreed to a contract extension that made him the highest-paid player in the NFL at the time.

 The Cowboys faced third-and-5 from the Cleveland 21-yard line on their first possession of the season.

 "We knew when we got down in the red zone fringe," Cooks said, "Cleveland at that time liked to bring Cover 0 [no deep safeties]. We're in three-by-one and I'm at the three [closest to the offensive linemen]. [Browns safety] Grant Delpit , he's inside on me and Dak sees at the line it's Cover 0 and he checks. We both see it."

 As he surveyed the defense, Prescott signaled tight end Jake Ferguson tighter to the formation to face defensive end Myles Garrett . Having a tight end block an All-Pro edge rusher alone is never the best answer, but Prescott knew he would be getting the ball out quickly.

 "Not ideal," Prescott said. "But all Jake has to do is get in his way."

 

 At the snap, the picture changed. The Cowboys had six blockers in for the six Browns defenders. They should have been protected.

 Browns linebacker Jordan Hicks , however, ran free between left tackle Tyler Guyton and left guard Tyler Smith , with a direct line on Prescott -- whose eyes were looking downfield.

 "It's Game 1. [Smith] is an All-Pro. He just makes a little [missed assignment]," Prescott said. "Trust me, I've done them. I do it here and there; interceptions."

 Hicks sprinted six steps and raised his left arm as Prescott cocked back to throw. His mechanics weren't great. His legs were almost parallel to the line, and the pass was all arm strength as he drifted back to the 30-yard line.

 "That's a flash of color," Prescott said. "I'm looking at that corner."

 Cooks was at the 14 as Prescott started to throw the ball. Delpit was at the 9 but flat-footed.

 "I actually throw this ball much earlier than I want to," Prescott said. "I would love to be able to get this ball all the way into that pylon box because I'm having to throw it now and in an awkward stance and Brandon's not there."

 The pass is high, but he had to let it go early so Cooks could run under it. During the week of practice, the two discussed Cooks looking up in the air, not back to Prescott, knowing the type of throw it would take.

 "Just putting air under it, boom! Thankfully the safety didn't play it very well," Prescott said. "Thankfully we caught him flat-footed, which happens in zero because he expects the blitz to get home."

 

 Cooks, who recently joined the San Francisco 49ers , counts his time with Prescott as a plus.

 "I was fortunate enough to play with a lot of the greats, and I'll put Dak in that variety when it comes to that at-the-line-of-scrimmage, pre-snap ability to read and think it through," Cooks said. "They've got to get through so much. They've got to know the protection, get the check to the offensive line to pick up that pressure, then they need to know the receiver's [job]. 

 "Not every quarterback can do it, but when you can, it makes your offense a lot better. Guys like Dak, [Tom] Brady , Drew [Brees] , they're an extension of the coach at that point."

 

 Prescott's work ethic shines on game days 
 For Prescott, it all started to click in 2018 after the Cowboys made a trade for wide receiver Amari Cooper . It was Prescott's third year and he was making his 40th regular-season start when the Cowboys played the Tennessee Titans in Cooper's first game.

 The Cowboys lost 28-14 and Prescott was 21-of-31 for 243 yards, two TDs and one INT, but something changed that day in how he saw the game. 

 "When [the game] slows down is when you understand the only little things you need to think about," Prescott said. "One of those football sayings is, 'See a little, see a lot; See a lot, see little.' 

 "And it's no different with the mind. If I'm trying to think about a lot, too much is going on. But if I know exactly what I need to do, if I know my purpose and my plan on this play, it's easy and it's simple."

 

 Since that game, Prescott has had four 4,000-yard seasons and all four of his 30-touchdown seasons (including a career-high 37 in 2021).

 The hours it takes to prepare for a game seem endless. Prescott's teammates marvel at the work he puts in.

 "Bro, his truck is the last one up here a lot of the days," Smith said. "I've stayed here a while after the final bell is rung and you can technically go home. For hours I've stayed here, and I'm leaving, his truck is still here.

 "If people think this is just natural talent -- well obviously he's naturally talented -- but if people think he's not working just as hard to be the best version of himself and be one of the best quarterbacks in the league, they're dead wrong. The body of work is put forth every day, and ultimately that body of work will show up."

 Said Cowboys receiver Ryan Flournoy : "As a receiver, there's a lot going through our mind, and we don't have to know what the linemen are doing, what the running back is doing. For him to dissect the defense, get everybody on board with one play, it's amazing. Even spitting out a play in the huddle, it's amazing, honestly."

 Each playcall can carry a check to another play, depending on what the defense is showing when the offense gets to the line of scrimmage. Sometimes it can be wordy, which can eat away at the time on the play clock. Offensive coordinator Klayton…

title: How Dolphins QB Malik Willis prepared for second chance
summary: Willis has worked for this opportunity in Miami, and he and the Dolphins believe he's ready for it.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Before Miami Dolphins fans got their first opportunity to see quarterback Malik Willis play inside Hard Rock Stadium, he showed his teammates why he was brought in to begin with.

 The Dolphins scheduled a stadium practice to mark the official end of training camp, and the night before, Willis spoke to his offensive teammates -- not because he saw anything that bothered him but to set a tone for the remainder of the summer.

 "I just wanted to talk to the offense and just have a man-to-man conversation," Willis said. "We got to understand this is a business and we got to take what we do personally. We got to take pride in it, and we got to do it to the best of our ability, regardless if we're calling plays to beat the defense or not. We're not calling plays to beat the defense. We're calling plays that we want to use throughout the year, and we're trying to get better."

 

 In short, he encouraged his teammates to believe in the process. It's a lesson he has learned himself in his time as a professional.

 While most of the Dolphins' offseason involved saving as much money as possible, first-year general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan made exactly one splash in free agency -- Willis, whom he signed to a three-year, $67.5 million contract that made him the only free agent to receive a multiyear deal from the Dolphins this offseason.

 Knowing 2026 would be a rebuilding year, the Dolphins identified the player they'd like to build around. Even one of the biggest moves they made in the spring, sending wide receiver Jaylen Waddle to the Denver Broncos in exchange for a first-round pick, was done with Willis in mind.

 "We're in a position with our roster where we need to get younger and cheaper -- and I just thought it was in the best interest of the Miami Dolphins to get two rookie players," Sullivan said after the trade. "If I do my job right ... they'll be on rookie contracts that we can grow with Malik. That's why we got [Willis] on a three-year deal, so we can put guys around him over the course of numerous draft classes. Next year, we'll have a little more flexibility in free agency, as we will in 2028, to grow this thing."

 Willis learned from an underwhelming start to his career with the Tennessee Titans , used a fresh start with the Green Bay Packers as an opportunity to fine-tune his game and ultimately showed enough in two seasons to convince Miami to build around him.

 For the first time since college, he entered this season as a starting quarterback and is now tasked with balancing his own development with the responsibility of leading the youngest offense in the NFL.

 "He's one of the leaders on our team. I mean, he's our quarterback," Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said. "Just imagine yourself in the huddle with three rookie receivers, a rookie tight end and a rookie fullback. And you're starting for the first time, and you got [six rookies] -- he's got a lot on his plate. I think he's handled that really well. Really well. And I don't think that's easy."

 The Dolphins aren't expected to win many games this season. Hafley has said repeatedly that success in 2026 will be defined more by players' development than wins and losses.

 There are multiple quarterbacks who have been deemed worthy of a high pick in the 2027 draft class, and fans could clamor for one of them if the Dolphins end up atop next year's draft order. But Willis isn't worried about whether his audition with the team lasts longer than one season. He has worked for this opportunity, and he and the Dolphins believe he's ready for it. And for now, they've handed him the keys to their franchise.

 "I think when I came into the league, I wasn't prepared, and that's not a knock toward my coaches or myself," Willis said. "That's just what it was coming from the system I came from, and I've had a chance to learn the last four years since I've been in the league.

 "I went through four different offenses and seen a bunch of different defenses, and I just think I've grown a lot and I'm grateful for the opportunity once again."

 

 

 'My first year didn't go great' 

 The Titans took Willis in the third round (86th overall) in the 2022 NFL draft after he threw for more than 5,000 yards and 47 touchdowns at Liberty.

 While he was considered by many draft pundits to be a potential first-round pick, his numbers at Liberty masked a raw quarterback prospect who often got by on his athleticism more so than fundamentals.

 "He was very much a compensator," said Sean McEvoy, a private quarterback coach who has trained Willis since he was in high school. "Where his natural athletic ability made up for the things mechanically that weren't as sound as most quarterbacks were at that time."

 

 McEvoy said it's not uncommon for athletic quarterbacks to rely on that athleticism in their developmental years.

 But doing so isn't sustainable.

 "You're going to hit your ceiling at some point when you play the position that way -- and it's just a matter of when you hit it," McEvoy said. "Some guys hit it as soon as they get to college, and some guys hit it when the pressure's put on them when they become a starter. And then some guys when they get to the league."

 Willis made six extended appearances as a rookie in 2022, completing 31 of 61 passes for 276 yards and three interceptions. After the season, he realized he could no longer purely get by on his athletic tools; as he put it to McEvoy, "I got my opportunity and I wasn't good enough."

 That offseason, he worked with McEvoy, Jacksonville-based quarterback coach Will Hewlett and arm-care coach Tom Gormely to refine his mechanics.

 "My first year didn't go great, so I went to figure out things that might help me," Willis said. "Using my hips and this lower body that I have, this strength that we work for, right, instead of just using all arm all the time -- it's just less consistent and it's more strain on your body, right?

 "So it's just working that over the last four years. I think it's been super beneficial. It's helped me become way more accurate and consistent."

 Hewlett described their work with Willis as a "controlled, monotonous, repeatable process" that centered around breaking his old movement patterns. They used motion capture and video analysis to break down each rep, focusing on the process instead of immediate results.

 Plyometric throwing, Hewlett said, was an "accelerator" for Willis and allowed him to practice his mechanics without worrying about hitting a target.

 "It's like you're throwing a little round tennis-ball-sized ball that ... it hits a wall and the only thing you have to go on is 'How did that feel?'" Hewlett said. "It was a process with very continuous feedback with video, like, 'Here's how much further forward your hips got on this, but your rotation was much greater based on your last rep.'"

 Willis' offseason work didn't stop the Titans from drafting quarterback Will Levis in the second round in 2023. Willis attempted five passes that season in just three appearances, and Levis finished the season as the team's full-time starter.

 Tennessee ultimately traded Willis to the Packers after the season, severing their faith in him after 11 appearances and three starts..

 

 

 'There's just no way this guy's a backup. There's no way.' 

 Packers quarterback Jordan Love suffered a sprained MCL in the 2024 season opener, paving the way for Willis' fourth and fifth career starts. In those opportunities, Willis completed a combined 25 of 33 passes for 324 yards and two touchdowns with 114 yards and another score on the ground.

 When Love returned, Willis ran the Packers' scout-team offense -- and sometimes had to be reigned in by then-Packers defensive coordinator Hafley.

 "A lot of times he really couldn't do what he does best," Hafley said. "Because I was sitting there telling him, if we were playing a drop-back guy and he started scrambling, I'd tell him, 'Hey, you got to stay in the…
