title: Why expansion to Houston makes too much sense for the NHL
summary: Commissioner Gary Bettman said the league is considering a new team, and Houston's viability is concrete.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Houston has been talked about as an NHL city before. There have been conversations, in group chats, on message boards and social media. Hockey fans have done it. So have Houston sports fans watching a game at any one of the several venues -- even during the time when the AHL was playing at Toyota Center.

 The conversations still exist, but now they're louder and more real because the voices include the NHL, its stakeholders, a potential owner and figures within Houston's political and sports landscape about how the city could land an expansion team.

 "I'm a big believer in that everything happens for a reason, right?" Harris County-Houston Sports Authority CEO Ryan Walsh said. "The right time, the right place, etc. Houston has been talked about as a destination for hockey for a long time. But I think Houston really is and has become a true destination for sports."

 NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said in late June the league is exploring adding a second team in Texas , with Houston and Austin as potential targets.

 Bettman said the league entered into an agreement with The Friedkin Group that gave them six months to explore putting a team in either city. It included agreeing to a $3.5 billion investment, including an expansion fee and building costs for an NHL arena.

 

 In late September, Bettman said the NHL is not in a formal round of expansion , noting that the NHL board of governors has taken a "wait-and-see attitude" when it comes to adding expansion franchises. He said there is an expectation that he'll know whether the board of governors prefers Austin or Houston as a potential expansion target by the end of the year.

 NHL deputy commissioner Bill Daly said there's a chance there might not be a vote on The Friedkin Group's bid by the NHL's next board meeting in December when the six-month exploration process has finished.

 Houston's viability as an option is concrete. As is the interest from influential figures in the city. But, much remains fluid when it comes to whether the NHL chooses to go to Houston, Austin or remain with 32 teams until a later time.

 For now, Houston remains the largest market in the U.S. without an NHL franchise. To get one would add to the city's distinction as one that heavily consumes sports. It already has MLB, the NBA, NFL, MLS and NWSL. Houston will see the return of the WNBA in 2027, with the Connecticut Sun relocating and becoming the Houston Comets.

 With that many professional teams, two FBS programs in Houston and Rice, one of the nation's strongest high school sports scenes and a host for other major events such as the World Cup, Houston's status can be viewed as a double-edged sword. There's an argument that adding the NHL would make it one of the most complete sports cities in the nation. Another suggests there could be such a thing as too much sports, and how it would be challenging for an NHL team to find its footing.

 Mainly, there are two questions at the heart of how Houston finds itself in this current position even when taking those differing perspectives into account.

 Why Houston? And why now?

 "Houston sells itself," Houston mayor John Whitmire said. "There are a lot of really fine cities, but there's only one Houston."

 
 Houston's hockey history 
 Minor league hockey first came to Houston in 1946, but the team ceased operations in 1949. It returned in 1965 with the Houston Apollos. They were the Montreal Canadiens ' farm team until 1969 when the team shuttered. The city got hockey back for a third time in 1972 with the arrival of the first iteration of the Aeros in the World Hockey Association.

 The Aeros were in Houston for six seasons, won two league titles and were led by Gordie Howe along with his sons Mark and Marty.

 "We knew absolutely nothing about Houston," Mark Howe said. "The first day we moved in -- Marty and I were still living at home at 18 and 19 -- I want to say there was a hurricane and you couldn't even see the house across the street. Then you go to the first day of training camp and it was 104 degrees outside. I think I sweated out 12 pounds."

 Howe said the front office had the players out in the community to attract fans while teaching people more about hockey. It worked; the Aeros were in the top five of WHA attendance three times over a five-year period.

 At the time, few U.S. cities had as many professional teams as Houston. The city was home to the Houston Astros, the Houston Oilers and the Houston Rockets.

 "Football, for me, is obviously the biggest thing down in Texas," Howe said. "All the high schools played on Friday nights. If the Aeros played on a Friday night, we would probably be on page five or six of the sports section because of high school football. That's the way it was."

 

 The Astros and Oilers called the Astrodome home. Even as Houston has changed and become much larger, there are still strong feelings about how the monument to advancement, which officially opened in 1965, remains the city's greatest achievement.

 For some people, the Astrodome is what put Houston on the map at the same time as the city was putting a man on the moon. This is what sports means to Houston.

 "They support everything and they're very proud of being Houstonians," said Tom Garrity, who was the president of the second version of the Houston Aeros for five seasons. "When you look at all their franchises, it's like anything. You have your ups and your downs. But I'd put Houston at the top of the list of supporting whatever is in town."

 The WHA played its final season in 1979, with four teams -- the Edmonton Oilers , Hartford Whalers, Quebec Nordiques and Winnipeg Jets -- joining the NHL.

 The Aeros disbanded a year earlier following the 1977-78 season.

 

 In 1994, the IHL granted Houston an expansion franchise, reusing the Aeros name in homage to the former WHA team. The new Aeros won a league championship in 1999 -- but the IHL folded in 2001. The Aeros joined the AHL, and became the farm team for the Minnesota Wild . The Aeros also spent one season as a farm team for the Dallas Stars .

 "It was a pretty traditional minor league hockey market. Weekend games were a way easier sell than a Tuesday night game," said Minnesota Wild broadcaster Joe O'Donnell, who spent five seasons with the Aeros. "You had a hardcore fanbase, a booster club, a season ticket holder base that was super passionate. Then, from a marketing standpoint, it was about how do you find a way to separate yourself and get the word out there."

 Drawing fans was a gradual process. Eventually, the team reached the top five in AHL attendance. O'Donnell said one of the items that helped was the team playing its games at Toyota Center, home of the Rockets.

 On the surface, the Aeros were playing in what might have been the nicest building in the AHL. They had future NHL players on their roster, won a league title in their second season and missed the playoffs only twice during their time in the AHL.

 Why leave Houston?

 "This is where the history of the owners of the Rockets and old Aeros comes into play," said David Walsh, a professor in the sports and fitness administration program at the University of Houston. "They were at each other's throats, egos, what have you. The old owner of the Aeros was Chuck Watson and the old owner of the Rockets was Les Alexander."

 
 An arena rights battle... and the end of the Aeros 
 Watson owned the Aeros, and also operated The Summit, the arena where the Aeros and the Rockets played before moving to the Toyota Center. Alexander, who purchased the Rockets in 1993, tried breaking the lease agreement. Watson denied the move, and Alexander was forced to honor the original lease agreement that was set to end in 2003.

 Alexander and Watson agreed to an arena deal in 1997 that gave both teams equal control, but Harris County voters rejected it in a 1999 referendum.

 Around this same time, Alexander sought to purchase the Edmonton Oilers…

title: Are Texans and Chargers this bad? And how do we bet the Rams one month in?
summary: Four weeks into the NFL season, what do we know, and what can we expect moving forward?
full_text:
Four weeks into the NFL season, the Houston Texans and Los Angeles Chargers are winless, a deeper stumble than anticipated. Which team can rebound, and which problems are real? The San Francisco 49ers look strong, as predicted, but is that start sustainable? Meanwhile, the Los Angeles Rams are Super Bowl favorites, yet their regular-season win total still offers a fade.

 The Texans aren't this bad, the preseason thesis just cracked 
 Texans: 0-4, 0-4 ATS (45-1 to win Super Bowl, 18-1 entering Week 1) 

 The biggest preseason concern for Houston was whether the offense could finally complement an elite defense. Instead, the defense has become part of the problem. Houston is allowing 27 points per game after allowing 17 PPG last season. More concerning, the offseason investment in the run game hasn't translated. David Montgomery is averaging just 2.7 yards per carry, leaving C.J. Stroud responsible for creating most of the offense (again).

 

 Stroud has actually been solid, throwing for 1,141 yards with five touchdowns and no interceptions. It's the lack of red zone execution -- top half of the league in attempts, bottom 10 in touchdowns scored. There's reason to expect improvement: Houston has essentially matched its opponents in total yardage, owns a positive turnover margin and has lost two games by four points or less. This looks more like an underperforming team than a terrible one.

 The fix starts with the run game, even if that means leaning more on Woody Marks or adjusting the blocking approach rather than forcing Montgomery into something that isn't working. Defensively, Houston has to limit explosive passes; the pass rush is still getting home, so the secondary needs to capitalize on that pressure.

 There's room for regression toward competence, but it shouldn't involve Stroud becoming Superman -- just play complementary football. Houston's season win total was 9.5 going into the season. At 0-4, the market has dropped them to 7.5. Seven wins is the new benchmark.

 

 The Chargers lost their foundation before it ever had an identity 
 Chargers: 0-4, 0-3-1 ATS (100-1 to win Super Bowl, 17-1 entering Week 1) 

 The Chargers were a preseason regression candidate because last year's 11 wins were helped by a soft schedule and close-game success. The bad news: their 0-4 start goes beyond regression.

 

 The offense Mike McDaniel was supposed to unlock has been undermined by the exact concern identified preseason: offensive line health. OT Rashawn Slater is doubtful, OT Joe Alt and G Trevor Penning are questionable, and C Tyler Biadasz is on injured reserve. Justin Herbert is pressing behind unstable protection, turning the ball over and failing to create explosive plays.

 The defense has declined without coordinator Jesse Minter, though it has created opportunities, forcing five turnovers against Buffalo -- yet losing the game anyway. The fix is simplification: lean on Omarion Hampton and Keaton Mitchell , use motion and quicker throws, and stop asking Herbert to rescue every possession.

 The Chargers are probably better than 0-4, but the schedule still limits their recovery. Under 5.5 wins at +118 is worth a look, and I would keep fading them as favorites until this offense proves itself.

 
 Check out the latest Super Bowl odds and major NFL awards futures . 

 

 The 49ers' season win total is ahead of schedule, the championship case remains untested 

 San Francisco's 4-0 start has validated my preseason OVER 9.5 prediction. I'm still not quite ready to validate the 49ers as a Super Bowl team, not at the +850 price. Kyle Shanahan has kept the offense efficient despite injuries, and Brock Purdy has been outstanding. The receiving additions are producing, the run game has multiple answers, and San Francisco is winning without relying heavily on turnovers or unusual kicking luck.

 

 Still, context matters. The opener against the Rams was played abroad, Miami might be the NFL's worst team, Arizona is rebuilding, and Denver has a strong defense without a punishing offense. The 49ers handled that stretch as a good team should. My problem with the hype is that the opening schedule hasn't forced the Niners to show that their limited pass rush and vulnerable secondary can survive against elite quarterbacks.

 Their Super Bowl price has shortened from 14-1 to +850. That move is a reflection of the current record more than actual substantial proof. If you have a preseason ticket, great. I wouldn't buy +850 now.

 NFL futures prediction: Rams UNDER 10.5 wins (+116) 

 The Rams being Super Bowl favorites and going under 10.5 wins can both make sense. The Super Bowl market is pricing their ceiling, with Sean McVay, a healthy Matthew Stafford and a roster capable of beating anyone in January.

 The win total is about surviving 13 more regular-season games with almost zero wiggle room. The Rams are 2-2, so the over requires a 9-4 finish. That's a demanding pace for a team facing a difficult schedule, with Stafford showing turnover volatility and Myles Garrett on injured reserve.

 The number has dropped from 11.5 preseason to 10.5, so protection with the 11-win middle is lost. Still, the +116 keeps the under playable. The Rams can still be one of the NFL's best teams, reach the playoffs and even win the Super Bowl while finishing 10-7. We know what the ceiling for the Rams can be. This wager is betting against regular-season perfection.

title: Irsay-Gordon's presence on Colts sideline reignites debate
summary: Carlie Irsay-Gordon's game-day routine isn't typical for owners, but she said it "helps to understand and to ask questions."
full_text:
INDIANAPOLIS -- The camera finds Carlie Irsay-Gordon. This becomes apparent during any Indianapolis Colts game telecast, when images of the team's primary owner are sure to be captured as she watches the action from the sideline.

 It's the fact that Irsay-Gordon is one of one: The only NFL owner known to routinely be stationed on the sideline during games while listening to a coach's headset communications and referencing a play sheet.

 Irsay-Gordon's longtime practice predates her 2025 ascension to primary owner by several years. Still, it continues to be a subject of fascination -- and debate -- for many.

 But, according to team sources, don't expect it to change anytime soon.

 There has not been any discussion of a change to the practice, just as there is no expectation she'll stop attending the various position and staff meetings she routinely sits in. If there's a question to be asked, it's perhaps this: Is Irsay-Gordon's approach having its intended effect?

 She went on record long ago to explain why she is on the sideline during games and why she's listening to headset transmissions.

 "I need to be able to say, 'Is this person full of B.S.? Do they even know what they're talking about?'" Irsay-Gordon said last year. She referred to a football team as "a complex organism" and explained how listening to coaches' conversations during games helps her decipher why plays did and did not work, for instance.

 

 All of this helps inform her day-to-day management of the team. It helps her, sources say, ask more probing questions during her respective weekly meetings with general manager Chris Ballard and coach Shane Steichen, for instance.

 "I like to say on a good day I have like a fifth-grade reading level understanding of the game and just the basic concepts of what we're trying to do, depending on the week and depending on our opponent and depending on the situation," Irsay-Gordon told "Front Office Sports Tonight" in London, where the Colts beat the  Washington Commanders   30-13  on Sunday. "But I think, then, it just helps to understand and to ask questions, because I think one of the things, in my opinion, like being a good leader is about listening, really to understand. And I think that's what the best teams do."

 Irsay-Gordon and her youngest sister, Kalen Jackson, took an active role in the team's extensive coaching search that produced Steichen's hiring on Feb. 14, 2023. To that end, gaining a deeper understanding of the team's operation better positioned her to decipher whether they are getting sufficient answers from job candidates, Irsay-Gordon has said.

 Asked what someone might glean from listening to conversations on a headset during games, Colts offensive coordinator Jim Bob Cooter said "there's a lot to learn from what is said."

 He added, "One of the things I really enjoy [about] coaching at the NFL level is the detail that goes into some of the strategic decisions and questions and problems that we solve."

 To be clear, an owner listening to a coach's headset is atypical.

 When Irsay-Gordon first began the practice -- long before her father, longtime Colts owner Jim Irsay, died last year -- it was initially seen as a surprising development for the former coaching staff, a source told ESPN.

 Some coaches were said to be more mindful of what they might say into their headsets, knowing a member of ownership was listening in. Ultimately, though, it didn't prove problematic. Now, it's mostly an afterthought because she has been at it since at least 2020.

 Irsay-Gordon's management style likely helped her gain acceptance despite making what is a bold move for an owner. She is ever present at Colts headquarters, working long hours alongside coaches and front-office executives through the week. She has forged genuine relationships with people at the highest levels of the organization as well as lower-level support staff. Around the building, everyone refers to her simply as "Carlie."

 

 Additionally, it was former head coach Frank Reich who encouraged Irsay-Gordon to make the habit of wearing a headset permanent as part of her effort to better educate herself on the team's machinations. His endorsement of the idea might have helped eased tensions.

 Her exact role on game day is also important to emphasize: She is not an active participant, according to Steichen and other staffers. Footage of Irsay-Gordon questioning an assistant coach on the sideline Sunday in London were shared widely online and described as disruptive in some corners. But the images were from before the game, not during the team's win.

 During games, Irsay-Gordon is equipped with a walkie-talkie connected to headphones. The device provides her the ability to listen to coaches' transmissions but not to join the conversation. She is generally positioned off to the side and not at the center of the activity unfolding on the sideline.

 And you should expect Irsay-Gordon to be in her usual spot Sunday, when the Colts travel to face the Pittsburgh Steelers  ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 She is adamant her presence is not a hindrance, something she is very cognizant of and has discussed with coaches and players.

 "What's funny is, I think my biggest concern going through this transition [to owner] was making sure I wasn't a distraction," Irsay-Gordon told ESPN earlier this year. "It's so interesting. Even a lot of the [players] were like, 'Why are people so focused on this now? You've been around for years. This doesn't make sense.'"

 It was just the confirmation Irsay-Gordon needed, she said. Because she's not going anywhere.

 "I'm glad it's normal for them," Irsay-Gordon told ESPN. "Because I still have a lot more to learn."

title: Why Jaguars play 26 of next 30 regular-season games away from Jacksonville
summary: The Jaguars will become the first NFL team since 1926 to play in 12 or more stadiums in a single season -- including Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday.
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. --  Jaguars cornerback Jourdan Lewis likes to go bird-watching when his team is playing on the road.

 He'll do it from inside the team bus when it pulls up to the opponent's stadium, and he doesn't have to look too long to find one. He doesn't need a field guide to identify the type, either.

 "I love seeing the fans pull up middle fingers and flip the bird at us," Lewis said. "It gets the juices flowing."

 He had better get used to seeing that regularly, because the Jaguars aren't going to be spending much time at EverBank Stadium over the next 23 months. They'll play just four of the next 30 regular-season games in Jacksonville, a stretch necessitated by the $1.4 billion renovation to their stadium  that is forcing the Jaguars to play 2027 home games in Orlando at Camping World Stadium, a two-hour drive south.

 As daunting as that odyssey might be, the Jaguars aren't grumbling about it. They've embraced it and turned it into a slogan: Anywhere, anytime, anybody.

 "We're not going to use it as an excuse," Jacksonville coach Liam Coen said. "It is what it is, and our mindset and mentality is going to be: Drop us off on a plane anywhere and we'll go play you."

 

 By the time the 2026 regular season ends, the Jaguars will become the first NFL team since the Duluth Eskimos in 1926 to play in 12 or more stadiums in a single season. The Eskimos from Minnesota had just one home game that campaign and played in 14 stadiums. The Jaguars will play in 12 stadiums in 2026 -- not including any potential away playoff games -- with seven of their final 10 contests on the road.

 The Jaguars beat the New England Patriots 35-6 at home on Sept. 27, and the next time they'll play there will be Nov. 1 against the Indianapolis Colts . That 34-day break is allowing for -- weather permitting -- uninterrupted work on EverBank Stadium. The Jaguars and the city of Jacksonville are splitting the cost of the renovation (team owner Shad Khan is responsible for all cost overruns), and work began following the team's playoff loss to the Buffalo Bills in January.

 International games are a significant part of the Jaguars' pilgrimage -- starting this week. They leave Thursday for London (approximately a nine-hour flight) to play back-to-back designated home games against the Philadelphia Eagles  at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday ( 9:30 a.m. ET, NFL Network ) and the Houston Texans  on Oct. 18 at Wembley Stadium ( 9:30 a.m. ET, NFL Network ). Those will be the 15th and 16th games the franchise has played in London dating back to the 2013 season. No other NFL team has played more than eight international games (Bills).

 When the Jaguars face Philadelphia, Jacksonville punter Logan Cooke will play in his NFL-record 10th international game, breaking a tie with former Jags offensive lineman Tyler Shatley . It's a record that Cooke said really means one thing: He has been around a long time for a team that makes regular trips to play games out of the country.

 "I didn't use to enjoy the trip at all," said Cooke, a seventh-round draft pick in 2018 who is the longest-tenured Jacksonville player. "The first few years we would stay at just a place downtown in a hotel on the street and there wasn't a whole lot to do. Once you saw the town one time, that was it. But now, we get to stay [at a resort on the outskirts of London], get to play some golf every now and then. Every morning, we'll get a cup of coffee and go walk around, walk the course before practice and meetings. It feels 50s outside, you get a cup of coffee, there's pheasant running across the golf course and ducks flying, and it's just real peaceful."

 

 Three lockers down from Cooke sits wide receiver Jakobi Meyers . He has been in the NFL since 2019 but has not yet played an international game. Meyers said he's looking forward to his first trip to Europe, and he has spoken with teammates about their experiences staying 11 days in London and playing back-to-back games, something the Jaguars did in 2023 and 2024.

 However, he isn't worried about the length of the trip or the 26 games the Jaguars will play away from Jacksonville between now and the 2028 season. He has fully embraced anywhere, anytime and anybody.

 "Whether it's here, whether it's there, it really doesn't matter for real," Meyers said. "It's a chance to go play in another city or another country or whatever it is, but it's more so the football part that I'm looking forward to.

 "I just like to play ball, so it really doesn't matter where you put [the game] for real. Let's just go hoop and have a good time."

 The stadium agreement between the city of Jacksonville and the Jaguars includes a clause that allows them to play a maximum of three international games in 2027, though none is scheduled at this point.

 The Jaguars have had success away from Jacksonville in Coen's 21 games as head coach. They lost three of their first five road games (including last season's London matchup with the Los Angeles Rams ), but they have since won five of their past six. Five of the Jaguars' next six are away, including at the  Baltimore Ravens  and the New York Giants .

 Though coaches and players generally avoid talking about games other than the next one, Coen addressed the ambitious road schedule with the team during training camp. He wanted to make sure the players understood the focus is still on winning.

 

 "I think just being honest, like, 'Hey guys, if you're a part of this organization right now, this is the reality,'" Coen said. "This is our truth, this is our reality, and nobody in this league and in this fanbase is going to care at the end of the day. Like, nobody. It's not going to be an allowed excuse or an allowed reason, because the results are what they are at the end of the season.

 "Your record's your record, and nobody's going to look at it and say, 'Oh, well, they had to go play a lot of games away from home.' I mean, it is what it is."

 The travel is not ideal, Jags center Robert Hainsey said, but everyone will just have to deal with it. Will there be grumbling? Yes. Will that become an issue? He says no.

 "We're so process-oriented and we're such creatures of habit as NFL players that you just do the same thing," Hainsey said. "We know exactly what it's going to look like, so there's no surprises. It's not like, 'What's going to happen on this away game?' The schedule's the same every time. So, it's easy to just stick with your routine and you just go through it.

 "As far as next year goes, who knows? We'll deal with that when we get there, but I'm not too worried about that yet."

 There is one benefit, though: a lot more chances for Lewis to go bird-watching. "It's always fun," he said.

title: Jets searching for identity as losses become 'tough to stomach'
summary: After a Week 1 win, New York has fallen to 1-3 and has struggled to assert itself the way it wants.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- The New York Jets still haven't established their identity. Four games should be enough time to form a style -- a brand, if you will -- but they're still searching.

 And that's troubling, especially as they embark on a four-game stretch (including three at home) that could define their season and the future of coach Aaron Glenn.

 The Jets have said they want to be a physical team that controls the trenches, punishing opponents with their running game and disrupting quarterbacks with a combination of ferocious rush and sticky coverage.

 Oh, they've had moments, maybe nine quarters of efficient football, but encouraging stints often don't equate to wins. And they haven't for the Jets (1-3), who have dropped three straight after a dominating victory over the winless Tennessee Titans in Week 1.

 

 "To me, your identity is, 'What does the other team say about you?'" Glenn said in training camp.

 Let's examine that thought. After pounding the Jets on Sunday, Chicago Bears linebacker Devin Bush told reporters, "Probably one of the easiest NFL games I done played in, and I'm not sore at all."

 Glenn dismissed the comments, saying Bush probably was alluding to the lopsided time of possession and not directly criticizing the Jets. In fact, Bush did mention the staggering possession disparity -- 42:45 to 17:15. But even if he wasn't trying to throw shade at the Jets, it was perceived that way after the video clip went viral. When a player refers to an "easy" win, regardless of context, it's bound to raise eyebrows.

 Such is life for the Jets.

 "Three straight losses is tough to stomach," center Josh Myers said.

 They have lost 17 of 21 games under Glenn, who is trying to eradicate the losing mentality that has enveloped the franchise for years. The fanbase has turned on Glenn, once a popular player for the Jets, and he needs to come up with answers -- quickly.

 After going 0-3 against the NFC North, the Jets have reached the so-called "soft" part of their schedule -- but it's not nearly as soft as it appeared to be in August. They host the Cleveland Browns (3-1) on Sunday, followed by a road game against the New England Patriots (2-2), followed by home dates with the Miami Dolphins (0-4) and Las Vegas Raiders (3-1). The Raiders and Browns, both led by first-year coaches, are among the year's biggest surprises. Still, these are games the Jets can't afford to squander.

 "We've got the biggest part of our season starting now," wide receiver Garrett Wilson said after the 23-12 loss in Chicago.

 Glenn's challenge is to define the team's identity, something it can hang its hat on. He can start with the defense, his pride and joy.

 

 After a promising start -- No. 1 in yards allowed after two weeks -- the defense has regressed over the last six quarters. It has allowed 44 points and 727 total yards over that span, in large part because of a pass rush that has disappeared. The Bears' Tyson Bagent , who started for the injured Caleb Williams , was barely touched.

 The front four, which includes No. 2 pick David Bailey , has registered zero sacks and only four quarterback hits over the last two full games. Glenn acknowledged the issue, saying they must "improve" their rush plan.

 "That's something that I have to do a better job at," Glenn said, "making sure that I get our guys to understand that."

 The Jets invested heavily in their front, drafting Bailey, trading for nose tackle  T'Vondre Sweat  and signing Joseph Ossai to a three-year, $34.5 million contract. They haven't received much bang for the buck.

 Glenn, who took over playcalling this season, has the seventh-highest blitz rate (38%) -- but they're still not affecting the quarterback. The first interception of the Glenn era came Sunday, when safety Minkah Fitzpatrick ended the longest drought in NFL history -- 20 games.

 The Jets had gone 643 pass attempts without a pick. Mathematically, the odds of a defense going exactly 643 attempts without an interception are 1 in 1.63 million, assuming a standard league-average interception rate of 2.28%.

 That's a damning trend for any coach, let alone a defensive-minded head coach whose philosophy is predicated on ball disruption.

 Offensively, can the Jets rediscover the ground game? It looked so good in the opener, with Breece Hall rushing for 102 of the 152 yards, but they've managed 67, 58 and 59 yards in the three games since. They certainly miss Hall (quadriceps), who sat out Sunday, but the offensive line -- supposedly one of the team's strengths -- is underperforming.

 

 When the ground game sputters, it ripples through the entire team, forcing adjustments.

 "Obviously, we're all frustrated and disappointed," said Myers, who insisted, "We're going to win games."

 Meanwhile, the pressure is mounting on Glenn, whose record after 21 games is the second worst in franchise history. Only Rich Kotite (3-18), who coached in 1995 and 1996, won fewer games in his first 21. Glenn knows the history; he played on those Kotite teams.

 Glenn is convinced that he has the right winning formula, and that the team is making progress even though it's not apparent in the standings. Ultimately, he will be judged by owner Woody Johnson.

 "There are some positives that came out of this [last loss]," Glenn insisted. "Sometimes everybody just focuses on the negative part of it, but our deal is we're going to make sure we try to continue to improve on that and hopefully, from the outside, our fans will see that."

title: Eagles offensive state of affairs in limbo
summary: The offensive line has long been the lifeblood of this franchise.
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA -- The Philadelphia Eagles  started the week with an identity issue on offense and a host of injuries to key players and in some ways, that feels like simpler times.

 Since then, All-Pro right tackle Lane Johnson abruptly retired , ending a 13-plus year run in which he anchored two Super Bowl championship teams, helped pave the way for Saquon Barkley 's historic 2024 campaign and became one of the best offensive linemen of his generation.

 A day after Johnson announced he was stepping away, general manager Howie Roseman traded interior lineman Cam Jurgens along with a 2027 seventh-round pick to the Baltimore Ravens for a 2027 fifth-round pick and a 2028 second-round selection.

 And just like that, two offensive line starters were removed from a group that was already struggling and dealing with the absence of left guard Landon Dickerson  who is on injured reserve with a knee injury.

 Add in injuries to Barkley (hamstring) and DeVonta Smith (hamstring) and you have an offense that heads into Sunday's London game against the Jacksonville Jaguars a shell of itself (9:30 a.m. EST, NFL Network).

 In terms of the particulars, it will be rookie Markel Bell at right tackle for Johnson. Willie Lampkin is expected to move into the starting lineup for Jurgens, who last played left guard. They'll account for two-fifths of a makeshift O-line that also includes left tackle Jordan Mailata , right guard Tyler Steen and center Drew Kendall .

 

 There is sound logic behind the Jurgens trade. The Eagles received really good value for a player that was not performing at a high level and hasn't regained his form since dealing with a back injury which required surgery during the 2024 season. They free up money and have built up a nice cache of picks for the talent-heavy 2027 and 2028 drafts.

 The Eagles' front office has been very good at keeping their organization competitive over long periods of time, and have earned the benefit of the doubt that they'll find a way to reload on the fly.

 But there is still the issue of the 2026 season. Just four games deep, it's becoming harder and harder to paint scenarios in which they stay above water, let alone reach the lofty expectations heading into the year.

 The offensive line has long been the lifeblood of this franchise. It has been at the core of their extended run of success that dates back to the early 2000s at the dawn of the Andy Reid era. In the rare seasons that have gone poorly during that stretch, it usually comes back to issues in the trenches, brought on by injury or otherwise.

 This season in particular was about installing a new offensive system and figuring out how primary players, most notably quarterback Jalen Hurts , fit in it. But that was under the premise the offensive line -- typically one of the best in football in recent years -- would continue to be a strength. 

 It becomes much harder to judge Hurts' performance or offensive coordinator Sean Mannion 's play-calling abilities if the front can't hold up.

 The discussion coming off Sunday's loss to the  Los Angeles Rams  centered around Hurts and coach Nick Sirianni's acknowledgment that the offense still hadn't found its identity. Should they lean more into the under-center, heavy play action style of play that Mannion brought with him from Green Bay, or lean on the elements that Hurts & Co. have majored in over previous seasons?

 It all becomes moot if defenders are constantly in the backfield.

 Maybe that won't happen. Maybe Bell, Kendall and Lampkin will prove to be quick studies. Maybe Dickerson will soon return from injured reserve (he recently said he's feeling much better health-wise) and help stabilize things. Maybe the Eagles can undergo a changing of the guard along the front while remaining competitive.

 There is also a world in which players, already stinging from the loss of Johnson and adjusting to life without revered offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, question why management would remove another starter in Jurgens from a room needing all the help it can get. The learning curve could be steep for the newcomers, leaving little hope that an already reeling offense continues to spiral.

 This is not the position the Eagles normally find themselves in. Then again, the offensive line outlook hasn't been this shaky in quite some time.

title: Fantasy football buzz: Six trades you should consider making today

full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values in fantasy football.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

 

 Oct. 7: Trade for or trade away? SOS says make these six moves today 

 By Tristan H. Cockcroft 

 We're at that time of season where the fantasy football trade market is either heating up or is already at peak temperature.

 There's inevitably a 0-4 team in your league, grasping to hopes of a miracle comeback. And it can be done, especially if I remind you that all you probably need is a 7-3 hot streak to make the playoffs as an I-sure-don't-want-to-face-them No. 4 seed. Trades -- especially bigger, badder and bolder ones -- are the best way to turn around a slow start.

 One way to unearth the highest-ceiling trades is to lean heavily upon the upcoming schedule. Mix and match your way into the playoffs and be that maddening team to face! This week, Mike Clay has released his initial version of the rest-of-season schedule rankings at each position -- kickers and defenses, too!

 It's a great tool for determining how fluky your player's extreme hot-or-cold start to the season might have been, as well as which players are in the best positions to thrive over the remaining 13 weeks of the fantasy season.

 Here are six trade-related takeaways to consider as you start offering deals:

 
 Bryce Young has been an unexpected early breakthrough , going from a No. 186 overall ADP and 11.1% opening-week roster rate to scoring the third-most fantasy points among quarterbacks through four weeks. He has certainly capitalized upon a soft schedule, the seventh-best at the position thus far. Young and his Carolina Panthers are on bye, but they have the position's third toughest the rest of the year. Young might be a tough player to trade based upon his past history, but considering his schedule and how bruised and battered the quarterback position on the whole, he's a name worth floating if you're confident in your QB1. 
 He might seem like an unappealing fantasy RB2 , but Aaron Jones Sr . could be one of the sneakiest running back values amongst that valuation tier, particularly over the next six weeks. Since Jordan Mason landed on IR , Jones' 78% snap and 73% rushing shares both rank fourth, and his 41.5 fantasy points are 14th, among running backs. Jones and the Minnesota Vikings also face the third most-favorable remaining schedule at the position, including nothing but upper-half matchups (aside from a Week 6 bye) the next seven weeks (@NO, bye, IND, @DET, BUF, @GB, @SF). 
 Colston Loveland 's fantasy managers are surely displeased after the No. 37 overall pick in terms of ADP has placed just 19th in target share (14.9%) and 31st in fantasy points (20.1) among tight ends through four weeks. His  Chicago Bears ' remaining schedule offers some hope of recovering TE1 value, as theirs has been the third toughest at the position thus far but the third most- favorable the rest of the year. Examining alternatives, I can't find more than five tight ends ( Trey McBride , Brock Bowers , George Kittle , Tyler Warren and Sam LaPorta ) I'd clearly prefer to Loveland the rest of the year. 
 It's difficult to envision Christian McCaffrey having as strong a finish as he had in 2025. The San Francisco 49ers have been more conservative with his workload through four weeks in 2026 (67% snap and 43% rushing shares) than at the same point in 2025 (83% and 65%), and he faces the most challenging remaining schedule among running backs. This isn't to persuade McCaffrey's managers to swiftly trade him for whatever they can get, but rather to caution that he might fall shy of expectations. Adjust your running back plan accordingly. 
 The hype surrounding Trevor Lawrence exiting Week 1 has dissipated , but there's still a lot to like about him and his receivers moving forward. Remember, Lawrence scored the second-most fantasy points among all players (and the most among quarterbacks) from Week 5 forward last year, and two of his toughest matchups all year are already in the rearview (Week 2-3's @DEN, NE). Between him and 2-fantasy-points-in-Week 4 WR Parker Washington , they're among my favorite trade targets right now. 
 The Seahawks' defense has again excelled early , their 40 fantasy points second among D/STs. What lies ahead, though, is the worst schedule for a defense, including two games apiece against the Los Angeles Rams and 49ers, and single meetings with the Kansas City Chiefs , Chicago Bears and Dallas Cowboys . Here's your almost daily reminder: Stream defenses! 
 

 

 Oct. 6: Jalen Hurts' job gets a lot tougher with Lane Johnson retirement 
 

 By Michael F. Florio 

 Lane Johnson announced his retirement from the NFL on Tuesday. That will leave a massive hole on the offensive line for an Eagles team that is missing a ton of star players. Saquon Barkley hurt a hamstring, and he is expected to miss Week 5. DeVonta Smith was out last week due to a hamstring injury, and he seems unlikely for Week 5. And Dallas Goedert remains sidelined with a knee injury.

 

 Jalen Hurts  has struggled in games without Johnson, having averaged 174 passing yards and 1.1 passing touchdowns per game when Johnson sat. On top of that, the quarterback faces a Jacksonville Jaguars team that has allowed three passing touchdowns and has six interceptions this season. Jacksonville can get after the QB, as well, producing 10 sacks through four weeks, eighth most in the NFL. That's problematic without Johnson.

 Perhaps Hurts' rushing ability saves the day, but he has not ran as much this season. He has fewer than 20 rushing yards in two of his past three games and one rushing touchdown this campaign. Plus, the Jaguars have allowed the second-fewest rushing yards and just two rushing touchdowns so far in 2026.

 Some QBs I would play over Hurts are Matthew Stafford , Jacoby Brissett , Kyler Murray and Jordan Love . The "floors" here are not safe, but Jameis Winston and Aaron Rodgers are upside options this week in favorable matchups.

 Falcons' offense has come alive under Michael Penix Jr. 
 

 By Michael F. Florio 

 The Atlanta Falcons are hitting their stride with Michael Penix Jr . They scored 45 points Monday night against the New Orleans Saints and have 80 total in Penix's two starts. Penix threw for 223 yards and one touchdown, finishing with 12.72 fantasy points. He has yet to crack 15 and is primarily a superflex option, although all the QB injuries could change that.

 

 Penix's impact on the Falcons offense cannot be overstated. Bijan Robinson went for 147 total yards and two touchdowns Monday, and in 16 career games with Penix at the helm he has 2,181 scrimmage yards and 17 touchdowns. Robinson saves his best for primetime, which means fantasy managers are in luck, as the Falcons play the Baltimore Ravens on "Sunday Night Football" next week.

 Penix also continues to elevate Drake London . After going for 194 yards in Week 3, London was held to a modest 96 yards on five catches Monday. He has 105 catches, 1,576 yards and nine touchdowns in 16 career games with Penix. He has to be viewed as an elite fantasy option as long as Penix is healthy.

 And Brian Robinson Jr . had himself a night, turning 15 opportunities into 67 yards and three touchdowns. He has double-digit touches in each of his past three games and has four total touchdowns in the past two games. Robinson should be added off the waiver wire if he is out there. Not only is he one of the top insurance backs, but he is carving out a role with standalone value. He can be a flex option with byes coming up and due to all the injuries.

title: Is it time to panic about 49ers' injuries? Breaking down IR, trade deadline plan
summary: The 49ers are again among the most injured teams in the NFL. We answered questions about their injuries and how they will affect the 2026 season.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- In what has become a part of their in-season reality, the San Francisco 49ers are once again on pace to be among the most injured NFL teams in 2026.

 Four weeks into the season, the Niners have the most games missed by players because of injury (75),  according to CBS Sports . They have the ninth-most annual salary value on their injured reserve (IR), physically unable to perform list (PUP) and non-football injury/illness list,  according to OverTheCap.com . That doesn't even account for stars such as defensive end Nick Bosa and fullback Kyle Juszczyk , who are injured but not on a reserve list.

 And though it's a distinction they'd prefer not to have, the Niners have again showed they are well equipped to handle a lengthy injury list. They're 4-0 with 16 players on IR and two more on PUP.

 "Of course, you never want your guys going down," linebacker Fred Warner said. "You want your best players out there. But this is the NFL, it's football, it's a violent game, things are going to happen."

 Plenty of injuries happened even before the opener against the Los Angeles Rams . In August, receiver  Ricky Pearsall had season-ending surgery on a right knee injury from the 2025 season. Then, in early September practices, defensive tackle  Alfred Collins ( torn patellar tendon ) and end  Sam Okuayinonu (foot) were injured. And in each of the ensuing weeks of the regular season, the 49ers have lost key players to in-game or practice injuries of varying severity.

 Here's a breakdown of the injuries by designation:

 
 Physically unable to perform list: DL Mykel Williams , RB Isaac Guerendo 
 Designated to return from IR: WR Christian Kirk , OL Austen Pleasants 
 Players currently on IR: DT Alfred Collins , DL Andrew Farmer II , S Darrick Forrest , DB Nate Hobbs , DL Mikail Kamara , LB Nick Martin , DE Sam Okuayinonu , WR Ricky Pearsall , WR Demarcus Robinson , WR De'Zhaun Stribling , TE Jake Tonges , OL Brett Toth , DT C.J. West , OL Nick Zakelj 
 Injured but not on a reserve list: DE Nick Bosa , FB Kyle Juszczyk , S Marques Sigle , CB Upton Stout , DT James Thompson Jr . 
 
 As San Francisco prepares for Sunday's NFC West showdown with the Seattle Seahawks  (3-1), let's answer a few pressing questions about the team's injured players.

 

 On a scale of 1-10 how panicked should the 49ers be about their injuries? 
 7 . It's high, but the good news? With the notable exceptions of Collins, Pearsall and tight end Jake Tonges  ( torn right MCL in Week 1 ), the rest of the 22 injured players should return at some point in 2026.

 San Francisco expects some players, such as Bosa ( calf injury in Sept. 24 practice ) or Juszczyk ( sprained right knee on Sunday ), to return in October. Others, such as wideout De'Zhaun Stribling  ( ankle surgery after Week 1 injury ) and defensive tackle C.J. West  ( right knee surgery in September ), might not be back until late November or early December if their recoveries go as planned.

 

 Injuries have hit the 49ers especially hard at receiver and on the defensive line. In the latter group, the only players available to play from the initial 53-man roster are DT  Osa Odighizuwa , DT  Gracen Halton , DE  Romello Height and DE  Keion White . In their stead, the Niners have gotten contributions from former practice squad players such as DT  Sebastian Valdez and street free agents such as DE  Khalid Kareem .

 "This is the first time that being in a situation where there's only four guys left out of the 10 guys you started with two weeks prior to that," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "To have that many new guys, practice squad guys, all those guys getting out there and stepping it up ... I've been real happy with them."

 There's a scenario in which those practice squad players hold their positions throughout October. Then, the return of injured players could set up the 49ers well for the stretch run.

 But that assumes there won't be more injuries in the meantime. With this team, that would be a bold assumption.

 
 Are the Niners really 'out' of injured reserve return designations? 
 In theory, yes. In practicality, not really. 

 Each team can designate eight players to return from IR during the regular season. Teams can designate up to two of those players when rosters trim to the initial 53 players at the end of the preseason. From there, every team can wait and see before opening a 21-day practice window for an injured player. Once a player is designated to return, they can play only after they've missed at least four games.

 Because the 49ers designated OL Austen Pleasants and WR Christian Kirk  to return on cutdown day, they technically have six IR spots remaining. They are hopeful Kirk will return to practice as soon as next week.

 There are undoubtedly at least six more players on IR they'd like to bring back. That doesn't mean all of them will return, however.

 From the list, Robinson, Stribling and West are the best bets to return if and when they recover. Robinson suffered a high right ankle sprain in the 49ers' Week 2 win over the Dolphins .

 The rest of the list largely comprises solid depth players who are more likely to return if more injuries happen at their positions.

 Yes, it behooves the Niners to refrain from placing more players they want to have available on IR. But it's not quite as dire of a situation as it might appear given the overall lack of long-term injuries to starters.

 

 
 What about the players on the physically unable to perform list? 
 Players on the PUP list have injuries suffered prior to training camp and also have to miss at least four games before they can return to playing in games. One difference: They are allowed to begin practicing as soon as Week 3, according to a new NFL rule this season.

 Williams, who tore an ACL last November , has a chance to be the first 49er to return from PUP on Sunday. The team opened his practice window last week and, if this week of practice goes well, he could be active against the Seahawks. That would be a big boost for the depleted defensive line.

 Guerendo (pectoral injury in April) is also on the PUP list, but he's likely more of an option to come back if there's an injury to any of the three running backs -- Christian McCaffrey , Kaelon Black and Jordan James  -- on the depth chart.

 

 How might these injuries affect the Niners' trade deadline plans? 
 The 49ers will get some key players back from injury before or around the Nov. 10 trade deadline , but that's unlikely to stop them from being aggressive in their pursuit of adding help. That's especially true on the defensive line and, to a lesser degree, wide receiver.

 San Francisco would be smart to invest in insurance policies for Bosa, West, Thompson and Okuayinonu in case their recoveries don't go as planned. A run-stuffing defensive tackle and another edge rusher capable of getting after the quarterback have to be among the top priorities for the Niners as the season goes on. Currently, they're 22nd in defensive rushing success rate and 26th in sacks per dropback.

 It's a safe bet that even with players coming back from injury, the Niners will look to add more options. As recent history has proved, the 49ers will need all the healthy and capable players they can get.
